fullOrganEntries.question: Define hepatocellular carcinoma.
fullOrganEntries.answer: Source definition: Most common primary malignant liver tumor, usually arising in cirrhotic liver. Refined definition based on medical consensus: Primary malignant epithelial tumor showing hepatocellular differentiation, usually developing in the setting of chronic liver injury/cirrhosis. Boundary condition: It is a primary hepatocellular malignancy, not metastatic liver disease and not cholangiocarcinoma. Synonyms: Hepatoma; primary liver cancer.

fullOrganEntries.question: Why does cirrhosis create the substrate for hepatocellular carcinoma?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Normal liver parenchyma is organized as hepatocyte plates/trabeculae with sinusoidal perfusion and portal tracts distributed through the native hepatic architecture. In chronic liver injury, repeated hepatocyte injury and regeneration occur within increasingly fibrotic parenchyma, and the article/Core support progression through regenerative nodules and dysplastic nodules toward HCC. As fibrosis partitions liver into nodules and the normal architecture becomes distorted, some nodules acquire atypia and progress to early then overt HCC. This cirrhotic nodular substrate explains why HCC often arises in a background of chronic liver injury and why precursor nodules and early malignancy can overlap on imaging before the lesion develops its full malignant vascular behavior. External literature source (not stated in Core/RadPrimer/STATdx/Radiopaedia). Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10093043/ Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4918274/

fullOrganEntries.question: Why is portal vein tumor thrombus such a strong clue to hepatocellular carcinoma?
fullOrganEntries.answer: HCC develops within hepatic parenchyma and has a strong tendency toward local venous invasion, especially into the portal venous system. Once tumor extends into the portal vein lumen, the intravascular material contains viable neoplastic tissue rather than bland clot alone, so the vein may expand and the thrombus may enhance because the tumor continues to receive arterial blood supply. That is why enhancing expansile tumor-in-vein is a major clue favoring HCC and is much less typical of most hypervascular metastases. External literature source (not stated in Core/RadPrimer/STATdx/Radiopaedia). Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3666429/

fullOrganEntries.question: Why can hepatocellular carcinoma contain fat and show signal dropout or fatty hypodensity on imaging?
fullOrganEntries.answer: The provided pathology states that HCC may contain increased fat and glycogen in the cytoplasm. When enough lipid is present, microscopic fat can produce signal dropout on opposed-phase MRI, while more extensive fat can make parts of the lesion hypodense on CT or echogenic on ultrasound. This matters diagnostically because fat within a hepatic mass, especially in cirrhotic liver and combined with classic HCC enhancement behavior, supports hepatocellular origin rather than many common mimics.

fullOrganEntries.question: Why can hepatocellular carcinoma develop a capsule, mosaic architecture, necrosis, and hemorrhage?
fullOrganEntries.answer: As HCC enlarges, it becomes structurally heterogeneous because different parts of the tumor show variable differentiation, fibrosis, fat, necrosis, and hemorrhage. The resulting internal compartmental heterogeneity produces the mosaic appearance seen in larger HCC. Marginal fibrotic reaction and/or compressed surrounding tissue can contribute to a capsule or pseudocapsule appearance, while rapidly growing abnormal tumor tissue is prone to necrosis and hemorrhage. These gross growth effects explain why larger HCC is often heterogeneous rather than uniformly solid and why mosaic pattern, necrosis, hemorrhage, and capsule support the diagnosis. External literature source (not stated in Core/RadPrimer/STATdx/Radiopaedia). Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3666429/ Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4918274/

fullOrganEntries.question: Why does infiltrative hepatocellular carcinoma appear ill-defined and often involve portal vein thrombus rather than a single clean spherical mass?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Not all HCC grows as a discrete expansile nodule. In the infiltrative form, malignant hepatocellular tissue spreads in a permeative, poorly marginated pattern through a broad territory of hepatic parenchyma rather than producing one sharply circumscribed mass. Because this growth pattern extends along and through native hepatic vascular structures, portal vein invasion/tumor thrombus is common, and the imaging result is diffuse or segment-spanning heterogeneous signal/attenuation with architectural distortion instead of one neat round lesion. This explains why infiltrative HCC can mimic other diffuse hepatic processes but portal vein tumor thrombus remains a key clue favoring HCC. External literature source (not stated in Core/RadPrimer/STATdx/Radiopaedia). Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3666429/

fullOrganEntries.question: What major pitfall can occur when evaluating multiple hypervascular liver lesions, and what imaging check helps avoid it?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Trap: Mistaking multifocal HCC for hypervascular metastases. Safety check: Look specifically for portal vein tumor thrombus and for the classic arterial hyperenhancement with washout pattern on multiphasic imaging. Key discriminator: Enhancing expansile tumor-in-vein strongly favors HCC; metastases may be multifocal and hypervascular but rarely invade the portal vein. Why the error happens: Both entities can present as multiple arterialized hepatic lesions, especially on arterial-phase imaging alone.

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the key pitfall when evaluating a cirrhotic liver nodule, and what imaging maneuver prevents the mistake?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Trap: Calling a cirrhotic nodule regenerative/dysplastic and missing HCC, or calling every nodule HCC without checking the full major-feature pattern. Safety check: Use multiphasic CT or MR and assess for the major HCC features together: arterial phase hyperenhancement, washout, capsule/pseudocapsule, and other supporting malignant behavior rather than relying on one feature in isolation. Key discriminator: Regenerative and dysplastic nodules often overlap with early HCC, but they usually lack the full classic arterialization-washout-capsule pattern. Why the error happens: Cirrhotic livers are nodular and heterogeneous, so both overcalling and undercalling are easy if evaluation is based on a single phase or a single sign.

fullOrganEntries.question: Where do Most HCC arises?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Most HCC arises in cirrhosis/chronic liver injury; the article states cirrhosis is present in 60–90% of cases. Exam pivot: In a cirrhotic liver, a new suspicious mass should be treated with a high prior probability for HCC and evaluated with proper multiphasic technique.

fullOrganEntries.question: Relationship between HCC and Hepatitis C
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hepatitis C accounts for ~ 1/3 of HCC cases in the USA. Exam pivot: Chronic HCV history meaningfully raises pretest probability for HCC, especially once cirrhosis has developed.

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the most common malignant primary liver tumor?
fullOrganEntries.answer: HCC is the most common primary malignant liver tumor and accounts for 80–90% of all primary liver malignancies. Exam pivot: When asked for the dominant primary malignant hepatic tumor, HCC is the default unless imaging strongly supports another entity.

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the special relationship between hepatitis B and cirrhosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hepatitis B can lead to HCC, and onset may precede development of cirrhosis. Exam pivot: Do not exclude HCC solely because overt cirrhosis is absent in a patient with chronic HBV.

fullOrganEntries.question: MRI appearance pivot for hepatocellular carcinoma: what is the key MRI signal/enhancement pattern (as stated in source)?
fullOrganEntries.answer: T1WI: HCC may be hypo-, iso-, or hyperintense to liver; fat or hemorrhage may make it hyperintense. T2WI: Usually hyperintense to liver. Post-gadolinium: Heterogeneous arterial hyperenhancement with washout on portal venous/delayed phases. Exam pivot: The classic MRI pattern is an arterially hyperenhancing lesion that becomes relatively dark later, often with mild T2 hyperintensity.

fullOrganEntries.question: MRI appearance pivot for hepatocellular carcinoma: besides gadolinium, what other contrast agents can you use in order to further ascertain whether a mass is a HCC? What is a caveat?
fullOrganEntries.answer: On the 20-minute delayed hepatobiliary phase after gadoxetate, most HCCs are hypointense focal masses; rare well-differentiated HCC may show delayed persistent enhancement. Exam pivot: Hepatobiliary-phase hypointensity is a strong clue to HCC, especially for small lesions and in cirrhotic liver.

fullOrganEntries.question: MRI appearance pivot for hepatocellular carcinoma: what is the diffusion-weighted imaging clue?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Diffusion-weighted MR: restricted diffusion within HCC often appears as bright signal in the focal lesion. Exam pivot: Restricted diffusion adds sensitivity and specificity to MR detection and should raise suspicion for HCC in a cirrhotic liver mass.

fullOrganEntries.question: What threshold growth criterion is listed as a major LI-RADS feature for hepatocellular carcinoma?
fullOrganEntries.answer: ≥ 50% increase in size in ≤ 6 months. Exam pivot: Rapid interval growth is a major malignant feature and upgrades concern for HCC even when morphology alone is borderline.

fullOrganEntries.question: What are the Milan criteria for liver transplantation in hepatocellular carcinoma?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Solitary HCC ≤ 5 cm, or up to 3 HCC nodules each ≤ 3 cm, with no vascular invasion or extrahepatic tumor. Exam pivot: These are the key transplant-selection size/number thresholds to know for board-style HCC questions.

fullOrganEntries.question: Surveillance/curability pivot for hepatocellular carcinoma: what tumor-size goal is emphasized for curative detection?
fullOrganEntries.answer: The surveillance goal is to detect tumors < 3 cm and limited to the liver, because small tumors without vascular invasion are potentially curable with resection, ablation, or transplantation. Exam pivot: The whole surveillance strategy is built around finding small, liver-limited HCC before vascular invasion develops.

fullOrganEntries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Cirrhosis with portal-hypertension changes and dysplastic nodule Keyword findings: widening of the fissures right lobe atrophy large varices innumerable small splenic lesions relative hypertrophy of the lateral segment of the left lobe with lenticular shape dysplastic nodule is hypointense The paired MR images show classic morphologic remodeling of cirrhosis with fissural widening, right-lobe atrophy, varices, and left-lateral-segment hypertrophy. The additional nodule is caption-labeled dysplastic, fitting the premalignant nodular spectrum seen in cirrhotic liver rather than uncomplicated diffuse cirrhosis alone. Differential: Budd-Chiari syndrome Nodular regenerative hyperplasia Cirrhosis with hepatocellular carcinoma

fullOrganEntries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Cirrhosis with portal hypertension Keyword findings: cirrhotic liver large varices enlarged caudate lobe caudate lobe as wide as the right lobe This CT shows classic cirrhotic morphology with marked caudate enlargement plus large varices indicating portal hypertension. Caudate hypertrophy relative to the right lobe is a strong structural clue to cirrhosis rather than isolated portal venous abnormality. Differential: Budd-Chiari syndrome Primary portal vein thrombosis Nodular regenerative hyperplasia

fullOrganEntries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Cirrhosis Keyword findings: nodular contours of the liver coarse echotexture On grayscale ultrasound, a nodular hepatic surface together with coarse parenchymal echotexture is a classic diffuse morphologic pattern of cirrhosis. This favors chronic architectural distortion from fibrosis and nodularity rather than a focal or purely vascular process. Differential: Advanced hepatic fibrosis Nodular regenerative hyperplasia Pseudocirrhosis

fullOrganEntries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Cirrhosis Keyword findings: hypertrophy of the lateral segment of the left lobe lenticular shape atrophy of the medial segment This T2-weighted MR demonstrates the classic lobar remodeling pattern of cirrhosis, with hypertrophy of the left lateral segment and atrophy of the medial segment. That characteristic volume redistribution supports cirrhosis rather than a focal hepatic mass process. Differential: Budd-Chiari syndrome Nodular regenerative hyperplasia Pseudocirrhosis

fullOrganEntries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Cirrhosis with portal hypertension Keyword findings: extensive ascites gastroesophageal varices Extensive ascites together with gastroesophageal varices is a classic complication pattern of portal hypertension. In this topic build, that combination most strongly supports decompensated cirrhosis rather than an isolated ascitic process. Differential: Portal hypertension from portal vein thrombosis Budd-Chiari syndrome Cardiac hepatopathy with ascites

fullOrganEntries.answer: Budd-Chiari syndrome Primary portal vein thrombosis Nodular regenerative hyperplasia

fullOrganEntries.question: Define cirrhosis.
fullOrganEntries.answer: 1) Source definition: Chronic liver disease characterized by diffuse parenchymal injury, extensive fibrosis, and conversion of liver architecture into structurally abnormal nodules. 2) Refined definition based on medical consensus: A chronic end-stage pattern of hepatic injury in which repeated hepatocyte injury and repair produce diffuse fibrosis with regenerative nodular architectural distortion of the liver. 3) Boundary condition: It is diffuse fibrotic and nodular architectural remodeling of the liver; it is not merely steatosis, hepatitis, or nodularity without fibrosis. 4) Synonyms: End-stage chronic liver disease; hepatic cirrhosis

fullOrganEntries.question: Why does cirrhosis produce a nodular, dysmorphic liver with segmental atrophy and hypertrophy?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Cirrhosis develops through the combined effects of hepatocyte loss, fibrosis, and regeneration. Repeated injury causes diffuse parenchymal damage, while extracellular matrix and fibrous tissue are deposited through the liver, separating surviving hepatocytes into islands and regenerative nodules. Those nodules are often encircled by fibrous bands, and the distorted parenchyma remodels unevenly rather than shrinking uniformly. As fibrosis and nodular regeneration progress, some regions undergo volume loss while others enlarge relatively, producing the characteristic pattern of right-lobe and medial left-lobe atrophy with relative caudate and left lateral segment hypertrophy. The gross result is a small hard nodular liver in advanced disease, with widened fissures, expanded gallbladder fossa, and a nodular contour. Imaging shows these dysmorphic volume shifts because chronic fibrotic remodeling and regenerative nodularity reorganize the liver’s architecture instead of preserving normal lobar proportions.

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the pitfall when a tiny arterial-phase hyperenhancing focus is seen in a cirrhotic liver, and what is the safety check that prevents overcalling it?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Trap: Mistaking a small arterioportal shunt for hepatocellular carcinoma. Safety check / maneuver: Check whether the focus is a small peripheral wedge-shaped arterial-phase-only abnormality and assess for lack of true mass behavior on follow-up multiphasic CT or MR. Key discriminator: The article states that AP shunts are usually peripheral, wedge-shaped, small, and seen only on arterial phase, whereas HCC is a true nodule or mass with characteristic tumor behavior rather than a transient perfusion phenomenon. Why the error happens: Cirrhotic vascular derangement creates focal arterialized perfusion abnormalities that can look hypervascular like tumor on arterial-phase imaging.

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the current most common cause of cirrhosis in the USA according to the source?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hepatitis C (~25%). Exam pivot: Do not default to alcohol as the leading cause; source specifically states alcohol is no longer the most common cause in the USA and Europe.

fullOrganEntries.question: What percentage of cirrhosis cases in the USA are attributed to alcoholic liver disease according to the source?
fullOrganEntries.answer: ~20%. Exam pivot: Alcohol is a major cause, but not the most common cause in this source, which helps rank etiologies correctly.

fullOrganEntries.question: What percentage of cirrhosis cases in the USA are classified as cryptogenic according to the source?
fullOrganEntries.answer: ~20%. Exam pivot: A substantial fraction is labeled cryptogenic, and the source notes most of these are believed to be due to nonalcoholic steatohepatitis.

fullOrganEntries.question: What percentage of cirrhosis cases in the USA are due to combined hepatitis C and alcohol according to the source?
fullOrganEntries.answer: ~15%. Exam pivot: Mixed etiologic injury is board-relevant because cirrhosis causation is not always attributable to a single exposure or disease.

fullOrganEntries.question: What percentage of cirrhosis cases in the USA are due to hepatitis B (with or without hepatitis D) according to the source?
fullOrganEntries.answer: ~15%. Exam pivot: Viral etiologies remain a major share of cirrhosis, so hepatitis B must stay high in the etiologic differential even when hepatitis C leads the list.

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the sex distribution of cirrhosis according to the source?
fullOrganEntries.answer: M > F. Exam pivot: Male predominance slightly raises the prior probability, though it is not specific enough to diagnose the cause.

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the worldwide prevalence and mortality ranking of cirrhosis according to the source?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Affects 360/100,000 and is the 12th leading cause of mortality worldwide. Exam pivot: This is not a rare disease; its population burden is high enough that classic imaging patterns should be immediately recognizable.

fullOrganEntries.question: What caudate:right lobe ratio strongly suggests cirrhosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: > 0.65 strongly suggests cirrhosis.

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the normal width relationship of the caudate lobe to the right lobe?
fullOrganEntries.answer: The caudate lobe is normally no more than 60% of the width of the right lobe.

fullOrganEntries.question: MRI appearance pivot for siderotic regenerative nodules: what is the key MRI signal pattern?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Sequence: T1WI → hypointense to isointense Sequence: T2WI → low signal intensity becomes more conspicuous Sequence: T2 gradient-echo / FLASH → markedly hypointense (best sequence for detection) Exam pivot: Iron within siderotic nodules creates a low-signal pattern, especially on GRE-type sequences, helping separate them from many other cirrhotic nodules.

fullOrganEntries.question: MRI appearance pivot for dysplastic regenerative nodules: what is the key MRI signal/enhancement pattern?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Sequence: Usually > 1 cm Sequence: T1WI → hyperintense Sequence: T2WI → hypointense (low grade) Sequence: Vascularity → minimal Sequence: Delayed hepatobiliary phase → take up and retain hepatobiliary contrast agents Exam pivot: The T1-bright / T2-dark pattern with hepatobiliary contrast retention helps distinguish dysplastic nodules from HCC.

fullOrganEntries.question: MRI appearance pivot for hepatocellular carcinoma in a cirrhotic liver: what is the key MRI pattern stated in the source?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Sequence: T1WI → iso-, hypo-, or hyperintense Sequence: T2WI → hyperintense Sequence: Postcontrast T1 → arterial-phase hyperenhancement with washout to hypointense on venous and delayed phases, with rim enhancement Sequence: DWI → restricted diffusion (bright signal) Sequence: Hepatobiliary contrast → rarely take up or retain it Exam pivot: Arterialization plus washout, T2 hyperintensity, restricted diffusion, and lack of hepatobiliary retention favor HCC over dysplastic nodules.

fullOrganEntries.question: MRI appearance pivot for fibrosis in cirrhosis: what is the key MRI pattern stated in the source?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Sequence: Fat-saturated T2WI → fibrosis is hyperintense Sequence: Delayed contrast imaging → fibrosis may show persistent enhancement Exam pivot: Persistent delayed enhancement favors fibrosis over HCC, which typically shows washout on delayed imaging.

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the most specific test stated in the source to distinguish a dysplastic regenerative nodule from HCC?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Delayed-phase hepatobiliary contrast-agent behavior on MR: dysplastic nodules take up and retain hepatobiliary contrast agents, whereas HCC rarely does. Exam pivot: Hepatobiliary contrast retention is a key discriminator against HCC in a cirrhotic liver.

fullOrganEntries.question: At what fibrosis stages does the source state diagnostic accuracy increase for elastography-based assessment?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Diagnostic accuracy increases from significant fibrosis (stage 2) to advanced fibrosis (stage 3) and cirrhosis (stage 4). Exam pivot: Elastography performs better as fibrosis becomes more advanced, so test confidence rises with later-stage disease.

fullOrganEntries.question: What change in MR elastography stiffness suggests histologic fibrosis progression according to the source?
fullOrganEntries.answer: A 15% increase in stiffness suggests histologic fibrosis progression. Exam pivot: This gives a concrete progression threshold for longitudinal fibrosis assessment.

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the pathologic grading scale for fibrosis/cirrhosis in the METAVIR system?
fullOrganEntries.answer: F0: no fibrosis F1: portal fibrosis without septa F2: portal fibrosis with few septa F3: numerous septa without cirrhosis F4: cirrhosis

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the approximate sampling-error rate of liver biopsy stated in the source?
fullOrganEntries.answer: ~33.1%. Exam pivot: Even though biopsy is the pathologic reference standard, sampling error is substantial enough that imaging-based fibrosis assessment matters.

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the normal direction of portal venous flow, and what direction indicates severe portal hypertension?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hepatopetal flow is normal. Hepatofugal flow is a sign of severe portal hypertension. Exam pivot: Reversed portal flow is a hemodynamic severity marker, not just a descriptive Doppler curiosity.

The combination of multiplicity and hypovascular ring-enhancing lesions favors metastases over a benign multifocal process. The key board pivot is arterial-phase dependence for detection of hypervascular metastatic disease. fullOrganEntries.question: Define lymphoma.
fullOrganEntries.answer: Source definition: Neoplasm of lymphoid tissues. Boundary condition: This is a malignant lymphoid neoplasm, not merely reactive lymphoid proliferation or nonspecific hepatic masslike infiltration. Synonyms: lymphoid malignancy

fullOrganEntries.question: Why can hypervascular hepatic metastases be conspicuous on arterial-phase imaging but become difficult to recognize on portal venous images?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hypervascular metastases have relatively greater arterial perfusion than surrounding liver, so they enhance strongly during the arterial phase and stand out against background hepatic parenchyma. As contrast redistributes on later phases, the lesion may become nearly isodense or much less conspicuous relative to the enhancing liver, especially on portal venous imaging. This perfusion behavior explains why these lesions can be missed if arterial-phase imaging is omitted and why biphasic liver CT is critical for suspected hypervascular primaries.

fullOrganEntries.question: Why can a treated hepatic metastasis appear as a near-water-density cystic lesion and mimic a simple hepatic cyst?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Some metastatic lesions undergo treatment-related loss of viable soft tissue and develop marked internal low attenuation, producing a near-water-density appearance on follow-up imaging. Because the gross lesion may then resemble a simple cyst, the key interpretive problem is false benign classification. Residual malignant architecture such as mural nodularity, along with temporal comparison to prior studies showing an earlier solid metastasis, explains why the lesion remains metastatic despite its cystlike attenuation.

fullOrganEntries.question: Why can hepatic lymphoma encase hepatic vessels yet preserve vessel patency and cause little vascular distortion?
fullOrganEntries.answer: The article repeatedly describes lymphoma as a soft infiltrative process that can surround portal or hepatic vascular structures without causing the aggressive invasion, thrombosis, or distortion expected from many epithelial malignancies. Because the tumor tends to track as pliable infiltrative soft tissue rather than destroy or obstruct the vessel wall, vessels may remain patent and can even be seen penetrating the mass. This explains the classic imaging clue of vascular encasement with preservation of flow and contour.

fullOrganEntries.question: Why can diffuse hepatic metastatic infiltration mimic steatosis on CT?
fullOrganEntries.answer: When metastatic disease becomes diffuse rather than discretely mass-forming, the liver may appear enlarged and globally low in attenuation with only subtle focal abnormalities. That diffuse reduction in attenuation can visually resemble fatty infiltration on CT because the dominant pattern is hepatic low density rather than sharply marginated masses. The malignant nature becomes apparent only when other modalities reveal innumerable lesions or metabolic activity, explaining why diffuse metastatic infiltration can masquerade as steatosis on CT alone.

fullOrganEntries.clinicalContext: 52-year-old patient with abdominal pain and flushing M8T4Q1Z7L2XC [BT1]
fullOrganEntries.question: What is the imaging trap here, and what acquisition step prevents the mistake?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Trap: Missing a hypervascular hepatic metastasis because it is nearly isodense or difficult to recognize on portal venous images alone. Safety check / maneuver: Obtain biphasic liver CT with an arterial phase when a hypervascular primary is known or suspected. Key discriminator: Hypervascular metastases may be conspicuous on arterial phase but become much less visible on venous phase. Why the error occurs: The lesion’s conspicuity depends on arterial perfusion, so venous-phase-only imaging can undercall or miss it.

fullOrganEntries.clinicalContext: 60-year-old patient with abdominal discomfort and weight loss R5N2K8W4P1DV [BT1]
fullOrganEntries.question: What is the imaging trap here, and what specific check helps prevent the mistake?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Trap: Mistaking a cystic hepatic metastasis for a simple hepatic cyst. Safety check / maneuver: Look carefully for mural nodularity and compare with prior imaging to see whether the lesion was previously solid. Key discriminator: A simple cyst should not have malignant mural nodularity or documented evolution from a prior soft tissue metastasis. Why the error occurs: Treated metastases can become near-water-density and deceptively benign in appearance.

fullOrganEntries.clinicalContext: 59-year-old woman with liver dysfunction and abdominal pain C5L8N2V4T7QM [BT1]
fullOrganEntries.question: What is the imaging trap here, and what follow-up check helps prevent the mistake?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Trap: Miscalling diffuse hepatic metastatic infiltration as benign steatosis. Safety check / maneuver: Use complementary imaging such as contrast-enhanced CT, PET/CT, or ultrasound to look for innumerable focal lesions or FDG-avid abnormal liver. Key discriminator: True steatosis does not produce diffuse FDG-avid malignant replacement or innumerable hypoechoic metastatic nodules. Why the error occurs: Diffuse metastatic infiltration may lower liver attenuation globally and visually simulate fatty liver on CT.

fullOrganEntries.clinicalContext: 60-year-old woman with abdominal pain and flushing Q4M8T1L6V2PX [BT1]
fullOrganEntries.question: What is the imaging trap here, and what modality principle helps avoid the mistake?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Trap: Calling an echogenic hepatic metastasis a hemangioma on ultrasound. Safety check / maneuver: Confirm with CT or MR rather than relying on sonography alone for characterization of a solid hepatic mass. Key discriminator: The lesion may mimic a hemangioma on ultrasound but show the typical appearance of metastasis on cross-sectional imaging. Why the error occurs: Some hypervascular metastases are echogenic and overlap sonographically with benign vascular lesions.

fullOrganEntries.clinicalContext: 55-year-old patient with abdominal distention and pain K2V8P4M1Q7LX [BT1]
fullOrganEntries.question: What is the imaging trap here, and what check helps separate it from true cirrhosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Trap: Mistaking treatment-related pseudocirrhosis for primary chronic cirrhosis. Safety check / maneuver: Look for residual metastatic lesions and the source-supported history of lesion shrinkage with fibrosis producing contour distortion. Key discriminator: Pseudocirrhosis reflects post-treatment metastatic contraction and scarring rather than primary diffuse cirrhotic remodeling. Why the error occurs: Both processes can produce a nodular contour, fissural widening, and capsular retraction.

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the most common malignant tumor of the liver?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Liver metastases. Exam pivot: When evaluating malignant hepatic masses, metastatic disease should rank ahead of primary malignant liver tumors by default unless the imaging and clinical setting strongly support a primary hepatic malignancy.

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the ratio of liver metastases to primary malignant liver tumors in the source?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Approximately 18:1 in favor of liver metastases. Exam pivot: This materially shifts the default prior toward metastatic disease when multiple malignant liver lesions are encountered.

fullOrganEntries.question: What percentage of oncology patients have liver metastases at autopsy according to the source?
fullOrganEntries.answer: 55%. Exam pivot: This emphasizes how common hepatic metastatic involvement is in systemic malignancy and supports keeping metastases high in the differential for malignant liver lesions.

fullOrganEntries.question: What percentage of metastatic cancer cases in the liver are from colon cancer according to the source?
fullOrganEntries.answer: 50% of cases of metastatic cancer. Exam pivot: In a patient with hepatic metastases, colorectal primary should rank very high among candidate sources.

fullOrganEntries.question: In hepatic lymphoma, which is more common: primary or secondary hepatic involvement?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Secondary hepatic involvement is more common; primary hepatic lymphoma is rare. Exam pivot: A lymphomatous liver lesion should usually be interpreted in the context of systemic lymphoma rather than assumed to be primary hepatic lymphoma.

fullOrganEntries.question: In hepatic lymphoma, which is more common: non-Hodgkin lymphoma or Hodgkin disease?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is more common than Hodgkin disease. Exam pivot: When lymphoma involves the liver, NHL should be the default subtype prior unless the broader disease context suggests otherwise.

fullOrganEntries.question: MRI appearance pivot for hepatic metastases: what is the key MRI signal/enhancement pattern stated in the source?
fullOrganEntries.answer: T1WI: Usually hypointense. T2WI: Moderate to high signal. DWI: Restricted. T1WI C+: Hypovascular metastases often show low signal center with peripheral rim enhancement; hypervascular metastases show hyperintense arterial-phase enhancement. Exam pivot: Multiplicity plus typical T1-dark/T2-bright restricted lesions with appropriate enhancement behavior strongly supports metastases; melanoma is an important T1-bright exception.

fullOrganEntries.question: MRI appearance pivot for hepatic lymphoma: what is the key MRI signal/enhancement pattern stated in the source?
fullOrganEntries.answer: T1WI: Hypointense. T2WI: Diffusely hyperintense or hypointense with a peripheral rim of hyperintensity. DWI: Restricted. T1WI C+: Minimal enhancement; may be heterogeneous or target-like; no distortion of vasculature or biliary ducts. Exam pivot: Restricted hypoenhancing hepatic lesions that preserve vessels favor lymphoma over many primary epithelial hepatic malignancies.

fullOrganEntries.question: MRI appearance pivot for melanoma liver metastases: what is the key MRI signal pattern stated in the source?
fullOrganEntries.answer: T1WI: May be hyperintense due to melanin. Exam pivot: T1 hyperintensity is an important exception to the usual T1-dark metastasis pattern and should raise melanoma as a candidate primary.

fullOrganEntries.question: With hepatobiliary contrast agents such as gadoxetate, what is the key delayed MRI appearance of hepatic metastases?
fullOrganEntries.answer: On delayed scans, normal liver is brightly enhanced and metastases are conspicuous as hypointense focal lesions. Exam pivot: Gadoxetate can reveal additional small metastases that are less evident on routine MR or CT.

fullOrganEntries.question: When should biphasic CT of the liver be obtained according to the source?
fullOrganEntries.answer: When a known or suspected hypervascular primary tumor is present, including endocrine tumors, renal cell carcinoma, thyroid carcinoma, carcinoid, pheochromocytoma, and some sarcomas, breast cancers, and melanomas. Exam pivot: Hypervascular metastases may be missed or undercalled if arterial-phase imaging is omitted.

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the reported per-patient sensitivity of gadoxetate-enhanced MR for colorectal liver metastases in the source?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Up to 96%. Exam pivot: When the question is maximal detection of hepatic metastatic burden, especially small lesions, gadoxetate-enhanced MR can outperform routine MR and CT.

fullOrganEntries.question: For lesion-size performance, what is the key source-stated advantage of gadoxetate-enhanced MR over CT?
fullOrganEntries.answer: All modalities do better for lesions greater than 1.5 cm, but gadoxetate-enhanced MR is much better than CT for lesions smaller than 1.5 cm. Exam pivot: When small hepatic metastases could change surgery or ablation candidacy, gadoxetate-enhanced MR is the highest-yield escalation step.

fullOrganEntries.question: In the absence of a known primary tumor or other metastases, what is the source-stated significance of hepatic lesions that are “too small to characterize”?
fullOrganEntries.answer: They rarely represent metastases. Exam pivot: Do not overcall tiny indeterminate liver lesions as metastatic disease when there is no corroborating primary or metastatic context.

fullOrganEntries.question: In the absence of a known primary tumor or other metastases, what is the source-stated significance of hepatic lesions that are lower than blood density on NECT?
fullOrganEntries.answer: They rarely represent metastases. Exam pivot: A very low-density tiny liver lesion on NECT without oncologic corroboration should not be reflexively labeled metastatic.

fullOrganEntries.question: What does peripheral rim enhancement in a hypovascular liver metastasis represent according to the source?
fullOrganEntries.answer: It indicates vascularized viable tumor in the periphery and a hypovascular or necrotic center; rim enhancement may also reflect compressed normal parenchyma. Exam pivot: Rim-enhancing metastases are not simple cystic lesions, and the rim should be interpreted as viable tumor or compressed liver rather than a benign wall.

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the source-stated liver-specific board pivot for hepatic lymphoma involving vessels and bile ducts?
fullOrganEntries.answer: A periportal hepatic mass may encase vascular or biliary structures without vascular occlusion or thrombosis; postcontrast MR may show no distortion of vasculature or biliary ducts. Exam pivot: Encasement with preserved patency/distortion is a classic clue favoring lymphoma over more aggressively invasive primary epithelial malignancies.

fullOrganEntries.question: Define Inflammatory hepatic adenoma.
fullOrganEntries.answer: Source definition: Most common hepatic adenoma subtype, including lesions previously called telangiectatic hepatic adenoma, associated with oral contraceptives, obesity, and alcohol use. Boundary condition: It is an HA subtype with persistent hypervascularity and bleeding risk, not FNH despite possible mimicry. Synonyms: Inflammatory HA; telangiectatic HA legacy terminology.

fullOrganEntries.question: Define HNF1A-mutated hepatic adenoma.
fullOrganEntries.answer: Source definition: Second most common hepatic adenoma subtype, associated with diabetes and familial hepatic adenomatosis, characterized by diffuse lipid deposition within adenomas. Boundary condition: It is a fat-rich adenoma subtype, not focal fat or FNH. Synonyms: HNF1A-mutated HA; HNF-alpha 1 mutated adenoma.

fullOrganEntries.question: Define CTNNB1-mutated hepatic adenoma.
fullOrganEntries.answer: Source definition: Least common hepatic adenoma subtype associated with beta-catenin mutation, more likely in men, androgenic steroid users, metabolic syndrome, and glycogen storage disease, with highest malignant transformation risk. Boundary condition: It is a high-risk HA subtype, not conventional HCC, although malignant transformation can occur. Synonyms: Beta-catenin-mutated HA; CTNNB1-mutated HA.

fullOrganEntries.question: Define Hepatic adenomatosis.
fullOrganEntries.answer: Source definition: No strict definition; generally more than 10 adenomas, associated with glycogen storage disease, steatosis, and diabetes. Boundary condition: It is a multiplicity pattern of adenomas, not a separate malignant diagnosis. Synonyms: Adenomatosis.

fullOrganEntries.question: Define Focal nodular hyperplasia.
fullOrganEntries.answer: Source definition: Benign liver mass that contains Kupffer cells and biliary ductules and may be confirmed with sulfur colloid or HIDA behavior in the proper context. Refined operational definition based on the allowed source set: A benign hepatocellular lesion that typically homogeneously enhances and retains hepatobiliary contrast, used as the key benign mimic of hepatic adenoma. Boundary condition: It is not hepatic adenoma; presence of bile ductules/Kupffer cells explains uptake behavior. Synonyms: FNH.

fullOrganEntries.question: Define Hepatocellular carcinoma.
fullOrganEntries.answer: Source definition: Most common primary liver tumor, classically a hypervascular liver mass in a patient with cirrhosis or chronic hepatitis until proven otherwise. Boundary condition: It is malignant and locally invasive; invasion, metastases, and tumor-in-vein distinguish it from benign adenoma when present. Synonyms: HCC.

fullOrganEntries.question: Why does hepatic adenoma usually lack HIDA uptake and hepatobiliary-phase retention compared with FNH?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Core and RadPrimer describe hepatic adenoma as hepatocellular tissue without bile ducts/bile ductules. HIDA uptake depends on biliary handling, and hepatobiliary-phase gadoxetate retention requires functioning hepatobiliary uptake/excretion behavior. FNH contains bile ductules and Kupffer cells, so it can show HIDA uptake and sulfur-colloid/hepatobiliary retention; adenoma usually lacks that machinery, so it shows paucity of HIDA uptake and often no substantial delayed gadoxetate retention. This mechanism is the key imaging discriminator between adenoma and FNH.

fullOrganEntries.question: Why does HNF1A-mutated hepatic adenoma show opposed-phase signal dropout?
fullOrganEntries.answer: The source states that the mutated HNF1A gene promotes lipogenesis and hepatocellular proliferation, producing diffuse lipid deposition within the adenoma. When fat and water are present within the same voxel, opposed-phase GRE T1 imaging cancels part of the signal, so the lesion loses signal compared with in-phase imaging. This connects the subtype biology to the practical MR discriminator: homogeneous intralesional fat favors HNF1A-mutated adenoma.

fullOrganEntries.question: Why can inflammatory hepatic adenoma show persistent hypervascularity and T2 hyperintensity/atoll-type appearance?
fullOrganEntries.answer: RadPrimer attributes persistent hypervascularity through arterial and venous phases to sinusoidal dilation, peliotic areas, and abnormal vessels. Those vascular/sinusoidal spaces create a hypervascular lesion and can produce T2 hyperintensity, including a peripheral atoll-type distribution in a subset of inflammatory adenomas. The imaging pivot is that this vascular inflammatory subtype can mimic FNH, so subtype risk factors and hepatobiliary-phase behavior must be checked.

fullOrganEntries.question: Why are hepatic adenomas prone to hemorrhage and why does size matter?
fullOrganEntries.answer: The source describes hepatic adenoma as a hepatocellular neoplasm with absent portal/central veins and bile ducts and scattered thin-walled unpaired vascular channels. This abnormal vascular architecture, combined with arterial supply and subtype-specific vascularity, explains why adenomas can hemorrhage or rupture. Larger lesions have more tissue and vascular substrate at risk, which is why incidentally discovered adenomas greater than 5 cm are usually resected and why hemorrhage is a central board complication.

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the pitfall when a hepatobiliary-phase liver lesion looks like FNH, and what safety check prevents the error?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Trap: Assuming hepatobiliary-phase uptake/retention always proves FNH. Safety check: Check for inflammatory HA risk factors and the full imaging pattern, because a minority of adenomas are iso- to hyperintense on hepatobiliary phase and inflammatory HA can mimic FNH. Key discriminator: FNH usually retains gadoxetate and contains bile ductules/Kupffer cells; adenoma often lacks substantial retention, but exceptions exist. Why it happens: Both lesions are hepatocellular and hypervascular, so hepatobiliary-phase behavior can overlap.

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the pitfall when a hepatic adenoma is found in a man or in glycogen storage disease, and what safety check prevents the error?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Trap: Treating all adenomas as low-risk benign lesions. Safety check: Identify malignant-risk factors: male sex, glycogen storage disease, anabolic steroid use, CTNNB1-mutated subtype, and size greater than 5 cm. Key discriminator: CTNNB1-mutated adenoma carries the highest malignant transformation risk and is relatively more associated with men and glycogen storage disease. Why it happens: The word adenoma sounds benign, but the subtype/risk context changes management urgency.

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the nuclear medicine pitfall in separating FNH from hepatic adenoma, and what safety check prevents the error?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Trap: Assuming sulfur colloid alone always separates FNH from adenoma. Safety check: Remember FNH can be variable on sulfur colloid, while HIDA helps because FNH contains biliary ductules and adenoma lacks bile ductules. Key discriminator: FNH should demonstrate HIDA uptake; hepatic adenoma usually shows paucity/lack of HIDA uptake. Why it happens: Kupffer-cell sulfur colloid behavior can vary, especially in FNH, so the bile-ductule-based HIDA discriminator is often cleaner.

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the sex distribution of hepatic adenoma stated by the source, and why does it matter?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Fact: 98% are seen in females; males are uncommon unless anabolic steroid use or glycogen storage disease is present. Exam pivot: A hepatic adenoma in a man should trigger higher concern for high-risk context and malignant transformation.

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the typical age group for hepatic adenoma stated by the source?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Fact: Young women in the childbearing age group, predominantly in the 3rd and 4th decades. Exam pivot: This demographic helps rank HA above HCC in a young noncirrhotic woman with a hypervascular hepatic mass.

fullOrganEntries.question: What proportion of hepatic adenomas are inflammatory subtype?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Fact: Inflammatory HA is the most common subtype, accounting for 40-50% of HAs. Exam pivot: Inflammatory subtype should be a default subtype consideration when a hepatic adenoma is hypervascular and hemorrhagic.

fullOrganEntries.question: What proportion of hepatic adenomas are HNF1A-mutated subtype?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Fact: HNF1A-mutated HA is the 2nd most common subtype, accounting for 30-35% of HAs. Exam pivot: Diffuse intralesional fat with opposed-phase signal dropout should raise this subtype strongly.

fullOrganEntries.question: What proportion of hepatic adenomas are CTNNB1-mutated subtype?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Fact: CTNNB1-mutated HA is the least common subtype, accounting for 10-15% of HAs. Exam pivot: Even though least common, it is the highest malignant-risk subtype, especially in men/steroid/glycogen-storage contexts.

fullOrganEntries.question: What percentage of patients with von Gierke type I glycogen storage disease have multiple adenomas according to the source?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Fact: Multiple adenomas occur in 60% of affected patients. Exam pivot: Multiple adenomas in glycogen storage disease should not be treated as a routine low-risk incidental multiplicity pattern.

fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic adenoma, what is the key subtype/risk framework?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Inflammatory HA: most common; persistent hypervascularity; highest bleeding risk. HNF1A-mutated HA: diffuse lipid/opposed-phase dropout; least aggressive. CTNNB1-mutated HA: least common; highest malignant transformation risk. Unclassified: does not fit other subtype profiles. Exam pivot: subtype changes imaging expectations and risk stratification.

fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic adenoma, what CT attenuation and enhancement pattern is expected?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Noncontrast CT: hemorrhage may appear as hyperdense foci; fat may be present; calcification is focal and about 5%. Postcontrast: typically arterial hyperenhancement, becoming iso- or hypoattenuating to liver on portal venous/delayed phases. Capsule: pseudocapsule/encapsulation may be present and can enhance late. Exam pivot: fat/hemorrhage and arterial hypervascularity support HA, but overlap with other hypervascular liver lesions remains.

fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic adenoma, what MRI signal and enhancement pattern is expected?
fullOrganEntries.answer: T1WI: heterogeneous; increased signal from fat/recent hemorrhage; decreased signal from necrosis, calcification, or old hemorrhage. T2WI: heterogeneous; increased signal from old hemorrhage/necrosis; decreased signal from fat/recent hemorrhage. Postcontrast: heterogeneous arterial hypervascular enhancement; delayed pseudocapsule may be hyperintense. Exam pivot: MR is better than CT for lipid and hemorrhage.

fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic adenoma, what gadoxetate-enhanced MRI behavior is source-supported?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Many adenomas show no substantial uptake or retention on delayed imaging. Up to 26% of adenomas are iso- to hyperintense to liver; 8% of FNHs may show hypointensity. Inflammatory HA can mimic FNH. Exam pivot: hepatobiliary-phase signal is highly useful but not absolute.

fullOrganEntries.question: For HNF1A-mutated hepatic adenoma, what MRI appearance is expected?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Diffuse lipid deposition within HA. Most evident as signal dropout on opposed-phase GRE T1WI due to homogeneous intralesional fat. Hyper- to isointense on T1WI; iso- to slightly hyperintense on T2WI. Only moderate arterial enhancement and no persistent venous/delayed enhancement. Exam pivot: homogeneous opposed-phase dropout is the subtype clue.

fullOrganEntries.question: For inflammatory hepatic adenoma, what MRI appearance is expected? What about percentages of some of the expected findings?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Persistent hypervascularity through arterial and venous phases. Iso- to mildly hyperintense on T1WI. Increased T2 signal, homogeneous or peripheral atoll distribution in 40% of cases. MR/clinical evidence of hemorrhage up to 30%. Exam pivot: hypervascular hemorrhagic adenoma with atoll-type T2 signal can mimic FNH.

fullOrganEntries.question: For CTNNB1-mutated hepatic adenoma, what MRI appearance is source-supported?
fullOrganEntries.answer: No distinctive MRI pattern is established. Usually hypervascular with evidence of hemorrhage or necrosis within tumor. Exam pivot: recognize the subtype mainly by risk context and malignant potential rather than a specific MRI signature.

fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic adenoma, what sonographic appearance is source-supported?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Core: no specific ultrasound features distinguish adenoma from other hepatic masses; it may be hyperechoic, isoechoic, or hypoechoic. RadPrimer: complex heterogeneous hyper-/hypoechoic mass with anechoic areas; capsule may be seen. Color Doppler: hypervascular tumor, large peripheral arteries/veins, and intratumoral veins. Exam pivot: intratumoral veins are absent in FNH and can help distinguish adenoma.

fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic adenoma, what nuclear medicine appearance is source-supported?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Tc-99m sulfur colloid: usually photopenic; RadPrimer states cold in 80% and warm in 20%. HIDA: usually lack of uptake because adenoma lacks biliary ductules; RadPrimer notes increased activity in some. Gallium: no uptake. Exam pivot: HIDA uptake favors FNH over adenoma because FNH contains biliary ductules.

fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic adenoma, what are the key source-supported malignant transformation risk factors?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Male sex: 10x more frequent malignant degeneration than in women on a per-case basis. Concomitant glycogen storage disease; anabolic steroid use; CTNNB1-mutated subtype. Mass size greater than 5 cm. Exam pivot: these features change an adenoma from routine benign lesion to high-risk lesion.

fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic adenoma, what are the main source-supported treatment pivots?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Adenoma less than 5 cm: observation and discontinuation of oral contraceptives or other steroids. Adenoma greater than 5 cm and near surface: surgical resection; consider transcatheter embolization. Any beta-catenin adenoma: resection independent of size. Pregnancy should be avoided due to increased rupture risk. Exam pivot: size, surface location, pregnancy risk, and beta-catenin status drive management.

fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic adenomatosis, what threshold and consequence are source-supported?
fullOrganEntries.answer: No strict definition; generally more than 10 adenomas. May number more than 100 adenomas. Associated with glycogen storage disease, steatosis, and diabetes. May cause hepatic dysfunction and hemorrhage. Exam pivot: multiplicity can be a disease-risk framework, not just incidental multiple benign masses.

fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic adenoma versus FNH, what is the key hepatobiliary/nuclear medicine discriminator?
fullOrganEntries.answer: FNH: contains Kupffer cells and bile ductules; may retain gadoxetate and demonstrate HIDA uptake. Hepatic adenoma: lacks bile ducts/bile ductules; often no delayed gadoxetate retention and paucity/lack of HIDA uptake. Exam pivot: FNH is usually the benign mimic to actively separate from adenoma.

fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic adenoma, what is the best imaging tool recommended by the source?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Use a combination of chemical shift, T2, and T1 pre- and postcontrast MRI, with optional gadoxetate-enhanced MRI. Exam pivot: MR characterizes lipid, hemorrhage, enhancement, and hepatobiliary behavior better than a single CT or ultrasound feature.

fullOrganEntries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Transient hepatic attenuation difference due to portal vein thrombosis Keyword findings: thrombosis of the posterior branch of the right portal vein compensatory increased flow through the hepatic artery ascites uniform enhancement of the liver portal vein thrombus Reasoning: Arterial-phase regional hepatic hyperenhancement occurs in the territory of a thrombosed portal vein branch, and the liver becomes uniformly enhancing on portal venous phase while the thrombus remains visible. This supports a transient perfusion abnormality from decreased portal inflow with compensatory arterial flow. Differential: Hypervascular liver mass Focal confluent fibrosis Hemangioma Focal sparing with fatty liver

fullOrganEntries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Peripheral arterioportal shunt-related THAD Keyword findings: peripheral, small, wedge-shaped, hypervascular foci no lesion peripheral, subcapsular location small size wedge shape no corresponding lesion on venous or delayed-phase imaging Reasoning: The arterial-phase finding is small, peripheral, subcapsular, and wedge-shaped, and it has no corresponding lesion on portal venous imaging. The article specifically states that this favors arterioportal shunt over heterogeneously hypervascular tumor. Differential: Hypervascular liver mass Focal confluent fibrosis Hemangioma Focal sparing with fatty liver

fullOrganEntries.clinicalContext: 67-year-old man with midepigastric pain and weight loss C8M2L5Q7R9VX
fullOrganEntries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: THAD caused by small hepatic metastasis at the apex of the wedge Keyword findings: wedge-shaped THAD small hypoattenuating liver metastasis low-attenuation pancreatic mass very small metastasis apex of the triangular THAD Reasoning: A wedge-shaped arterial perfusion abnormality can be downstream from a small neoplastic lesion. The decisive clue is the very small metastasis at the apex of the triangular THAD, matching the diagnostic checklist warning to search the apex of the wedge. Differential: Hypervascular liver mass Focal confluent fibrosis Hemangioma Focal sparing with fatty liver

fullOrganEntries.clinicalContext: 57-year-old woman with abdominal pain and weight loss D2P9K4L8Q6ZA
fullOrganEntries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Left lobar THAD due to cholangiocarcinoma-related biliary obstruction Keyword findings: dilated left main bile duct left lobar THAD dilated bile ducts left lobe THAD biliary obstruction focal increased sinusoidal pressure regionally decreased portal flow Reasoning: A lobar THAD should have an identifiable cause. Here, biliary obstruction from cholangiocarcinoma produces focal increased sinusoidal pressure and regionally decreased portal flow, accounting for the left lobar perfusion abnormality. Differential: Hypervascular liver mass Focal confluent fibrosis Hemangioma Focal sparing with fatty liver

fullOrganEntries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Biopsy-caused arterioportal shunt with THAD Keyword findings: hyperenhancement of a portion of the lateral segment of the liver early enhancement of the portal vein branch arterioportal shunt prior biopsy of the liver portal venous-phase CECT appears normal Reasoning: Early enhancement of a portal vein branch draining the hyperenhancing segment indicates arterioportal shunting. Normal appearance on portal venous phase supports a transient perfusion phenomenon rather than a persistent mass. Differential: Hypervascular liver mass Focal confluent fibrosis Hemangioma Focal sparing with fatty liver

fullOrganEntries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: HCC-associated THAD/perfusion abnormality Keyword findings: enlarged branch of the right hepatic artery brightly enhancing lesion in the right lobe wedge-shaped zone of hypervascularity multiple hypervascular tumor foci portal venous radicle washout of contrast from the HCC masses overestimation of tumor size Reasoning: This case shows tumor and perfusion abnormality together. The wedge-shaped hypervascular zone peripheral or distal to the tumor is THAD rather than tumor, while the masses show portal venous washout. Separating the two prevents overestimation of tumor size. Differential: Hypervascular liver mass Focal confluent fibrosis Hemangioma Focal sparing with fatty liver

fullOrganEntries.clinicalContext: 71-year-old man with weight loss and abdominal pain G9L2X5Q8R1MP
fullOrganEntries.question: 6 month later Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: THAD with subsequent metastatic lesion in the same region Keyword findings: area of enhancement blends in with the liver parenchyma on the venous phase no discreet underlying lesion findings are consistent with THAD 6 months later discreet metastatic lesion previously seen region of THAD Reasoning: The initial arterial enhancement behaves like THAD by blending into liver on venous phase with no discrete lesion. The follow-up image demonstrates why oncology-context THAD regions need careful scrutiny: a metastatic lesion later appears in the same region. Differential: Hypervascular liver mass Focal confluent fibrosis Hemangioma Focal sparing with fatty liver

fullOrganEntries.clinicalContext: Adult patient with chest discomfort H4Q7N2L9X5RK
fullOrganEntries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Third-inflow THAD from SVC obstruction with collateral venous flow Keyword findings: hyperdense enhancement of the medial left lobe collateral veins that traverse the chest wall diaphragm, and liver parenchyma obstruction of the superior vena cava (SVC) occlusion of the SVC chest wall collateral veins intrahepatic collaterals densely opacified medial segment Reasoning: Medial left lobe hyperenhancement occurs via collateral venous pathways in SVC obstruction. This is a third-inflow phenomenon rather than a primary hepatic mass. Differential: Hypervascular liver mass Focal confluent fibrosis Hemangioma Focal sparing with fatty liver

fullOrganEntries.clinicalContext: Adult man with abdominal pain J2K8M5Q1L7RX
fullOrganEntries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: THAD due to septic thrombosis of the anterior right portal vein branch Keyword findings: hyperenhancement of the anterior right lobe segments of the liver septic thrombosis anterior branch of the right portal vein Reasoning: Anterior right lobe arterial hyperenhancement is explained by septic thrombosis of the corresponding anterior right portal vein branch, producing decreased portal inflow with compensatory arterial perfusion. Differential: Hypervascular liver mass Focal confluent fibrosis Hemangioma Focal sparing with fatty liver

fullOrganEntries.clinicalContext: Older man with abdominal pain K5P9L2Q7M1ZA
fullOrganEntries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: THAD from septic thrombophlebitis with anterior right portal vein thrombosis Keyword findings: septic thrombophlebitis due to diverticulitis hyperperfusion of the anterior right lobe of the liver thrombosis of the anterior branch of the right portal vein compensatory increased flow from the hepatic artery Reasoning: The anterior right lobe hyperperfusion corresponds to anterior portal branch thrombosis from septic thrombophlebitis, with compensatory hepatic arterial flow producing the THAD pattern. Differential: Hypervascular liver mass Focal confluent fibrosis Hemangioma Focal sparing with fatty liver

fullOrganEntries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: THAD due to liver abscess Keyword findings: hyperenhancement of the right lobe of the liver right lobe of the liver liver abscess Reasoning: The right lobe hyperenhancement is described as THAD due to a liver abscess. This fits the article mechanism in which abscess or infection can alter regional inflow and produce a perfusion abnormality. Differential: Hypervascular liver mass Focal confluent fibrosis Hemangioma Focal sparing with fatty liver

fullOrganEntries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Transient hepatic intensity difference (THID) on MRI Keyword findings: THID in the arterial phase iso-intense on the venous phase absence of corresponding abnormality on precontrast T2 MR images vascular phenomenon small vessel thrombosis Reasoning: Arterial-phase MRI hyperenhancement that becomes isointense on venous phase and lacks a corresponding precontrast or T2 abnormality supports THID as a vascular phenomenon rather than a structural lesion. Differential: Hypervascular liver mass Focal confluent fibrosis Hemangioma Focal sparing with fatty liver

fullOrganEntries.question: CT abdomen with contrast. Based on the images, name 4 key differentials and give one best discriminator for each.
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hypervascular liver mass Focal confluent fibrosis Hemangioma Focal sparing with fatty liver

fullOrganEntries.clinicalContext: 67-year-old man with midepigastric pain and weight loss C8M2L5Q7R9VX [DD2]
fullOrganEntries.question: CT abdomen with contrast. Based on the images, name 4 key differentials and give one best discriminator for each.
fullOrganEntries.answer: THAD from small hepatic tumor Hypervascular liver mass Hemangioma Focal confluent fibrosis

fullOrganEntries.clinicalContext: Adult patient with chest discomfort H4Q7N2L9X5RK [DD3]
fullOrganEntries.question: CT abdomen with contrast. Based on the images, name 4 key differentials and give one best discriminator for each.
fullOrganEntries.answer: Third-inflow THAD from SVC obstruction Hypervascular liver mass Focal sparing with fatty liver Hemangioma

fullOrganEntries.question: MRI abdomen. Based on the images, name 3 key differentials and give one best discriminator for each.
fullOrganEntries.answer: THID Hypervascular liver mass Hemangioma

fullOrganEntries.question: Define transient hepatic attenuation/intensity difference (THAD/THID).
fullOrganEntries.answer: Source definition: Transient increase in hepatic attenuation, or intensity on MRI, appearing as segmental wedge-shaped areas of enhancement during arterial-phase CT or MRI, which become isoattenuating/isointense during portal venous phase due to regional variations in the balance between hepatic arterial and portal venous blood flow. Boundary condition: It is a transient perfusion phenomenon, not a mass by itself; a separate underlying lesion may still be present. Synonyms: THAD = transient hepatic attenuation difference; THID = transient hepatic intensity difference.

fullOrganEntries.question: Why can decreased portal venous inflow produce THAD or THID?
fullOrganEntries.answer: In the arterial phase, iodinated contrast reaching the liver through the hepatic artery is normally diluted in the sinusoids by unopacified portal venous blood in an approximate 3:1 portal-to-arterial contribution. If portal venous inflow is decreased by segmental portal vein thrombosis, compression/occlusion by mass, extrinsic compression, or elevated sinusoidal pressure, the affected territory receives relatively greater arterial contribution. This produces arterial-phase regional hyperenhancement, which becomes isoattenuating/isointense once portal venous enhancement equilibrates in later phases.

fullOrganEntries.question: Why can increased arterial inflow produce THAD or THID?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Any process that increases hepatic arterial inflow can make a region of liver enhance more strongly during arterial-phase imaging. Source-supported causes include peripheral AP shunts in cirrhosis, hypervascular masses drawing increased arterial flow by sump or siphon effect, and posttraumatic or congenital AV fistula. The abnormality is transient because the portal venous phase restores more uniform parenchymal enhancement, so the perfusion territory fades relative to liver.

fullOrganEntries.question: How does SVC obstruction create medial left lobe or segment 4 THAD?
fullOrganEntries.answer: SVC obstruction can divert venous return through collateral pathways: subclavian vein -> internal mammary vein -> recanalized paraumbilical vein -> left portal vein -> medial left lobe/quadrate lobe -> hepatic veins -> IVC -> right atrium. This alternative venous inflow can densely opacify the medial left lobe or segment 4 during arterial-phase CT or MRI, producing a third-inflow THAD. The same collateral-flow physiology explains the hot quadrate/medial segment sign on Tc-sulfur colloid scans in SVC obstruction.

fullOrganEntries.question: Why can biliary obstruction produce a lobar THAD?
fullOrganEntries.answer: The source states that biliary obstruction or cholangitis can elevate sinusoidal pressure and regionally decrease portal flow. When portal inflow is reduced in the affected territory, hepatic arterial contribution becomes relatively more conspicuous during arterial-phase imaging. This produces a lobar or segmental THAD that fades when portal venous phase enhancement becomes more uniform.

fullOrganEntries.clinicalContext: 67-year-old man with midepigastric pain and weight loss C8M2L5Q7R9VX [BT1]
fullOrganEntries.question: What is the major pitfall on this case, and what safety check prevents it?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Trap: Calling the perfusion wedge the whole lesion and missing the small causative tumor. Safety check: Inspect the apex of every wedge-shaped THAD on portal venous-phase and arterial-phase images. Key discriminator: The THAD is wedge-shaped and perfusional, while the causative tumor is a small rounded lesion at the apex of the wedge/triangle. Why it happens: The perfusion abnormality can be larger and more conspicuous than the small mass that causes it.

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the major pitfall on this case, and what safety check prevents it?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Trap: Overestimating HCC tumor size by including adjacent THAD/perfusion abnormality as tumor. Safety check: Compare arterial and portal venous phases and separate the discrete tumor foci from the transient wedge-shaped perfusion territory. Key discriminator: The HCC masses show washout, while the THAD becomes less evident on portal venous phase. Why it happens: Tumor and adjacent perfusion abnormality can both be hypervascular on arterial phase.

fullOrganEntries.clinicalContext: Adult patient with chest discomfort H4Q7N2L9X5RK [BT3]
fullOrganEntries.question: What is the major pitfall on this case, and what safety check prevents it?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Trap: Misinterpreting medial left hepatic lobe enhancement from collateral venous flow as a hepatic mass. Safety check: Look for SVC occlusion, chest wall collateral veins, intrahepatic collaterals, and densely opacified medial segment/segment 4. Key discriminator: Third-inflow enhancement follows collateral venous pathways rather than forming a discrete spherical or oval mass. Why it happens: Alternative venous inflow can create focal hepatic hyperenhancement and nuclear medicine hot pseudolesions.

fullOrganEntries.question: For THAD, what CT appearance is expected?
fullOrganEntries.answer: - Arterial phase: peripheral wedge-shaped increased attenuation with straight margins. - Portal venous/delayed phases: becomes isodense and inconspicuous. - CT may show the cause: focal hepatic/perihepatic mass, portal vein thrombosis, or hepatic vein thrombosis. Exam pivot: If it persists or behaves like a mass, do not call it pure THAD.

fullOrganEntries.question: For THID, what MRI appearance is expected?
fullOrganEntries.answer: - Arterial phase gadolinium-enhanced MRI: areas of hyperenhancement. - Venous/delayed phases: becomes isointense to liver. - T2/DWI: no corresponding signal abnormality unless an underlying lesion is present. Exam pivot: Absence of a T2/DWI correlate supports vascular phenomenon rather than structural lesion.

fullOrganEntries.question: For THAD/THID, what ultrasound appearance is source-supported?
fullOrganEntries.answer: - Ultrasound: no corollary findings are expected. - Exception: contrast-enhanced ultrasound with microbubble contrast agent may show a correlate. Exam pivot: Do not invent grayscale or Doppler findings for THAD unless contrast-enhanced ultrasound is specifically being used.

fullOrganEntries.question: For THAD/THID, what nuclear medicine pseudolesions are source-supported?
fullOrganEntries.answer: - Tc sulfur colloid: hot accumulation in the left lobe/quadrate region can occur with SVC obstruction. - FDG PET/CT: hot accumulation can occur within a THAD. Exam pivot: Tracer hot spots caused by perfusion/third inflow can be misinterpreted as tumor.

fullOrganEntries.question: What are the three major mechanism buckets for THAD/THID?
fullOrganEntries.answer: - Decreased portal flow: portal vein thrombosis, mass compression/occlusion, elevated sinusoidal pressure. - Increased arterial inflow: AP shunts, hypervascular masses, AV fistula. - Third inflow: alternative venous supply such as gallbladder venous drainage or paraumbilical/paradiaphragmatic collaterals. Exam pivot: The enhancement pattern is the clue; the mechanism tells you where to search for the cause.

fullOrganEntries.question: What contrast timing/protocol details are source-supported for evaluating THAD/THID?
fullOrganEntries.answer: - Best tool: CECT with arterial and portal venous-phase imaging. - Arterial phase: 25-40 seconds after IV bolus. - Contrast: >100 mL volume and >=3 mL/sec injection rate. - Portal venous phase: 60-80 seconds after IV bolus. Exam pivot: The diagnosis depends on proving arterial conspicuity with venous/delayed fading.

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the diagnostic checklist pearl for a wedge-shaped THAD?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Look carefully for a small hepatic tumor at the apex of the wedge-shaped THAD. Exam pivot: The THAD may be the larger perfusion sign, while the true neoplastic cause may be a small rounded lesion at the apex.

fullOrganEntries.question: How do the main THAD mimics differ from true THAD?
fullOrganEntries.answer: - Hypervascular liver mass: spherical/oval, may wash out, and should be separate from THAD. - Focal confluent fibrosis: delayed-phase wedge with capsular retraction/volume loss, often segment 4. - Hemangioma: nodular discontinuous peripheral enhancement or flash fill, tracking blood pool. - Focal fatty sparing: high-attenuation normal liver in fatty liver, often segments 4A/4B near gallbladder fossa, more evident on nonenhanced CT/MRI. Exam pivot: Shape, phase behavior, and background liver separate perfusion from mimic.

fullOrganEntries.question: Which tumors are source-stated to invade or obstruct hepatic veins/portal veins in THAD-related cases?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Tumor invading or obstructing veins: hepatocellular carcinoma > cholangiocarcinoma > metastases. Exam pivot: Portal venous invasion/obstruction can create THAD and carries poor prognosis related to the underlying tumor.

fullOrganEntries.question: What phase behavior distinguishes THAD from a true hypervascular mass?
fullOrganEntries.answer: THAD is arterial-phase wedge hyperenhancement that becomes isoattenuating/isointense on portal venous and delayed phases; a true mass is spherical/oval and may persist or wash out.

fullOrganEntries.clinicalContext: 38-year-old after liver transplant. Portal venous Doppler ultrasound panel ABDDOP01
fullOrganEntries.question: What Doppler pitfall is shown, and what should it not be mistaken for?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Helical flow in the main portal vein after liver transplant; do not mistake it for true hepatofugal portal venous flow. Core concept: helical flow is spiral/secondary flow superimposed on overall portal venous inflow. In liver transplants, it commonly occurs when donor and recipient main portal veins are discrepant in size, especially with marked diameter mismatch.Logic behind the finding: Color Doppler: alternating red and blue bands within the main portal vein do not automatically mean the entire portal vein is reversed. In a helical stream, one side of the spiral is moving relatively toward the transducer and another side is moving relatively away from it, so opposite colors can coexist in the same vessel lumen. Spectral Doppler: sampling through the helix can show components above and below the baseline, creating an apparent bidirectional/hepatopetal-hepatofugal pattern. That reflects rotational flow within the sample volume rather than necessarily true net hepatofugal flow. Anatomic/hemodynamic basis: donor-recipient portal vein diameter mismatch changes vessel geometry at/near the anastomosis. The caliber transition disturbs laminar flow, causes flow separation, and produces circular/helical streamlines. The source article notes this is accentuated when the portal-vein diameter discrepancy is greater than 50%. How not to overcall it: confirm the net direction by checking intrahepatic portal vein branches and using the vessel course/angle. If intrahepatic branches remain hepatopetal, the red/blue mixture in the main portal vein is a pitfall pattern, not true global hepatofugal portal flow. Persistent helical flow with high velocity can still be a clue to portal vein stenosis, so do not ignore the anastomosis. Reference: Fig. 3 and teaching text from Altered Doppler flow patterns in cirrhosis patients: an overview, PMC4701371. The article describes helical flow as secondary spiral flow from disturbed laminar flow; after liver transplant it is attributed to donor/native portal vein diameter discrepancy and is accentuated when the discrepancy is greater than 50%. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4701371/

fullOrganEntries.clinicalContext: Adult with abdominal pain, ascites, abnormal liver tests, and hypercoagulable history. Portal venous phase liver MRI panel GILIVBCS01A
fullOrganEntries.question: What vascular liver disorder pattern is shown, and what background parenchymal finding supports it?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Budd-Chiari syndrome, with hepatic venous outflow obstruction and mosaic hepatic enhancement from venous congestion. Why: Budd-Chiari is defined by impaired hepatic venous drainage in the absence of right heart failure or constrictive pericarditis. Direct imaging signs are hepatic vein/IVC obstruction and venous collaterals. Indirect signs include ascites, caudate or spared-territory hypertrophy, fibrosis/atrophy of involved segments, portal hypertension, mosaic enhancement, and later regenerative nodules. Differential to think through: congestive hepatopathy from right heart failure, sinusoidal obstruction syndrome, cirrhosis with heterogeneous enhancement, portal vein thrombosis, and infiltrative hepatic tumor. Direct hepatic vein/IVC obstruction or collaterals is the key discriminator. Reference: Porrello G, Mamone G, Miraglia R. Budd-Chiari Syndrome Imaging Diagnosis: State of the Art and Future Perspectives. Diagnostics (Basel). 2023;13(13):2256. PMCID: PMC10341099. DOI: 10.3390/diagnostics13132256. Open access CC BY 4.0. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10341099/Differentiate from congestive hepatopathy by looking for a cardiac/right-heart cause and patent hepatic veins. Differentiate from primary cirrhosis by identifying hepatic venous outflow obstruction, venous collaterals, caudate hypertrophy, and the BCS pattern of focal regenerative nodules.

fullOrganEntries.clinicalContext: 36-year-old man with chronic liver disease, ascites, and prior TIPS. Multiphasic liver CT panel GILIVBCS02B
fullOrganEntries.question: In this vascular chronic liver background, what is the most likely interpretation of the multiple arterialized hepatic nodules?
fullOrganEntries.answer: FNH-like regenerative nodules / large regenerative nodules in chronic Budd-Chiari syndrome. Why: chronic hepatic venous outflow obstruction causes portal flow deprivation, congestion, fibrosis, and compensatory hepatic arterialization. Areas with relatively preserved outflow can undergo benign hepatocellular hyperplasia, producing multiple arterialized regenerative nodules. On CT they are often homogeneous arterial enhancing and become iso- or slightly hyperdense on portal venous/delayed phases. Trap: do not call every arterial enhancing nodule HCC in chronic Budd-Chiari. Multiplicity, homogeneous enhancement, T1 iso/hyperintensity on MRI, lack of restricted diffusion, central scar/perinodular congestion rim, and hepatobiliary iso/hyperintensity favor benign regenerative nodules. Differential to think through: HCC, adenoma, true FNH, dysplastic nodule, hypervascular metastases, hemangioma, and perfusion pseudolesion. Reference: Rizzetto F, Rutanni D, Carbonaro LA, Vanzulli A. Focal Liver Lesions in Budd-Chiari Syndrome: Spectrum of Imaging Findings. Diagnostics (Basel). 2023;13(14):2346. PMCID: PMC10378170. DOI: 10.3390/diagnostics13142346. Open access CC BY 4.0. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10378170/HCC is favored by a solitary/new dominant lesion, T1 hypointensity, T2 hyperintensity, restricted diffusion, heterogeneous arterial enhancement, enhancing capsule, portal/delayed washout, hepatobiliary hypointensity, portal venous invasion, and rising AFP. In BCS, APHE and washout alone have low specificity.

fullOrganEntries.clinicalContext: Known chronic hepatic venous outflow obstruction. Surveillance hepatospecific-contrast MRI shows an arterialized nodule with delayed washout-like appearance. Panel GILIVBCS03C
fullOrganEntries.question: What is the main diagnostic trap here, and what feature keeps you from overcalling malignancy?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Trap: calling a large regenerative/FNH-like nodule in chronic Budd-Chiari syndrome hepatocellular carcinoma solely because it has arterial hyperenhancement and washout-like behavior. Most likely diagnosis: benign FNH-like regenerative nodule / large regenerative nodule in chronic Budd-Chiari. Why the trap happens: BCS changes liver hemodynamics. Portal flow deprivation and increased arterialization make regenerative nodules hypervascular. Perilesional congestion can create relative delayed hypointensity, so 'washout' is less specific than it is in ordinary cirrhosis/HCC algorithms. What rescues the call: hepatobiliary-phase iso/hyperintensity means functioning hepatocytes and ductular proliferation are present, like FNH/FNH-like regenerative tissue. That pattern argues against HCC, which is usually HBP hypointense in this context. Differential to think through: HCC, hepatic adenoma, true FNH, dysplastic nodule, necrotic/infarcted regenerative nodule, hypervascular metastasis. If AFP rises, the lesion is solitary/dominant, HBP hypointense, diffusion restricting, T2 bright, rapidly growing, or atypical over serial exams, biopsy/focused workup is justified.
