Reference: Porrello G, Mamone G, Miraglia R. Budd-Chiari Syndrome Imaging Diagnosis: State of the Art and Future Perspectives. Diagnostics (Basel). 2023;13(13):2256. PMCID: PMC10341099. DOI: 10.3390/diagnostics13132256. Open access CC BY 4.0. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10341099/In chronic BCS, do not apply LI-RADS/AASLD-style APHE-plus-washout logic uncritically. HBP hyperintensity and lack of aggressive ancillary features favor FNH-like RN; HBP hypointensity, T2 hyperintensity, T1 hypointensity, restriction, capsule, vascular invasion, and AFP elevation favor HCC.

fullOrganEntries.clinicalContext: 49-year-old woman with chronic hepatic venous outflow obstruction. Multisequence liver MRI shows multiple hepatic lesions, including larger right-lobe lesions. Panel GILIVBCS04D
fullOrganEntries.question: What is the likely diagnosis of the larger right-lobe lesions, and why should size alone not make you call HCC?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Large FNH-like regenerative nodules in chronic Budd-Chiari syndrome. Why size is not enough: regenerative nodules in BCS can be large, increase in size, change enhancement, and even show washout-like behavior during follow-up. Those changes are not automatically malignant in this specific vascular liver disease context. Benign clues in this panel: multiple lesions, T1 hyperintensity, T2 iso-hypointensity with central scar-like signal, no meaningful diffusion restriction compared with liver, arterial enhancement without persistent malignant behavior, portal/delayed isointensity, perinodular congested rim, and hepatobiliary iso/hyperintensity. Differential to think through: HCC, hepatic adenoma, true FNH, hemangioma, dysplastic nodule, necrotic/infarcted regenerative nodule, hypervascular metastasis. The source also includes a hemangioma-like lesion as a separate lesion, which is a useful reminder not every lesion in the same liver is the same entity. Reference: Rizzetto F, Rutanni D, Carbonaro LA, Vanzulli A. Focal Liver Lesions in Budd-Chiari Syndrome: Spectrum of Imaging Findings. Diagnostics (Basel). 2023;13(14):2346. PMCID: PMC10378170. DOI: 10.3390/diagnostics13142346. Open access CC BY 4.0. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10378170/Favor HCC when the lesion is solitary/new dominant, HBP hypointense, T2 hyperintense, T1 hypointense, diffusion restricting, capsule-forming, vascular invasive, or associated with rising AFP. Favor FNH-like RN when nodules are multiple, T1 iso/hyperintense, T2 iso/hypointense, HBP iso/hyperintense, and lack aggressive ancillary features.

fullOrganEntries.clinicalContext: 67-year-old woman with chronic hepatic venous outflow obstruction and a new focal liver lesion. Multisequence hepatospecific MRI panel GILIVBCS05E
fullOrganEntries.question: In the same vascular liver disease background, what features should make you worry for true malignancy rather than a benign regenerative nodule?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hepatocellular carcinoma arising in Budd-Chiari syndrome. Why this is different from the regenerative nodule trap: the lesion is new/solitary, T2 hyperintense, T1 hypointense, diffusion restricting, arterial enhancing, then shows washout with an enhancing capsule and hepatobiliary-phase hypointensity. That combination is much more concerning for HCC than a T1-bright/HBP-bright FNH-like regenerative nodule. Key distinction: in BCS, arterial enhancement and washout alone are not enough because benign regenerative nodules can do that. Add the ancillary features: HBP hypointensity, restricted diffusion, T2 hyperintensity, T1 hypointensity, capsule, vascular invasion, growth pattern, and AFP. Differential to think through: HCC, necrotic/infarcted regenerative nodule, adenoma, cholangiocarcinoma, hypervascular metastasis, hemangioma. Necrotic regenerative nodules can mimic HCC by T2 hyperintensity, T1 hypointensity, diffusion restriction, and HBP hypointensity; lack of enhancement through dynamic phases favors necrotic RN rather than HCC. Reference: Rizzetto F, Rutanni D, Carbonaro LA, Vanzulli A. Focal Liver Lesions in Budd-Chiari Syndrome: Spectrum of Imaging Findings. Diagnostics (Basel). 2023;13(14):2346. PMCID: PMC10378170. DOI: 10.3390/diagnostics13142346. Open access CC BY 4.0. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10378170/HCC in BCS: often solitary/new dominant, T1 low, T2 high, DWI restriction, heterogeneous APHE, washout/capsule, HBP hypointensity, possible vascular invasion, and rising AFP. FNH-like RN: often multiple, T1 iso/high, T2 iso/low, little/no restriction, central scar/rim, and HBP iso/high.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/3 Image 2/3 Image 3/3 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Focal nodular hyperplasia (FNH) Keyword findings: - homogeneously and brightly enhancing mass - central scar - became isodense with liver on portal venous phase - retains contrast more than underlying liver - central scar does not take up or retain gadoxetate Reasoning: The combination of homogeneous arterial hyperenhancement, later isointensity, and hepatobiliary contrast retention by the mass with nonretention in the central scar is the FNH pattern.Key differentiators: FNH favors a T2-bright scar that enhances late with extracellular contrast and a lesion that retains hepatobiliary contrast. Fibrolamellar HCC instead has a fibrotic T2-dark scar; adenoma usually lacks biliary ductules and typically does not show the same hepatobiliary retention pattern; hemangioma should show peripheral discontinuous nodular blood-pool enhancement with progressive fill-in. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/3 Image 2/3 Image 3/3 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Giant cavernous hemangioma Keyword findings: - peripheral nodular enhancement - isodense to vessels - small focus of calcification - did not fill in on delayed imaging - very bright - well defined Reasoning: Blood-pool-matching peripheral nodular enhancement with progressive fill-in plus very bright T2 signal strongly supports hemangioma; giant lesions may contain a nonenhancing central scar/cystic region that can calcify.Key differentiators: Hemangioma favors peripheral discontinuous nodular enhancement matching vessels and marked T2 brightness. Fibrolamellar HCC may have a calcified scar but lacks the classic blood-pool fill-in pattern; FNH enhances homogeneously and typically has a T2-bright scar rather than a giant blood-pool lesion. Imaging specificity: Diagnostic in the right dynamic-enhancement context.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Conventional hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) Keyword findings: - large, heterogeneous, hypervascular mass - foci of necrosis - mottled or mosaic appearance - absence of calcification Reasoning: A large hypervascular mosaic mass with necrosis in an older patient and no scar calcification favors conventional HCC over fibrolamellar HCC in the source case.Key differentiators: Conventional HCC may show arterial hyperenhancement, washout, mosaic architecture, necrosis, and vascular invasion. Fibrolamellar HCC is favored in younger noncirrhotic patients and has a classic fibrotic scar that is often calcified. Imaging specificity: Requires correlation.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Conventional hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) Keyword findings: - large mass - eccentric scar - necrotic area - tumor invasion of portal vein Reasoning: Tumor invasion of the portal vein is a major discriminator favoring HCC when a large hepatic mass contains an eccentric scar-like or necrotic region.Key differentiators: Portal-vein tumor invasion supports HCC. Cholangiocarcinoma more characteristically pairs fibrous delayed enhancement with capsular retraction and biliary obstruction; fibrolamellar HCC is classically a young-patient tumor with a fibrotic central scar. Report-critical findings: Explicitly report tumor-in-vein/portal venous invasion when present. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hepatic adenoma Keyword findings: - heterogeneous mass in the left lobe - focus of high attenuation - hemorrhage - lower density foci - necrosis and fibrosis Reasoning: The central heterogeneity is explained by hemorrhage, necrosis, and fibrosis rather than a true central scar, a key adenoma pitfall.Key differentiators: Adenoma often appears heterogeneous because of fat or hemorrhage and can contain necrotic/fibrotic low-density regions that simulate a scar. Chemical-shift signal loss from intracellular lipid and lack of hepatobiliary/biliary-duct behavior help separate it from FNH. Imaging specificity: Requires correlation.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hepatic adenoma Keyword findings: - large, enhancing mass - central nonenhancing scar Reasoning: A central nonenhancing region in an adenoma can represent fibrosis/necrosis rather than a true FNH-type scar; the source uses this appearance as adenoma-pattern reinforcement.Key differentiators: Do not equate a central nonenhancing region with FNH. Adenoma is an arterialized hepatocellular lesion that may contain fat, hemorrhage, necrosis, or fibrous pseudocapsule; FNH is favored by homogeneous arterial enhancement and hepatobiliary contrast retention. Imaging specificity: Requires correlation.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/2 Image 2/2 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hepatic metastases from mucinous colon cancer Keyword findings: - multiple lesions - faint central calcification - central, low-density necrosis or fibrosis - calcification is more difficult to recognize on contrast-enhanced imaging Reasoning: Multiplicity plus central low-density necrosis/fibrosis and faint calcification in a mucinous-primary pattern supports hepatic metastases; noncontrast CT makes subtle calcification more conspicuous.Key differentiators: Metastases are usually hypovascular and best seen on portal venous phase. Mucinous metastases can calcify. EHE tends to be peripheral/subcapsular with capsular retraction, while regenerative nodules are tied to Budd-Chiari morphology and may retain hepatobiliary agent. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive with the clinical context.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/3 Image 2/3 Image 3/3 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Fibrolamellar hepatocellular carcinoma Keyword findings: - heterogeneous, hypervascular mass - large, calcified central scar - similar enhancement of tumor in a cardiophrenic node - central necrotic scar - calcified portions of the scar Reasoning: A large heterogeneous hypervascular mass in a young patient with a calcified central scar is the classic fibrolamellar HCC pattern; nodal disease reinforces aggressive behavior.Key differentiators: Fibrolamellar HCC favors a large fibrotic T1/T2-dark scar and scar calcification. FNH has a T2-bright scar with delayed enhancement and hepatobiliary retention; hemangioma shows blood-pool nodular enhancement with progressive fill-in; conventional HCC is favored by older/cirrhotic context and tumor-in-vein. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/2 Image 2/2 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Mass-forming intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma Keyword findings: - scar or necrosis - capsular retraction - occlusion of the portal vein - occlusion of the bile duct - progressive enhancement - fibrotic changes - nonenhancing central scar Reasoning: Progressive delayed enhancement from fibrotic stroma plus capsular retraction and biliary/portal obstruction is the cholangiocarcinoma pattern.Key differentiators: Cholangiocarcinoma favors progressive fibrotic enhancement, peripheral biliary dilation/occlusion, capsular retraction, and volume loss. Fibrolamellar HCC may retract the capsule but usually presents as a large young-patient hypervascular mass with a fibrotic scar. Report-critical findings: State biliary obstruction, portal venous obstruction, capsular retraction, and lobar volume loss when present. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/2 Image 2/2 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hepatic epithelioid hemangioendothelioma Keyword findings: - multiple peripheral hypovascular lesions - target appearance - subcapsular lesions - retraction of the overlying liver capsule - multiple peripheral and confluent masses - hyperintense central necrosis or scar Reasoning: A multifocal peripheral/subcapsular target-pattern process with capsular retraction and confluent lesions is the EHE pattern.Key differentiators: EHE characteristically forms multiple spherical subcapsular masses that may coalesce and may show a target/halo appearance with capsular retraction. Metastases can be multiple but do not have the same characteristic peripheral coalescent/retraction pattern in the source framework. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/5 Image 2/5 Image 3/5 Image 4/5 Image 5/5 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Large regenerative nodules / nodular regenerative hyperplasia in Budd-Chiari syndrome Keyword findings: - multiple hypervascular foci - hypointense central scar - persistent uptake and retention of the agent within the nodules - functional hepatocytes - multiple large, regenerative nodules - doughnut-like enhancement - central scar - trichrome stain shows green staining of the central scar Reasoning: Multiple hypervascular scar-containing nodules with hepatobiliary-agent retention, Budd-Chiari morphology/TIPS context, and trichrome-confirmed scar support large regenerative nodules rather than multifocal malignancy.Key differentiators: The key separator is the global Budd-Chiari setting plus multiplicity and retained hepatobiliary agent, indicating functioning hepatocytes. Chronic Budd-Chiari also produces caudate hypertrophy, peripheral atrophy, and prominent regenerative nodules. HCC remains an important mimic, especially if a nodule develops malignant enhancement or invasive behavior. Imaging specificity: Requires correlation.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: Why does FNH retain hepatobiliary contrast while its central scar does not?
fullOrganEntries.answer: FNH is a hamartomatous focus of disorganized but functioning liver tissue containing hepatocytes and biliary ductules. The hepatocytes take up hepatobiliary agents, so the lesion is iso- to hyperintense on the hepatobiliary phase. The central scar is composed of biliary ductules and venules rather than normal hepatocyte-rich parenchyma, so the scar does not retain gadoxetate. Radiologic pivot: lesion retention with scar nonretention strongly supports FNH over adenoma.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: Why does a cavernous hemangioma show peripheral discontinuous nodular enhancement with progressive centripetal fill-in?
fullOrganEntries.answer: A cavernous hemangioma is composed of disorganized endothelial-lined vascular spaces supplied from the periphery. Contrast first opacifies peripheral vascular lakes, producing discontinuous nodules that match the blood pool, then progressively fills more central vascular spaces on later phases. Giant lesions may have a central nonenhancing degenerative/fibrotic region. Radiologic pivot: blood-pool-matching peripheral nodules with delayed centripetal fill-in are virtually pathognomonic in the right setting.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: Why can hepatic adenoma mimic a scar-containing liver mass and why does it differ from FNH on biliary imaging?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Adenoma contains hepatocytes and scattered Kupffer cells but no bile ducts. It is supplied by the hepatic artery, so it is often arterially hyperenhancing. Hemorrhage, intracellular fat, necrosis, fibrosis, and a fibrous pseudocapsule can create heterogeneous low- or high-signal regions that mimic a central scar. Because biliary ductules are absent, HIDA uptake is reduced and hepatobiliary behavior differs from FNH. Radiologic pivot: pseudo-scar heterogeneity plus absent biliary-duct behavior favors adenoma over FNH.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: Why does mass-forming cholangiocarcinoma enhance progressively and retract the liver capsule?
fullOrganEntries.answer: The tumor has abundant fibrous/desmoplastic stroma. Contrast progressively accumulates within this fibrotic matrix, producing delayed/progressive enhancement rather than an early blood-pool pattern. Fibrosis contracts and distorts adjacent parenchyma, accounting for capsular retraction and volume loss; growth along/around bile ducts can also cause peripheral biliary obstruction. Radiologic pivot: progressive fibrotic enhancement plus capsular retraction and biliary obstruction strongly favors cholangiocarcinoma.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: Why can Budd-Chiari syndrome produce multiple hypervascular regenerative nodules that mimic HCC?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hepatic venous outflow obstruction causes chronic perfusion stress and parenchymal remodeling. Chronic disease produces peripheral hepatic atrophy with compensatory caudate hypertrophy and prominent regenerative nodules. These nodules contain functioning hepatocytes and can become hypervascular; hepatobiliary-agent retention therefore supports regenerative tissue rather than a nonhepatocellular metastasis. Radiologic pivot: interpret the nodules together with the global venous-outflow morphology and hepatobiliary retention rather than calling multifocal HCC from arterial hyperenhancement alone.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: What scar-based pitfall can make FNH look like fibrolamellar HCC, and what imaging checks prevent the error?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Trap: Treating every central scar as equivalent. Safety check: Compare scar T2 signal, calcification, enhancement timing, and hepatobiliary contrast behavior. Discriminator: FNH has a T2-hyperintense scar that enhances late with extracellular contrast and a lesion that retains hepatobiliary agent; fibrolamellar HCC has a fibrotic T1/T2-hypointense scar and commonly a calcified scar. Why it happens: Both may be large hypervascular liver masses with a central scar.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: When a liver mass has a calcified central scar, how do you avoid mistaking giant hemangioma for fibrolamellar HCC?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Trap: Letting scar calcification alone decide the diagnosis. Safety check: Evaluate dynamic enhancement and T2 signal. Discriminator: Hemangioma shows peripheral discontinuous nodular enhancement matching blood pool with progressive fill-in and very bright T2 signal; fibrolamellar HCC is a heterogeneous tumor with a fibrotic scar rather than a blood-pool fill-in pattern. Why it happens: Both can be large masses with calcified central scar-like regions.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: What is the pseudo-scar trap in hepatic adenoma, and what should you check before calling FNH?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Trap: Calling any central nonenhancing or low-density focus a true scar. Safety check: Look for hemorrhage, necrosis, fibrosis, intracellular fat, and hepatobiliary/biliary-duct behavior. Discriminator: Adenoma heterogeneity commonly reflects fat, hemorrhage, necrosis, or fibrosis; FNH favors homogeneous arterial enhancement and hepatobiliary retention. Why it happens: Nonenhancing central material can visually imitate a scar.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: How can a large conventional HCC mimic fibrolamellar HCC, and which clues help separate them?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Trap: Assuming a large heterogeneous hypervascular HCC with central necrosis must be fibrolamellar. Safety check: Assess patient age/cirrhosis context, scar calcification, and venous invasion. Discriminator: Conventional HCC is favored by older/cirrhotic context and tumor-in-vein; fibrolamellar HCC favors a young noncirrhotic patient with a classic fibrotic often calcified scar. Why it happens: Both can be large, heterogeneous, hypervascular masses.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: What prevents a scar-like cholangiocarcinoma from being mistaken for FNH or fibrolamellar HCC?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Trap: Focusing only on the central scar-like region. Safety check: Inspect enhancement kinetics, capsule contour, bile ducts, and portal veins. Discriminator: Progressive delayed fibrotic enhancement, capsular retraction, peripheral biliary obstruction, portal venous obstruction, and volume loss favor cholangiocarcinoma. Why it happens: Central fibrosis or necrosis can simulate the scar of other liver masses.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: How do you avoid overcalling multiple hypervascular regenerative nodules in Budd-Chiari syndrome as multifocal HCC?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Trap: Treating arterial hyperenhancement alone as malignant. Safety check: Assess multiplicity, the global Budd-Chiari morphology, hepatobiliary-agent retention, and invasive behavior. Discriminator: Regenerative nodules may be numerous, scar-containing, and retain hepatobiliary agent because they contain functioning hepatocytes; chronic Budd-Chiari shows caudate hypertrophy and peripheral atrophy. Why it happens: Hypervascular regenerative nodules can closely mimic HCC.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For fibrolamellar HCC, what patient profile should materially raise it in the differential of a scar-containing liver mass?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Young patient without cirrhosis; AFP is typically not elevated. Exam pivot: In a young noncirrhotic patient with a large heterogeneous scar-containing mass, fibrolamellar HCC rises sharply over conventional HCC.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic adenoma, which clinical associations materially raise the pretest probability when evaluating a hypervascular liver mass?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Much more common in females, especially with prolonged oral contraceptive use; in males, association with anabolic steroid use. Exam pivot: These associations move adenoma upward when imaging shows a hypervascular lesion with fat or hemorrhage.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For conventional HCC, what clinical substrate should strongly raise the pretest probability of a hypervascular liver mass?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Cirrhosis is the major risk factor; chronic hepatitis B and fatty liver disease are additional important risks. Exam pivot: In a high-risk liver, a hypervascular mass with washout or tumor-in-vein should be treated as HCC until proven otherwise.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For a liver mass with a central or eccentric scar-like region, what compact imaging framework best organizes the differential?
fullOrganEntries.answer: 1) Scar calcification. 2) Dynamic enhancement of mass and scar. 3) Multiplicity. 4) Secondary clues: vascular invasion, biliary obstruction, capsular retraction, Budd-Chiari morphology. Exam pivot: These four buckets separate true scar lesions from necrosis/hemorrhage/fibrosis mimics.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For FNH, what CT contrast-phase pattern should be recognized?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Bright homogeneous arterial enhancement except for the central scar; later the lesion becomes isoattenuating to liver, with delayed scar enhancement around 5 minutes. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive. Recognition pivot: Homogeneous arterialization plus late scar enhancement is the classic CT pattern.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For FNH, what MRI and hepatobiliary-contrast pattern should be recognized?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Typically isointense to liver on routine MRI; central scar is subtly T2 hyperintense. Arterial hyperenhancement; delayed scar enhancement with extracellular agents. Hepatobiliary phase: lesion iso-/hyperintense from retained Eovist, while the scar does not retain it. Recognition pivot: Hepatobiliary retention strongly separates FNH from adenoma.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For FNH, what ultrasound and Doppler pattern should be recognized?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Ultrasound appearance is nonspecific; the central scar is rarely seen. Doppler may show a spoke-wheel configuration of arterial vessels. Imaging specificity: Nonspecific. Recognition pivot: Use Doppler as supportive, not definitive, evidence.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For FNH, what nuclear medicine behavior can help confirm the diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Tc-99m sulfur colloid may confirm Kupffer cells in about 1/3 of cases; HIDA can show bile-duct cell activity. Recognition pivot: Presence of Kupffer cells and bile ductules supports FNH over adenoma.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For cavernous hemangioma, what multiphasic CT/MRI enhancement pattern should be recognized?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Peripheral discontinuous nodular enhancement matching blood pool with progressive centripetal fill-in on later phases. Giant lesions may retain a central nonenhancing degenerative/fibrotic region. Imaging specificity: Diagnostic in the right context. Recognition pivot: Enhancement should behave like blood pool.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For cavernous hemangioma, what MRI T2 pattern should be recognized?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Typically T2 hyperintense and even more hyperintense on T2 fat-saturated imaging; giant lesions can have a very bright central region. Recognition pivot: Marked T2 brightness reinforces hemangioma when dynamic enhancement is classic.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For cavernous hemangioma, what ultrasound pattern should be recognized?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Circumscribed, homogeneously echogenic mass with no flow on color Doppler; posterior acoustic enhancement may be present. A hypoechoic halo/target sign should not be seen and suggests malignancy. Recognition pivot: Classic echogenic avascular morphology supports hemangioma in an otherwise normal liver.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: In a hepatic mass suspicious for HCC, which vascular finding must be explicitly inspected and reported?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Report-critical finding: Tumor-in-vein, especially portal venous invasion; internal enhancement or Doppler flow within thrombus supports tumor thrombus. Consequence: Confirms locally invasive behavior and changes staging/management. Report pivot: Always inspect the portal and hepatic veins/IVC.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic adenoma, what CT/MRI enhancement and heterogeneity pattern should be recognized?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Circumscribed arterial hyperenhancement, becoming iso- or hypoenhancing on portal venous/delayed phases. Heterogeneity may reflect fat or hemorrhage; a fibrous pseudocapsule may enhance late. Recognition pivot: Hypervascularity plus fat/hemorrhage raises adenoma, but imaging can remain nonspecific.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic adenoma, what chemical-shift MRI clue should be recognized?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Some adenomas contain intracellular lipid and show T1 hyperintensity with signal loss on out-of-phase images. Recognition pivot: Out-of-phase signal loss supports a fat-containing adenoma subtype and helps explain apparent central heterogeneity.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic adenoma, what nuclear medicine pattern helps distinguish it from FNH?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Adenomas are usually photopenic on Tc-99m sulfur colloid scintigraphy and generally lack HIDA uptake because they contain no bile ducts. Recognition pivot: FNH contains Kupffer cells and bile ductules; adenoma does not.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic adenoma, what size threshold changes management?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Incidentally discovered adenomas >5 cm are usually resected because of hemorrhage risk. Exam pivot: Size >5 cm is a management threshold, not just a descriptive measurement.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic metastases, what CT phase usually gives the best conspicuity?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Most metastases are hypovascular and are best appreciated on the portal venous phase as hypoattenuating masses. Recognition pivot: Portal venous phase is the default detection phase for most metastases, unlike hypervascular HCC.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic metastases, what MRI signal pattern should be recognized?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Typically T1 hypointense and T2 hyperintense; blood products and melanin can be T1 hyperintense. Recognition pivot: Use the pattern as a broad metastatic clue, then integrate enhancement and primary tumor context.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic metastases, what ultrasound pattern should be recognized?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Variable appearance; classic finding is a hypoechoic rim producing a target sign. Recognition pivot: A target lesion should raise malignancy/metastasis rather than classic hemangioma.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: Which primary or treatment contexts should make calcified liver metastases plausible?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Mucinous cancers including colon, gastric, and ovarian; osteosarcoma; treated lymphoma. Exam pivot: Central calcification in multiple liver lesions should raise mucinous metastases in the scar-mass differential.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For fibrolamellar HCC, what MRI scar pattern separates it from FNH?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Large heterogeneous mass with a classic fibrotic central scar that is hypointense on T1 and T2. FNH scar is T2 hyperintense and enhances late. Recognition pivot: T2-dark scar favors fibrolamellar HCC; T2-bright delayed-enhancing scar favors FNH.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For fibrolamellar HCC, what CT scar clue is especially important?
fullOrganEntries.answer: A large heterogeneous hypervascular mass with a large central scar; scar calcification strongly favors fibrolamellar HCC or giant hemangioma. Recognition pivot: In a young patient, a calcified central scar strongly raises fibrolamellar HCC.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For fibrolamellar HCC, what capsular contour finding can be seen?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Capsular retraction may be seen in 10% of cases. Exam pivot: Retraction does not exclude fibrolamellar HCC, but prominent biliary obstruction/progressive fibrosis should move cholangiocarcinoma upward.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For mass-forming intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, what contrast-enhancement pattern should be recognized?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Large relatively well-defined lobulated mass with delayed/progressive enhancement from fibrous stroma. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive with supporting findings. Recognition pivot: Progressive enhancement is the opposite of a blood-pool hemangioma pattern.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For mass-forming cholangiocarcinoma, which associated findings should be explicitly sought and reported?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Report-critical findings: peripheral biliary dilation/obstruction, capsular retraction, hepatic volume loss/lobar atrophy, and portal venous obstruction. Consequence: These findings support diagnosis and define local extent. Report pivot: Do not report the mass without mapping ductal and vascular obstruction.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, what CT/MRI pattern should be recognized?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Multiple spherical subcapsular/peripheral masses that may coalesce; halo/target appearance and capsular retraction are key clues. MRI: lesions are T1 hypointense and T2 hyperintense with peripheral target-pattern enhancement. Recognition pivot: Peripheral multiplicity plus retraction is the defining pattern.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, which contour change is a useful reportable clue?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Capsular retraction over subcapsular lesions is a characteristic clue. Report pivot: Mention retraction and peripheral coalescent distribution because they materially narrow the differential.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For chronic Budd-Chiari syndrome, what global liver morphology helps explain multiple regenerative nodules?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Chronic hepatic venous outflow obstruction produces caudate lobe hypertrophy, peripheral hepatic atrophy, and prominent regenerative nodules. Recognition pivot: Read the nodules in the context of venous-outflow morphology rather than treating each hypervascular nodule in isolation.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For large regenerative nodules in Budd-Chiari syndrome, what hepatobiliary MRI behavior supports benign regenerative tissue?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Persistent uptake/retention of gadobenate dimeglumine in the nodules indicates functioning hepatocytes; deficient biliary ducts help explain retention within the lesions. Recognition pivot: Hepatobiliary retention supports regenerative hepatocellular tissue rather than metastases.

fullOrganEntries.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
fullOrganEntries.question: For large regenerative nodules / NRH in Budd-Chiari, what multiplicity and size pattern should be recognized?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Multiacinar large regenerative nodules are usually multiple and less than 4 cm and may have central scars. Exam pivot: Numerous small-to-moderate scar-containing nodules in a Budd-Chiari liver should raise regenerative nodules before assuming multifocal malignancy.

fullOrganEntries.question: Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Uncomplicated simple hepatic cyst Mini-differential: Biliary cystadenoma/cystadenocarcinoma Hepatic abscess Cystic metastasis Key imaging findings: Homogeneous water-attenuation lesion with a smooth, nearly imperceptible wall and no debris or mural irregularity. Key differentiators: No enhancing solid tissue, thick wall, or mural nodule. Classic simple-fluid morphology supports a simple cyst.

fullOrganEntries.question: What complication of this large cyst should be reported?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Large hepatic cyst causing compression and obstruction of the intrahepatic bile ducts Mini-differential: Biliary cystic neoplasm Hepatic abscess Key imaging findings: Very large homogeneous cyst with adjacent intrahepatic ductal dilatation. Report-critical finding: Biliary compression/obstruction from mass effect. Benign fluid morphology does not exclude a clinically important complication.

fullOrganEntries.question: What accounts for the heterogeneous signal within these cysts on T2-weighted MRI?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hemorrhage within hepatic cysts Mini-differential: Hemorrhagic cyst Biliary cystic neoplasm Hepatic abscess Key imaging findings: Contiguous large cysts with areas of lower T2 signal than the remaining fluid. Key differentiator: Blood products explain the source-described signal complexity. This T2 image alone cannot exclude an enhancing neoplastic component; inspect the contrast-enhanced examination before classifying a complex cyst.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Polycystic liver disease; determine the hereditary subtype with clinical/family assessment Mini-differential: Biliary hamartomas Multiple simple hepatic cysts Caroli disease Key imaging findings: Innumerable water-attenuation cysts of varying size causing hepatomegaly; the caption describes only a few renal cysts and normal renal function. Key differentiators: Larger variable-size cysts favor polycystic liver disease over tiny irregular biliary hamartomas. Ductal communication favors Caroli disease. Imaging identifies the liver phenotype; renal and family/genetic assessment establish the syndrome.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Patient with subacute diverticulitis. Most likely diagnosis of this complex liver lesion?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hepatic pyogenic abscess Mini-differential: Cystic metastasis Amebic abscess Biliary cystic neoplasm Key imaging findings: Complex mass with innumerable septa and contents slightly higher than water attenuation; aspiration yielded pus. Key differentiators: Pyogenic abscess may ring-enhance and can show central T2 hyperintensity with restricted diffusion. Amebic abscess can be indistinguishable by imaging; cultures/clinical context may be required. Imaging specificity: Requires correlation.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/3 Image 2/3 Image 3/3 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Biliary hamartomas Mini-differential: Autosomal dominant polycystic liver disease Caroli disease Hepatic metastases Key imaging findings: Innumerable small, often irregular 2-15 mm CT lesions; smaller lesions are echogenic on US, while larger lesions appear cystic. MRCP shows noncommunicating T2-bright lesions. Key differentiators: Noncommunication argues against Caroli disease; a uniformly tiny lesion population favors hamartomas over the variable-size larger cysts of polycystic liver disease. Pitfall: The illustrated benign hamartomas have small enhancing wall nodules. Do not apply a solitary complex-cyst malignancy rule without considering the whole pattern.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Cystic hepatic metastasis (thyroid primary established in the source case) Mini-differential: Hepatic cyst Biliary cystadenoma/cystadenocarcinoma Hepatic abscess Key imaging findings: Multiple hypodense hepatic masses including a cystic lesion with a subtle mural nodule. Key differentiators: A mural nodule or enhancing solid component argues against a simple cyst and should raise neoplasm. Cystic metastases may occur from several primaries and after treatment. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive of neoplasm; primary-site correlation is required.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/2 Image 2/2 CT before and after treatment of a known gastric GIST. What explains the change in the hepatic lesion?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Metastatic gastric GIST with treatment-related cystic necrosis Mini-differential: Uncomplicated hepatic cyst Hepatic abscess Key imaging findings: A previously solid heterogeneous metastasis becomes cystic after imatinib (Gleevec) therapy in the source case. Interpretation pivot: Compare the two time points; treatment-related necrosis explains the change. A new fluid-like appearance does not reclassify a known metastasis as a benign cyst. Complete necrosis is the source case outcome, not a viability guarantee from a single CT image.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 What lesion category is favored, and can this CT establish the infectious cause?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hepatic abscess; amebic in the source case, but CT alone cannot distinguish amebic from pyogenic abscess Mini-differential: Hepatic pyogenic abscess Cystic metastasis Hydatid cyst Key imaging findings: Solitary shaggy encapsulated cystic mass with nonenhancing contents. Key differentiators: Amebic abscess is not reliably separable from pyogenic abscess by imaging alone; clinical presentation and serology are decisive in the described pattern. Imaging specificity: Requires correlation.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Three weeks after blunt traumatic liver laceration. What is the likely nature of this new collection?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Posttraumatic collection containing bile and blood Mini-differential: Hepatic cyst Hepatic abscess Cystic metastasis Key imaging findings: Lobulated cystic collection at the site of prior liver injury. Key differentiators: Trauma timing and comparison with prior CT favor a posttraumatic collection over a primary cystic neoplasm; CT appearance alone does not establish exact fluid composition. Outside clarification (NCI terminology): Biloma denotes collected bile; hematoma denotes collected blood; seroma denotes serous/clear fluid. The original caption incorrectly equates blood with seroma.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/2 Image 2/2 Liver transplant recipient. What complication does this pattern suggest, and which vessel requires evaluation?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Transplant biloma with suspected ischemic biliary injury; assess for hepatic artery thrombosis Mini-differential: Postoperative seroma Hepatic abscess Key imaging findings: Irregular cystic collections, dilated ducts, and peribiliary fluid in the allograft. Report-critical pivot: Assess hepatic arterial patency because hepatic artery thrombosis can cause biliary necrosis and biloma. The source cases had confirmed thrombosis; these fluid images alone do not prove the vascular diagnosis.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Febrile, immunosuppressed patient. What process is favored by these numerous small liver lesions?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Opportunistic hepatic microabscesses (candidiasis in the source case) Mini-differential: Other fungal microabscesses Mycobacterial infection Hepatic metastases Key imaging findings: Innumerable tiny hypodense hepatic lesions with irregular walls in a febrile immunosuppressed patient. Key differentiators: Clinical context favors opportunistic infection. Fungal and mycobacterial infections overlap; imaging alone cannot identify Candida. Microbiologic/clinical correlation is required.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Patient from an echinococcosis-endemic region of the Middle East. Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hepatic hydatid cyst Mini-differential: Biliary cystadenoma/cystadenocarcinoma Hepatic abscess Simple hepatic cyst Key imaging findings: Large multiseptate cystic masses containing peripheral daughter cysts. Key differentiator: Daughter cysts within a mother cyst, or a detached floating membrane, strongly support hydatid disease; exposure and serology support interpretation. Outside clarification (CDC): Scolices are microscopic parasitic structures, not the macroscopic daughter cysts seen on CT.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Biliary cystic neoplasm (biliary cystadenoma in the source case) Mini-differential: Biliary cystadenocarcinoma Hydatid cyst Hepatic abscess Key imaging findings: Large lobulated complex cystic mass with enhancing wall and septa. Key differentiators: Multiseptated architecture with enhancing wall/septa is typical for biliary cystic neoplasm. Cystadenoma and cystadenocarcinoma are not easily distinguished by imaging; mural nodules raise concern for malignant transformation. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive for biliary cystic neoplasm.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 A cystic hepatic lesion opacifies during ERCP, with surface nodularity in the ducts. What diagnosis is favored?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Intraductal biliary neoplasm (biliary IPMN in source terminology); associated cholangiocarcinoma was established in this case Mini-differential: Caroli disease Biliary cystadenoma/cystadenocarcinoma Simple hepatic cyst Key imaging findings: Dilated ducts and a cystic mass on CT; the source reports ERCP communication and intraductal surface nodularity. Key differentiator: Ductal communication plus nodularity favors intraductal neoplasm over simple cyst or uncomplicated Caroli disease. Invasive cholangiocarcinoma cannot be established from this CT image alone.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Woman with portal hypertension. Most likely explanation for these cyst-like liver lesions?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Caroli disease Mini-differential: Biliary hamartomas Autosomal dominant polycystic liver disease Multiple simple hepatic cysts Key imaging findings: Multiple cyst-like intrahepatic duct dilatations draped around central portal venous branches. Key differentiators: Communication with the biliary tree and the central-dot sign distinguish Caroli disease from noncommunicating cystic lesions. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive. Associated source finding: Congenital hepatic fibrosis accounts for the portal hypertension with splenomegaly and varices in this example.

fullOrganEntries.clinicalContext: Man with right upper quadrant pain YS4A3TOEWHKD
fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Aggressive cystic hepatic neoplasm with rupture (undifferentiated hepatic sarcoma in the source case) Mini-differential: Biliary cystic neoplasm Hepatic abscess Cystic metastasis Key imaging findings: Huge multiseptate cystic mass with enhancing peripheral components and intraperitoneal blood from capsular rupture. Key differentiators: Enhancing peripheral solid tissue and hemorrhagic rupture argue against a simple cyst and support aggressive neoplasm. Imaging specificity: Requires pathologic correlation. Report-critical finding: Hemoperitoneum from capsular rupture; the histologic tumor type requires pathology.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 29-year-old woman with a solid-appearing segment IV lesion on ultrasound; no enhancement on the complete MRI. Which cyst is suggested?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Ciliated hepatic foregut cyst Mini-differential: Simple hepatic cyst Biliary cystic neoplasm Hepatic abscess Key imaging findings: Segment 4 complex cystic-appearing mass on T2 MRI with no enhancement on other sequences; the lesion had appeared solid on ultrasound. Key differentiators: The US/MRI discrepancy is a pitfall; lack of enhancement supports a cystic lesion, but definitive diagnosis in the described case required resection. Imaging specificity: Requires correlation.

fullOrganEntries.question: Why do biliary hamartomas appear as multiple small cyst-like lesions that do not communicate with the biliary tree?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Abnormal development of small intrahepatic bile ducts leaves benign cystic ductal remnants disconnected from the functioning biliary tree. Imaging consequence: Numerous tiny, often irregular lesions; small lesions may be echogenic on US, and MRCP shows no biliary communication. Interpretation pivot: Noncommunication separates this pattern from the communicating ductal dilatation of Caroli disease.

fullOrganEntries.question: What anatomic mechanism produces the central-dot sign in Caroli disease?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Caroli disease is saccular dilatation of intrahepatic bile ducts around portal-tract branches. On contrast-enhanced imaging, an enhancing portal branch within a dilated duct produces the central-dot sign. Interpretation pivot: The dot together with ductal communication favors Caroli disease over noncommunicating cysts and biliary hamartomas.

fullOrganEntries.question: Why can treated hepatic GIST metastases become a cystic-mass pitfall on follow-up CT?
fullOrganEntries.answer: A solid metastatic GIST can undergo complete treatment-related necrosis. Necrotic tumor loses its prior solid appearance and becomes low-attenuation/cystic on CT. Imaging consequence: a previously solid metastasis may resemble a benign cyst after response. Interpretation pivot: compare with pretreatment imaging before calling a new cystic lesion benign.

fullOrganEntries.question: What is the main pitfall when innumerable small cyst-like liver lesions are seen, and how do you avoid confusing biliary hamartomas with Caroli disease or polycystic liver disease?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Trap: Treating every multicystic liver pattern as the same entity. Safety check: Assess lesion size/morphology, search for larger extrahepatic cysts, and determine whether the lesions communicate with the biliary tree. Discriminator: Biliary hamartomas are small and noncommunicating; Caroli disease is dilated communicating intrahepatic bile ducts; ADPLD is innumerable simple cysts and is supported by extrahepatic/familial evidence. Why it happens: all three can look like multiple hepatic cysts on cross-sectional imaging.

fullOrganEntries.question: How should known ADPKD change the interpretation of innumerable nonenhancing hepatic cysts?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Known ADPKD supports an associated polycystic liver phenotype rather than an unrelated multifocal tumor or infection. Interpretation pivot: Integrate the renal disease and family history with the simple-cyst morphology; do not rank innumerable cysts without that context. Outside clarification (NIDDK): Liver cysts are an extrarenal manifestation of ADPKD. The association does not by itself establish a separate isolated hereditary liver disorder.

fullOrganEntries.question: What age/sex pattern should increase the pretest likelihood of biliary cystadenoma when a solitary large multiseptated cystic liver mass is found?
fullOrganEntries.answer: A middle-aged woman with a solitary large multiseptated cystic mass and enhancing wall/septa has a pattern that raises concern for biliary cystic neoplasm. Pretest pivot: The demographic context helps rank the differential, but cannot distinguish benign from malignant histology.

fullOrganEntries.question: For a simple hepatic cyst, what CT appearance should be recognized?
fullOrganEntries.answer: CT: Homogeneous water attenuation (0-20 HU), a thin/nearly imperceptible wall, and no enhancement. Interpretation pivot: Thick enhancing wall, enhancing septa, or a true mural nodule requires characterization as a complex lesion; fluid attenuation alone is insufficient.

fullOrganEntries.question: What imaging pattern favors polycystic liver disease over biliary hamartomas?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Innumerable nonenhancing simple cysts of varying size, often including large cysts and causing hepatomegaly. Key differentiator: Biliary hamartomas are predominantly tiny and often irregular; Caroli disease communicates with the biliary tree. Correlate renal findings and family history to classify the hereditary syndrome.

fullOrganEntries.question: Which MRI feature supports pus within a suspected hepatic abscess?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Central T2 hyperintensity with restricted diffusion can support purulent content. Interpretation pivot: Combine this with a complex/rim-enhancing lesion and infection context; restriction alone is not sufficient to exclude necrotic tumor.

fullOrganEntries.question: For biliary hamartomas, what CT appearance should be recognized?
fullOrganEntries.answer: CT: Innumerable tiny, often irregular cyst-like lesions; the illustrated case spans 2-15 mm and includes small enhancing wall nodules. Interpretation pivot: Assess the full tiny-lesion distribution and MRCP noncommunication before assuming mural nodularity means malignant cystic masses. The nodular wall appearance is a described variant, not a required finding.

fullOrganEntries.question: For biliary hamartomas, what ultrasound appearance should be recognized?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Ultrasound: larger lesions can appear cystic, while smaller lesions may be hyperechoic to the liver. Recognition pivot: tiny echogenic lesions do not exclude a cystic biliary hamartoma process. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive in the correct multimodality pattern.

fullOrganEntries.question: For biliary hamartomas, what MRCP finding separates them from Caroli disease?
fullOrganEntries.answer: MRCP: innumerable small T2-hyperintense lesions that do not communicate with the biliary tree. Key differentiator: noncommunication favors biliary hamartomas; Caroli disease is dilated intrahepatic bile ducts that communicate. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive.

fullOrganEntries.question: In a cystic hepatic lesion, what CT finding should make metastatic or other neoplastic disease a leading concern?
fullOrganEntries.answer: A true mural nodule or enhancing solid component in an otherwise cystic mass raises concern for neoplasm; multiple lesions or a known cancer history increase concern for metastases. Pitfall: Nodularity does not establish a primary site or prove malignancy. The source also illustrates tiny biliary hamartomas with enhancing wall nodules.

fullOrganEntries.question: In a liver allograft, what cystic/biliary finding is report-critical because it should raise concern for hepatic artery thrombosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Biloma, peribiliary fluid, and/or biliary necrosis in the allograft should prompt assessment of hepatic arterial patency. Report pivot: Hepatic artery thrombosis is a consequential cause of ischemic biliary injury in this setting. Report the arterial assessment rather than attributing all postoperative fluid to an uncomplicated collection.

fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic fungal microabscesses/candidiasis, what CT/MRI pattern should be recognized?
fullOrganEntries.answer: CT: Innumerable tiny hypoenhancing lesions. MRI may show T2 hyperintensity and diffusion restriction. Interpretation pivot: In a febrile immunocompromised patient, this pattern favors opportunistic microabscesses. Imaging does not reliably identify the organism; absence of a particular MR feature does not exclude infection.

fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic fungal microabscesses, what ultrasound pattern should be recognized?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Multiple tiny hypoechoic liver lesions. Interpretation pivot: In a febrile immunocompromised patient this raises opportunistic microabscesses, but the US pattern is nonspecific and requires clinical/microbiologic correlation.

fullOrganEntries.question: Which cross-sectional imaging features favor hydatid disease over a simple hepatic cyst?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Daughter cysts within a mother cyst and/or a detached floating membrane; a peripheral cyst wall may calcify. Interpretation pivot: These internal structures, combined with exposure history, favor echinococcal disease over an uncomplicated simple cyst. Their absence does not establish a benign simple cyst.

fullOrganEntries.question: What produces the water-lily sign in a hepatic hydatid cyst?
fullOrganEntries.answer: A detached endocyst membrane floats or undulates within the cyst fluid. Interpretation pivot: A floating membrane supports hydatid disease rather than a simple hepatic cyst; it is distinct from fine echogenic hydatid sand. Outside clarification: The membrane definition is corroborated by the cystic-liver imaging review cited in the audit report.

fullOrganEntries.question: On ultrasound, how is hydatid sand different from daughter cysts or a floating membrane?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hydatid sand appears as fine internal echoes that may become more apparent with patient repositioning; daughter cysts are separate cystic structures, and a detached membrane produces the water-lily sign. Outside clarification (CDC and cystic-liver imaging review): Sand contains microscopic protoscolices and hooklets, not merely detached membrane sediment. This distinction prevents conflating three different hydatid signs.

fullOrganEntries.question: For biliary intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasm, what imaging feature proves that a cystic-appearing lesion is ductal in origin?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Demonstrated communication with the bile ducts, such as filling of the cystic component during ERCP, establishes a ductal connection. Key differentiator: Associated intraductal nodularity raises concern for an intraductal biliary neoplasm. Communication alone also occurs in Caroli disease and does not prove carcinoma.

fullOrganEntries.question: When HCC undergoes spontaneous or treatment necrosis and looks cystic, what residual imaging behavior points back to HCC?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Residual solid components that arterially hyperenhance and then wash out on portal venous/delayed imaging. Recognition pivot: a cystic/necrotic lesion with this viable solid enhancement pattern should not be mistaken for a benign cyst. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive in the appropriate liver-risk context.

fullOrganEntries.question: What ultrasound pitfall is described for ciliated hepatic foregut cyst?
fullOrganEntries.answer: It can appear complex or solid on US despite a nonenhancing cystic appearance on MRI, as in the segment IV source case. Interpretation pivot: Compare modalities and enhancement before assuming an apparently solid US lesion is a solid tumor. This pattern suggests a foregut cyst but does not establish its histology.

fullOrganEntries.question: Why is prior imaging especially important when evaluating a cystic hepatic mass?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Simple cysts usually change slowly, abscesses can change rapidly, and treated tumors can become cystic through necrosis. Recognition pivot: interval behavior can reclassify a lesion that is otherwise morphologically ambiguous on a single study.

fullOrganEntries.question: Why can an undifferentiated hepatic sarcoma appear solid on US but cystic on CT or MRI?
fullOrganEntries.answer: The article attributes the discordant appearance to myxoid stroma within a solid tumor. Outside clarification (radiologic-pathologic correlation): The high water content of this stroma produces low CT attenuation and high T2 signal despite solid tumor tissue. Interpretation pivot: Solid US appearance with fluid-like CT/MRI appearance and enhancing peripheral tissue should raise concern for neoplasm; pathology establishes the tumor type.

fullOrganEntries.question: How can the expected course of an uninfected posttraumatic or postprocedural hepatic collection affect interpretation?
fullOrganEntries.answer: The article notes that these collections may take weeks to months to resolve and may not require drainage when uninfected. Interpretation pivot: Persistence alone is not proof of tumor or infection; interpret interval change with the injury/procedure history and clinical state. This observation is not a blanket rule for symptomatic or complicated collections.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hepatic Cavernous Hemangioma Mini-differential: Focal Nodular Hyperplasia Hepatic Adenoma Hypervascular Hepatic Metastases Key imaging findings: Two hyperenhancing dome lesions with adjacent THAD and venous-phase contrast retention. Key differentiators: Small flash-filling hemangiomas may enhance rapidly and homogeneously, but their enhanced portions remain nearly isodense to blood vessels across phases. FNH instead blends toward liver on portal/delayed phases; HCC or metastases do not characteristically remain blood-pool equivalent. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/3 Image 2/3 Image 3/3 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hepatic Cavernous Hemangioma Mini-differential: Focal Nodular Hyperplasia Hepatic Adenoma Arterioportal Shunt Key imaging findings: The same small lesion remains isodense to blood pool on NECT, arterial, and portal venous CT. Key differentiators: Blood-pool matching across phases is the key hemangioma clue. FNH becomes nearly isodense to liver outside the arterial phase, whereas arterioportal shunts are perfusion phenomena that normalize to liver rather than a persistent blood-pool-equivalent mass. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Focal Nodular Hyperplasia Mini-differential: Hepatic Adenoma Hepatocellular Carcinoma Hepatic Cavernous Hemangioma Key imaging findings: Cloud-like arterial hyperenhancement with imperceptible blending into liver on portal venous phase; no visible scar in this example. Key differentiators: FNH is a stealth lesion outside the arterial phase. Adenoma is usually more heterogeneous and may contain fat, necrosis, or hemorrhage; HCC typically washes out to hypoattenuation; hemangioma follows blood pool rather than background liver. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/2 Image 2/2 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Focal Nodular Hyperplasia Mini-differential: Hepatic Adenoma Fibrolamellar Hepatocellular Carcinoma Hepatocellular Carcinoma Key imaging findings: Homogeneous arterial enhancement, near-isointensity to liver on portal venous MRI, and a persistent small central scar. Key differentiators: FNH typically returns toward background liver signal after the arterial phase. Fibrolamellar HCC is usually large and heterogeneous with a fibrotic scar; adenoma may be heterogeneous from fat or hemorrhage. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/2 Image 2/2 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Focal Nodular Hyperplasia Mini-differential: Fibrolamellar Hepatocellular Carcinoma Hepatic Adenoma Hepatocellular Carcinoma Key imaging findings: Arterial hypervascular mass with central scar that becomes isodense to liver on portal venous phase. Key differentiators: Portal-phase blending with background liver strongly supports FNH. Fibrolamellar HCC is typically large and heterogeneous and commonly has a calcified fibrotic scar; HCC more characteristically washes out to hypoattenuation. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Focal Nodular Hyperplasia Mini-differential: Hepatic Adenoma Hepatocellular Carcinoma Arteriovenous Malformation Key imaging findings: Homogeneous arterial hypervascularity, central scar, early draining veins, and isodensity to liver on other phases. Key differentiators: This combination matches the FNH vascular/hemodynamic pattern. Adenoma is usually more heterogeneous; HCC classically demonstrates washout; pure vascular shunts lack a true FNH-type mass architecture. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Arterioportal Shunt Mini-differential: Hepatocellular Carcinoma Transient Hepatic Attenuation Difference Focal Nodular Hyperplasia Key imaging findings: Arterial left-lobe hyperenhancement that normalizes on portal venous phase with early filling of the left portal vein. Key differentiators: Early portal-branch opacification is a key sign of arterioportal shunting. HCC is a true mass and more typically shows arterial enhancement with washout rather than transient perfusion change. Imaging specificity: Diagnostic in the stated procedural context.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Arterioportal Shunt Mini-differential: Hepatocellular Carcinoma Transient Hepatic Attenuation Difference Hepatic Metastases Key imaging findings: Multiple peripheral wedge-shaped arterial hyperenhancing foci with no corresponding venous-phase abnormality. Key differentiators: Shape, peripheral distribution, and complete disappearance on later phase favor arterioportal shunts over HCC or metastases, which are true masses. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Arterioportal Shunt Mini-differential: Hepatocellular Carcinoma Focal Nodular Hyperplasia Transient Hepatic Attenuation Difference Key imaging findings: Small arterial-only hypervascular focus, described as absent on NECT and portal venous images. Key differentiators: Small arterioportal shunts in cirrhosis are often ≤1.5 cm and may disappear on later phases. Peripheral wedge-shaped geometry, no corresponding precontrast T1/T2 abnormality, and early portal-branch filling favor shunting when present. Imaging specificity: Suggestive in the supplied case; arterial hyperenhancement alone does not establish HCC or a shunt.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Arterioportal Shunt Mini-differential: Hepatocellular Carcinoma Transient Hepatic Attenuation Difference Hepatic Metastases Key imaging findings: Peripheral capsular-based wedge-shaped arterial hypervascular foci that disappear on venous and delayed imaging. Key differentiators: A straight/wedge perfusion geometry and transient phase behavior favor arterioportal shunts over round true masses such as HCC or metastases. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/2 Image 2/2 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Transient Hepatic Attenuation Difference Mini-differential: Arterioportal Shunt Hepatocellular Carcinoma Hypervascular Hepatic Metastases Key imaging findings: Peripheral wedge-shaped arterial hyperperfusion that normalizes on portal phase, with portal-phase spherical metastases causing the perfusion abnormality. Key differentiators: THAD is a transient perfusion effect rather than a true mass. Larger or segmental THAD should prompt a search for a lesion compressing or occluding a portal branch. Imaging specificity: Diagnostic as a perfusion phenomenon when phase normalization and the causal portal-flow abnormality are demonstrated.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hepatocellular Carcinoma Mini-differential: Arterioportal Shunt Hepatic Adenoma Hypervascular Hepatic Metastases Key imaging findings: Heterogeneous arterial hyperenhancement with portal-venous washout to hypoattenuation. Key differentiators: HCC is a true mass with washout; arterioportal shunts are usually wedge-shaped and disappear on later phases. In the appropriate at-risk liver, the classic arterial-enhancement/washout pattern strongly favors HCC. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive in the supplied cirrhotic patient.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hepatocellular Carcinoma Mini-differential: Arterioportal Shunt Hepatic Adenoma Fibrolamellar Hepatocellular Carcinoma Key imaging findings: T2 hyperintensity, diffusion restriction, arterial hyperenhancement, venous washout, and capsular enhancement. Key differentiators: The combination of arterialization, washout, capsule, and diffusion restriction is a classic HCC pattern in an at-risk liver. Shunts lack a true mass and corresponding T2/DWI abnormality. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive in the supplied cirrhotic patient.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/2 Image 2/2 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hepatocellular Carcinoma Mini-differential: Hypervascular Hepatic Metastases Hepatic Adenoma Fibrolamellar Hepatocellular Carcinoma Key imaging findings: Large mass with mosaic arterial hypervascular enhancement and internal necrosis; much of the mass becomes isodense on portal phase. Key differentiators: The STATdx caption identifies mosaic hypervascular architecture as typical of a large HCC. This case shows that a large HCC need not display uniform visible washout on every supplied slice; internal necrosis and heterogeneous arterialization remain important clues. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hepatic Metastases Mini-differential: Hepatocellular Carcinoma Hepatic Adenoma Focal Nodular Hyperplasia Key imaging findings: Innumerable hypervascular liver lesions, some with ring enhancement. Key differentiators: Multiplicity, heterogeneity, and ring enhancement favor metastatic disease. The source specifically highlights endocrine/neuroendocrine, melanoma, and renal cell carcinoma as common hypervascular primaries. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hepatic Metastases Mini-differential: Hepatocellular Carcinoma Hepatic Adenoma Focal Nodular Hyperplasia Key imaging findings: Hypervascular hepatic lesions with a simultaneously visible hypervascular pancreatic neuroendocrine primary. Key differentiators: A hypervascular extrahepatic primary plus multifocal hepatic lesions strongly supports metastases rather than multiple primary benign liver masses. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/2 Image 2/2 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hepatic Adenoma Mini-differential: Focal Nodular Hyperplasia Hepatocellular Carcinoma Hepatic Angiomyolipoma Key imaging findings: Arterial hypervascularity with a capsule and relative hypointensity on the supplied delayed gadoxetate image. Key differentiators: Adenoma can be heterogeneous from fat, necrosis, or hemorrhage. Typical FNH shows homogeneous arterial enhancement and returns toward background liver on portal images. Gadoxetate hepatobiliary retention is a separate supportive FNH discriminator, but this source labels the second image only as delayed. Imaging specificity: Supports adenoma in this source case. Inflammatory subtype is the reported final diagnosis; these two images alone do not establish subtype.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/2 Image 2/2 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hereditary Hemorrhagic Telangiectasia Mini-differential: Arteriovenous Malformation Arterioportal Shunt Focal Nodular Hyperplasia Key imaging findings: Heterogeneous arterial-phase liver enhancement, enlarged tortuous hepatic arteries, early opacification of enlarged hepatic veins/IVC, and homogeneous portal-phase liver. Key differentiators: This is a diffuse hepatic vascular-shunting pattern rather than a focal mass. The article also notes marked enrichment of FNH in HHT. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive in the appropriate multisystem/family context.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/2 Image 2/2 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Nodular Regenerative Hyperplasia Mini-differential: Hepatocellular Carcinoma Focal Nodular Hyperplasia Arterioportal Shunt Key imaging findings: Multiple small arterial hypervascular nodules with persistent portal-phase hypervascularity in a liver with IVC occlusion, ascites, and collaterals. Key differentiators: In chronic Budd-Chiari, prominent regenerative nodules are expected and may resemble FNH. Persistent enhancement and the venous-outflow-obstruction context help avoid overcalling multifocal HCC. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive with vascular-context correlation.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/2 Image 2/2 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Nodular Regenerative Hyperplasia Mini-differential: Hepatocellular Carcinoma Focal Nodular Hyperplasia Arterioportal Shunt Key imaging findings: Multiple arterial hypervascular nodules, some with hypointense halos, and persistent portal-phase hyperintensity. Key differentiators: Persistent portal enhancement in Budd-Chiari supports large regenerative nodules. Interpret the nodules alongside hepatic venous outflow obstruction and collateral vessels before favoring multifocal HCC. Imaging specificity: Requires correlation with the vascular background.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/2 Image 2/2 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Fibrolamellar Hepatocellular Carcinoma Mini-differential: Focal Nodular Hyperplasia Hepatocellular Carcinoma Mass-forming Cholangiocarcinoma Key imaging findings: Large lobulated heterogeneous hypervascular mass with a large calcified central scar in a young patient without a cirrhotic-appearing liver. Key differentiators: Fibrolamellar HCC occurs in young patients without cirrhosis and classically has a fibrotic central scar; calcification within the scar is a major separator from typical FNH. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/2 Image 2/2 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Cholangiocarcinoma (Peripheral) Mini-differential: Hepatocellular Carcinoma Hepatic Cavernous Hemangioma Fibrolamellar Hepatocellular Carcinoma Key imaging findings: Large mass and porta-hepatis nodes with arterial hypervascular foci and heterogeneous persistent delayed enhancement that becomes hyperdense to liver and blood vessels. Key differentiators: Mass-forming cholangiocarcinoma classically demonstrates delayed/progressive enhancement. Unlike hemangioma, the delayed enhancing components do not simply track blood pool; capsular retraction is an additional article clue. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive; pathology confirmed the supplied case.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Hepatic Angiomyolipoma Mini-differential: Hepatic Adenoma Hepatocellular Carcinoma Key imaging findings: Hypervascular hepatic mass containing foci of macroscopic fat, with similar renal angiomyolipomas. Key differentiators: Nonfatty portions of hepatic AML are hypervascular; only about half show macroscopic fat on CT, so fat is highly helpful when present but its absence does not exclude AML. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive in this cross-organ context.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/1 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Angiosarcoma, Liver Mini-differential: Hepatic Cavernous Hemangioma Hypervascular Hepatic Metastases Peliosis Hepatis Key imaging findings: Multiple liver masses with peculiar eccentric enhancement and hypervascular foci; similar splenic lesions were described. Key differentiators: The article emphasizes bizarre enhancement that may resemble hemangioma and multifocal liver/spleen disease. This pattern is not specific enough for imaging-only certainty. Imaging specificity: Requires correlation.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/2 Image 2/2 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Superior Vena Cava Obstruction, Abdominal Manifestations Mini-differential: Transient Hepatic Attenuation Difference Arterioportal Shunt Focal Nodular Hyperplasia Key imaging findings: Bright left-lobe arterial enhancement with chest-wall/capsular collaterals and direct demonstration of SVC occlusion; the liver becomes homogeneous on venous phase. Key differentiators: This is collateral-driven pseudolesional enhancement without mass effect, not a true hypervascular tumor. Imaging specificity: Diagnostic when the obstructed SVC and collateral pathway are shown.

fullOrganEntries.question: Image 1/2 Image 2/2 Most likely diagnosis?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Peliosis Hepatis Mini-differential: Hepatic Cavernous Hemangioma Angiosarcoma, Liver Hypervascular Hepatic Metastases Key imaging findings: Continuous ring enhancement on arterial phase with progressive fill-in on later contrast imaging. Key differentiators: Peliosis may mimic hemangioma, but the supplied source emphasizes continuous/ring-like enhancement versus the classic discontinuous nodular peripheral enhancement of hemangioma. Imaging specificity: Nonspecific to strongly suggestive depending on the complete clinical/imaging context.

fullOrganEntries.question: Why does a THAD appear as arterial-phase hyperenhancement that disappears on portal venous imaging?
fullOrganEntries.answer: A THAD is a perfusion phenomenon caused by reduced portal venous inflow to a territory, commonly from obstruction or compression of a portal vein branch. Compensatory increased arterial flow makes the involved wedge of liver transiently hyperenhancing on arterial phase. Once portal venous enhancement equilibrates, the area becomes isodense to background liver; the key interpretation pivot is that there is no true persistent mass.

fullOrganEntries.question: In HHT, which additional diagnosis should be considered for a focal FNH-like hypervascular hepatic mass?
fullOrganEntries.answer: Focal nodular hyperplasia. The article reports markedly increased FNH prevalence in HHT (about 100-fold); this raises FNH in the differential when a focal mass has the matching enhancement pattern. Do not assume every HHT hepatic finding is simply diffuse shunting.

fullOrganEntries.question: For a suspected hepatic hemangioma, what unenhanced MRI signal feature is supportive?
fullOrganEntries.answer: T2 hyperintensity supports hemangioma when the dynamic enhancement pattern also matches blood pool. T2 brightness alone is not specific.

fullOrganEntries.question: For hepatic cavernous hemangioma, what ultrasound pattern should be recognized?
