candidates.question: What is cavernous transformation of the portal vein?
candidates.answer: Network of collateral venous channels replacing chronically thrombosed portal vein. example of case Cavernous transformation of portal vein | Radiology Case | Radiopaedia.org

candidates.question: Why can blunt impact larger than the orbital aperture produce an internal orbital blowout fracture?
candidates.answer: A large blunt object compresses the orbital contents and transmits force to the thin internal orbital walls. The favored hydraulic mechanism is acute rise in intraorbital pressure from compressed orbital contents; the alternative buckling mechanism is direct transmission of impact along the orbital walls. Either mechanism can fracture the orbital floor or medial wall, producing internal wall deformity with possible herniation of orbital fat or extraocular muscle through the defect. This is why CT shows floor or medial wall failure even when the orbital rim may be spared.

candidates.question: Why do parapelvic and peripelvic renal sinus cysts produce different effects on the collecting system?
candidates.answer: The key difference is the site of origin and growth pattern within the renal sinus. Parapelvic cysts are essentially simple renal cortical/parenchymal cysts that protrude or herniate into the renal sinus. Because they behave like a focal mass entering the sinus from adjacent parenchyma, they tend to be solitary and produce localized displacement/distortion of sinus structures rather than diffuse stretching of the infundibula and calyces. Peripelvic cysts are thought to be lymphatic in origin and arise within the renal sinus itself. Because they are typically multiple, confluent, and noncommunicating, they track alongside the pelvocalyceal system and can parallel, elongate, and stretch the infundibula/calyces rather than acting like one focal protruding cyst. Imaging pivot: this origin-based difference explains why a solitary sinus cyst without infundibular stretching favors a parapelvic cyst, whereas multiple sinus cysts that parallel/stretch the collecting system favor peripelvic cysts.

cards.question: Why can periportal edema be a normal early finding after liver transplantation?
cards.answer: Liver transplantation disrupts normal hepatic lymphatic channels. While lymphatic connections reform, transiently impaired lymphatic drainage can allow fluid to accumulate in the periportal interstitium. Imaging consequence: a periportal low-density collar may persist for weeks after transplantation and, by itself, does not imply allograft injury or rejection. The interpretation changes when separate vascular or biliary complications are present.

candidates.question: Why does the normal pineal gland enhance after contrast administration?
candidates.answer: The pineal gland lacks a blood-brain barrier, so it normally enhances after contrast administration. Its vascular supply is primarily from the medial posterior choroidal artery arising from P2 branches.

candidates.question: Why can FAST or DPL be falsely negative in splenic trauma?
candidates.answer: Source-stated limitation: 29% of all patients and 40% of children with splenic injury may not have hemoperitoneum. Exam pivot: A negative FAST/DPL does not exclude splenic injury, especially in children; CECT is the best diagnostic tool when clinical concern persists.

candidates.question: What Milan criteria are listed in the source for liver transplant in hepatocellular carcinoma?
candidates.answer: Single tumor 2-5 cm or 3 tumors Exam pivot: This is the source-stated transplant selection threshold and is a classic management-style board fact.

candidates.question: Why can a pseudoaneurysm after splenic trauma rupture if untreated?
candidates.answer: Core describes pseudoaneurysm as injury to the intima and media of the arterial wall, with rupture contained only by the adventitia. Because the normal arterial wall layers are disrupted and the containment is incomplete, the lesion remains a high-risk contained vascular injury rather than a stable hematoma. The imaging pivot is that a rounded contrast collection should not be dismissed as simple clot; it may require angiographic treatment even when not actively enlarging on delayed CT.

candidates.question: Why can the site of maximal tenderness be misleading in appendicitis?
candidates.answer: The inflamed portion (often the tip) may lie distant from the cecal tip, shifting pain localization.

candidates.question: What does peripheral rim enhancement in a hypovascular liver metastasis represent according to the source?
candidates.answer: It indicates vascularized viable tumor in the periphery and a hypovascular or necrotic center; rim enhancement may also reflect compressed normal parenchyma. Exam pivot: Rim-enhancing metastases are not simple cystic lesions, and the rim should be interpreted as viable tumor or compressed liver rather than a benign wall.

candidates.question: Why can orbital roof fractures produce both orbital and intracranial findings?
candidates.answer: The orbital roof is simultaneously the ceiling of the orbit and the floor of the anterior cranial fossa. A fracture can displace fragments inferiorly into the orbit or superiorly toward the cranial fossa and can create communication between the orbit and intracranial compartment. This explains why CT review must include the globe, retrobulbar hematoma, extraocular muscles, proptosis, optic canal/orbital apex region, pneumocephalus, and intracranial hemorrhage.

candidates.question: Why does periosteal entrapment cause persistent physeal widening and raise concern for growth arrest?
candidates.answer: The periosteum is tightly attached at the physis. In a displaced physeal fracture, periosteum can become interposed in the widened physeal gap instead of lying outside the fracture. This mechanical interposition prevents complete reduction, so persistent physeal widening greater than 3 mm after reduction suggests entrapment. Imaging consequence: MRI may show low-signal periosteum, ligament, or tendon trapped in the fracture; clinically this can require open reduction and is associated with higher likelihood of subsequent growth arrest.

candidates.question: Why does periosteal entrapment cause persistent physeal widening and raise concern for growth arrest?
candidates.answer: The periosteum is tightly attached at the physis. In a displaced physeal fracture, periosteum can become interposed in the widened physeal gap instead of lying outside the fracture. This mechanical interposition prevents complete reduction, so persistent physeal widening greater than 3 mm after reduction suggests entrapment. Imaging consequence: MRI may show low-signal periosteum, ligament, or tendon trapped in the fracture; clinically this can require open reduction and is associated with higher likelihood of subsequent growth arrest.

candidates.question: Why can early CT underestimate or miss pancreatic necrosis?
candidates.answer: Normal substrate: Imaging can only depict necrosis once enough perfusion failure and tissue devitalization have evolved to create a detectable enhancement abnormality. Primary insult: Severe pancreatitis evolves dynamically over time rather than reaching its full destructive extent immediately at presentation. Cellular / microanatomic consequence: Early after symptom onset, acinar injury, edema, and inflammatory hyperemia may already be present, but the full extent of microvascular collapse and irreversible tissue death may not yet be established. Propagation step: Ongoing enzyme-mediated injury, vascular compromise, and inflammatory amplification convert initially viable but injured tissue into frankly nonviable necrotic tissue over the next several days. Gross / mesoscopic pathologic consequence: The gland may initially appear only edematous or only subtly hypoenhancing, then later show far more extensive necrosis. Imaging manifestation: Early CT can therefore miss or underestimate necrosis, whereas repeat imaging after biologic evolution shows clearer nonenhancing devitalized tissue. Board pivot: This is a timing/biology problem, not merely a scanner problem; a negative early CT does not reliably exclude later-proven necrosis.

candidates.question: What report element should be included for traumatic splenic injury?
candidates.answer: Include the AAST-OIS splenic injury grade in reports detailing splenic traumatic injury. Exam pivot: The grade communicates injury severity and helps guide management, especially when vascular injury is present.

candidates.question: Why can partial or intermittent torsion have normal, decreased, absent, or even increased Doppler flow?
candidates.answer: Partial twist: Incomplete torsion may obstruct venous outflow and diastolic arterial flow without fully eliminating systolic inflow, so color flow can persist but be asymmetric. Intermittent twist: The cord may untwist before imaging, restoring perfusion. Reperfusion: Post-detorsion reactive hyperemia can temporarily increase flow and mimic orchitis. Imaging result: Side-to-side color and spectral comparison may reveal reduced velocity, high resistance, or absent diastolic flow during pain, while a direct whirlpool sign can remain the decisive clue.

cards.question: Why can hepatic-artery stenosis or thrombosis cause biliary necrosis and intrahepatic bilomas after liver transplantation?
cards.answer: The bile ducts depend on hepatic arterial perfusion. When the hepatic artery is severely stenosed or thrombosed, ischemic injury can affect the biliary tree before diffuse hepatic infarction develops. Duct walls become indistinct or necrotic and bile can leak into intrahepatic collections, producing bilomas. Imaging consequence: biliary necrosis, irregular/dilated ducts, and bilomas in a liver allograft should trigger assessment of hepatic arterial patency.

candidates.question: Why can pneumatosis cystoides intestinalis cause pneumoperitoneum in an asymptomatic patient?
candidates.answer: Cystic intramural gas collections can rupture, releasing gas into the peritoneal cavity; despite a concerning CT appearance, the underlying process can be benign and patients may be asymptomatic.

candidates.question: Why does chronic deep vein thrombosis become echogenic and contracted, and sometimes appear as a fibrous cord or calcified scar?
candidates.answer: In chronic DVT, thrombus that does not fully lyse is progressively organized into fibrous tissue. The article states that postthrombotic thrombus is invaded by fibroblasts and becomes organized as scar, with wall thickening, reduced luminal diameter, echogenic intraluminal material, synechiae, and sometimes a fibrous cord when recanalization fails. Some chronic scar may calcify. This tissue transformation explains why chronic thrombus no longer looks like the distended low-echo clot of acute DVT; instead, the vein becomes smaller, thicker walled, and more echogenic. The imaging pivot is that echogenic contracted venous abnormality favors chronic organized postthrombotic change over acute fresh clot.

candidates.question: Why does hepatic steatosis lose signal on opposed-phase GRE MRI?
candidates.answer: In steatosis, intracellular fat and water contribute signal within the same imaging voxel. Their signals add on the in-phase acquisition and partially cancel on the opposed-phase acquisition, producing signal loss. The comparison supports microscopic fat in the liver; the surrounding morphology and absence of mass effect help establish steatosis rather than a fat-containing mass.

candidates.question: Why can hepatic lymphoma encase hepatic vessels yet preserve vessel patency and cause little vascular distortion?
candidates.answer: The article repeatedly describes lymphoma as a soft infiltrative process that can surround portal or hepatic vascular structures without causing the aggressive invasion, thrombosis, or distortion expected from many epithelial malignancies. Because the tumor tends to track as pliable infiltrative soft tissue rather than destroy or obstruct the vessel wall, vessels may remain patent and can even be seen penetrating the mass. This explains the classic imaging clue of vascular encasement with preservation of flow and contour.

candidates.question: What Milan criteria are listed in the source for liver transplant in hepatocellular carcinoma?
candidates.answer: Single tumor 2-5 cm or 3 tumors Exam pivot: This is the source-stated transplant selection threshold and is a classic management-style board fact.

candidates.question: What sonographic threshold defines extrahepatic biliary ductal dilatation?
candidates.answer: Extrahepatic biliary ductal dilatation is defined as common hepatic/common bile duct > 6-7 mm or > 40% of the diameter of the adjacent portal vein. Exam pivot: These are the article’s explicit size criteria for abnormal extrahepatic duct dilatation and help separate a truly enlarged duct from a normal-caliber extrahepatic bile duct.

candidates.question: When HCC undergoes spontaneous or treatment necrosis and looks cystic, what residual imaging behavior points back to HCC?
candidates.answer: Residual solid components that arterially hyperenhance and then wash out on portal venous/delayed imaging. Recognition pivot: a cystic/necrotic lesion with this viable solid enhancement pattern should not be mistaken for a benign cyst. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive in the appropriate liver-risk context.

candidates.question: Why does occlusive portal vein thrombosis produce absent Doppler flow and faint intraluminal echoes on ultrasound?
candidates.answer: When thrombus fills the portal-vein lumen, normal moving blood is replaced by relatively static clot material, so there is little or no detectable forward venous signal on color or spectral Doppler. Because the lumen is occupied by thrombus rather than freely flowing blood, the vein may also contain visible internal echoes on grayscale US. In acute thrombosis the vein may be enlarged as thrombus fills the lumen; with more chronic occlusion the vein may become small, echogenic, or difficult to see. The imaging pivot is that true luminal thrombus explains the combination of absent flow plus intraluminal material, whereas very slow flow can mimic the first feature but does not create a truly thrombosed lumen.

candidates.question: Why can partial or intermittent torsion have normal, decreased, absent, or even increased Doppler flow?
candidates.answer: Partial twist: Incomplete torsion may obstruct venous outflow and diastolic arterial flow without fully eliminating systolic inflow, so color flow can persist but be asymmetric. Intermittent twist: The cord may untwist before imaging, restoring perfusion. Reperfusion: Post-detorsion reactive hyperemia can temporarily increase flow and mimic orchitis. Imaging result: Side-to-side color and spectral comparison may reveal reduced velocity, high resistance, or absent diastolic flow during pain, while a direct whirlpool sign can remain the decisive clue.

candidates.question: Why can FAST or DPL be falsely negative in splenic trauma?
candidates.answer: Source-stated limitation: 29% of all patients and 40% of children with splenic injury may not have hemoperitoneum. Exam pivot: A negative FAST/DPL does not exclude splenic injury, especially in children; CECT is the best diagnostic tool when clinical concern persists.

candidates.question: What is the pathologic grading scale for fibrosis/cirrhosis in the METAVIR system?
candidates.answer: F0: no fibrosis F1: portal fibrosis without septa F2: portal fibrosis with few septa F3: numerous septa without cirrhosis F4: cirrhosis

candidates.question: In SBO, what imaging diagnosis is crucial because it directs prompt surgical intervention?
candidates.answer: CT diagnosis of closed-loop obstruction or strangulating (ischemic) SBO is crucial because these represent complicated obstruction with vascular compromise risk and require prompt surgical intervention rather than conservative management.

cards.question: Why does hepatic schistosomiasis produce an echogenic periportal fibrotic mantle on ultrasound?
cards.answer: Schistosomal eggs embolize to portal venules and incite chronic periportal inflammation and fibrosis. Progressive fibrous thickening expands the portal tracts and surrounds the portal venous branches. Imaging consequence: ultrasound shows thick echogenic periportal tissue, classically described as clay-pipestem fibrosis; when viewed in cross-section an anechoic portal vein may sit within an echogenic fibrotic mantle.

candidates.question: Why does perforated cholecystitis produce a wall defect and adjacent pericholecystic fluid collection or abscess?
candidates.answer: Perforated cholecystitis usually evolves from severe progressive distention and necrotic wall injury. Continued obstruction and inflammation increase intraluminal pressure and compromise mural viability until a focal area of weakened, necrotic wall ruptures. Once the wall is disrupted, bile, inflammatory fluid, infected material, or stones can escape into adjacent tissues, producing a visible wall defect, focal pericholecystic collection, abscess, or extraluminal gallstones. This mechanism explains why perforation is more than severe cholecystitis: the defining imaging pivot is actual continuity loss of the wall with leakage into surrounding spaces.

candidates.question: Why do gallstones appear echogenic, produce posterior acoustic shadowing, and often move dependently on ultrasound?
candidates.answer: Gallstones are solid intraluminal concretions formed from bile constituents rather than soft tissue attached to the gallbladder wall. Because the stone surface and internal composition create a strong acoustic impedance difference relative to surrounding bile, the ultrasound beam is strongly reflected, producing a bright echogenic interface. When the stone is sufficiently large or dense, much of the beam is either reflected or attenuated so little sound continues beyond it, creating clean posterior acoustic shadowing. Very small stones may not shadow well because insufficient beam extinction occurs. Because the stones are free within bile rather than fixed to the wall, they usually move to the dependent portion of the gallbladder when patient position changes. This mechanism explains the classic discriminator set for gallstones—echogenicity, shadowing, and mobility—and helps separate them from polyps, which are wall-based and nonmobile, and from sludge, which may move but usually lacks clean shadowing.

candidates.question: How does the normal endometrium change across the menstrual cycle on ultrasound?
candidates.answer: During menstruation and early proliferative phase it is thin and mildly echogenic, then it gradually thickens and becomes more hypoechoic. Near ovulation it shows a trilaminar or striated appearance with a relatively hypoechoic inner layer, more hyperechoic peripheral layer, and a central echogenic line from apposed endometrial walls. During the secretory phase it becomes progressively thicker and more echogenic.

candidates.question: How does diabetic autonomic neuropathy produce the atonic stomach seen on imaging?
candidates.answer: Chronic hyperglycemia causes vagal autonomic neuropathy. Vagal dysfunction impairs gastric smooth muscle stimulation. Loss of coordinated antral contractions reduces propulsion of gastric contents. Functional stasis leads to retained food and contrast. This results in a dilated, atonic stomach on imaging.

candidates.question: Why does cirrhosis produce a nodular, dysmorphic liver with segmental atrophy and hypertrophy?
candidates.answer: Cirrhosis develops through the combined effects of hepatocyte loss, fibrosis, and regeneration. Repeated injury causes diffuse parenchymal damage, while extracellular matrix and fibrous tissue are deposited through the liver, separating surviving hepatocytes into islands and regenerative nodules. Those nodules are often encircled by fibrous bands, and the distorted parenchyma remodels unevenly rather than shrinking uniformly. As fibrosis and nodular regeneration progress, some regions undergo volume loss while others enlarge relatively, producing the characteristic pattern of right-lobe and medial left-lobe atrophy with relative caudate and left lateral segment hypertrophy. The gross result is a small hard nodular liver in advanced disease, with widened fissures, expanded gallbladder fossa, and a nodular contour. Imaging shows these dysmorphic volume shifts because chronic fibrotic remodeling and regenerative nodularity reorganize the liver’s architecture instead of preserving normal lobar proportions.

candidates.deck: Corebook::Ultrasound::Female Pelvis Basic::Hemorrhagic Cyst::Hemorrhagic Ovarian Cyst
candidates.question: Why can a hemorrhagic ovarian cyst evolve from an echogenic or solid-appearing lesion into a web-like or retracting-clot pattern on ultrasound?
candidates.answer: Hemorrhage enters a functional ovarian cyst, most often a corpus luteum. The source describes a changing mixture of liquid blood, fibrin, and clot: acutely, blood can make the cyst diffusely echogenic and mimic solid tissue; as clot organizes and retracts and the clot dissolves, fibrin strands and retracting clot create the characteristic web-like/reticular or geometric intracystic interfaces. Because these internal structures are blood products rather than perfused tissue, they remain avascular on Doppler. The cystic fluid background can still produce posterior acoustic enhancement, preserving the clue that the lesion is fundamentally cystic.

candidates.question: How do you distinguish an extrarenal pelvis from hydronephrosis on ultrasound?
candidates.answer: Extrarenal pelvis is located outside the renal hilum and shows absence of calyceal dilatation. Exam pivot: Central fluid near the renal sinus is not enough by itself to call hydronephrosis; you must confirm true calyceal dilation.

candidates.question: How does emphysematous cholecystitis change perforation risk?
candidates.answer: Emphysematous cholecystitis carries a 5x greater risk of gallbladder perforation. Exam pivot: Gas in the gallbladder is not just a variant finding; it should trigger concern for an especially dangerous complication-prone form of disease.

candidates.question: Why does a traumatic carotid-cavernous fistula show abnormal venous enhancement and enlarged superior ophthalmic vein on CTA?
candidates.answer: A traumatic carotid-cavernous fistula creates a direct arterial-to-venous shunt between the cavernous carotid and the cavernous sinus. Because arterial blood is delivered directly into the venous cavernous sinus, venous structures enhance abnormally during the arterial phase instead of only later in the venous phase. The increased venous outflow burden can distend the involved cavernous sinus and enlarge the ipsilateral superior ophthalmic vein. On CTA, that arterialized venous enhancement pattern is the discriminator that separates CCF from a simple fracture line or nonshunting venous abnormality.

candidates.question: Why does pancreatitis produce a sentinel loop sign?
candidates.answer: Normal substrate: Bowel loops adjacent to an inflamed organ often respond with localized adynamic ileus due to nearby inflammatory irritation. Primary insult: Pancreatic inflammation extends to neighboring small bowel loops. Cellular / microanatomic consequence: Local inflammatory signaling and irritation suppress motility in the adjacent loop without causing a true mechanical obstruction. Propagation step: That single nearby bowel segment accumulates gas and fluid because peristaltic propulsion is reduced. Gross / mesoscopic pathologic consequence: One focal small-bowel loop becomes mildly dilated while the remainder of the bowel does not show a generalized obstruction pattern. Imaging manifestation: Radiographs show a localized gas-filled, sometimes air-fluid-containing sentinel loop adjacent to the inflamed pancreas. Board pivot: The key is localized reactive ileus, which separates this sign from diffuse ileus or true mechanical bowel obstruction.

candidates.question: Why does portal hypertension produce slow portal venous flow and an increased congestion index?
candidates.answer: Portal hypertension increases resistance to forward portal venous transit, so portal venous velocity falls even before the main portal vein reverses direction. At the same time, the portal vein may enlarge. Because the congestion index is the ratio of portal vein cross-sectional area to main portal vein velocity, a larger vein plus slower flow increases the congestion index. Imaging consequence: grayscale may show a dilated main portal vein, while spectral Doppler shows reduced velocity despite preserved antegrade flow until portal hypertension becomes more severe.

candidates.question: How does the normal myometrium typically appear on ultrasound?
candidates.answer: Three layers are often discernible: a compact thin hypoechoic inner layer forming the subendometrial halo, a thicker relatively echogenic middle layer, and a thinner hypoechoic outer layer peripheral to the arcuate vessels.

cards.question: Why do peribiliary cysts parallel portal veins and mimic dilated bile ducts?
cards.answer: Peribiliary cysts arise from dilated peribiliary glands in the periportal connective tissue. Because these glands track along portal tracts, the resulting cystic/tubular structures run beside portal veins and can resemble dilated ducts on CT or T2-weighted MRI. The key architectural distinction is that peribiliary cysts do not communicate with the biliary tree.

candidates.question: Why can an infected renal cyst show wall or septal enhancement and mimic a more aggressive cystic lesion?
candidates.answer: When a renal cyst becomes infected, the main change is inflammatory reaction in the wall and septa rather than simple sterile fluid alone. The article explicitly notes that inflammatory or infected cysts may contain granulation tissue and that granulation tissue may enhance; angiographically, infected cysts may show neovascularity in this granulation tissue. That creates a thick wall, septations, and enhancement around or within the inflammatory tissue, sometimes with debris- or gas-fluid levels. The imaging pivot is that enhancement in this setting reflects inflamed vascularized granulation tissue rather than necessarily malignant tissue, which is why infected cysts can mimic neoplastic cystic masses.

candidates.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Portal Hypertension and varices
candidates.question: What does hepatofugal portal vein flow indicate?
candidates.answer: Reversal of portal flow consistent with advanced portal hypertension.

candidates.question: Why do biliary hamartomas appear as multiple small cyst-like lesions that do not communicate with the biliary tree?
candidates.answer: Abnormal development of small intrahepatic bile ducts leaves benign cystic ductal remnants disconnected from the functioning biliary tree. Imaging consequence: Numerous tiny, often irregular lesions; small lesions may be echogenic on US, and MRCP shows no biliary communication. Interpretation pivot: Noncommunication separates this pattern from the communicating ductal dilatation of Caroli disease.

candidates.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Anatomy: Veins and Venous Sinuses::Dural Sinuses
candidates.question: What is the key compartment rule for the cavernous sinus and its contents?
candidates.answer: The cavernous sinus is an irregular, trabeculated venous compartment along the sides of the sella. The cavernous internal carotid artery and cranial nerve number 6 are the only structures that lie within the cavernous sinus itself. Cranial nerve numbers 3 and 4 and divisions 1 and 2 of cranial nerve number 5 lie in the lateral dural wall. The medial dural wall is often inapparent on imaging.

candidates.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Orbit and Sinonasal Overview::Orbit Overview
candidates.question: Why is orbital fat one of the most important normal imaging landmarks in the orbit?
candidates.answer: Normal orbital fat outlines the globe, extraocular muscles, optic nerve-sheath complex, and vessels, making compartmental localization practical on CT and MR.

candidates.question: What is the key hepatobiliary-phase pitfall in HCC, and what safety check prevents it?
candidates.answer: Trap: Excluding HCC because a lesion is isointense or hyperintense on hepatobiliary phase imaging. Safety check: Do not let hepatobiliary-phase signal override the dynamic hallmark pattern; integrate arterial hyperenhancement, washout, capsule, and the rest of the study. Key discriminator: The article states that uptake is related to OATP8 receptor behavior and that most HCCs are hypointense, but up to 10% of HCCs can be isointense or hyperintense on hepatobiliary phase. Why this error occurs: Readers may overgeneralize the usual hepatobiliary-phase appearance into an absolute rule.

candidates.question: How does diverticulitis lead to portal venous thrombophlebitis and hepatic abscess formation?
candidates.answer: Infected pericolonic veins draining an inflamed diverticular segment become contaminated with enteric bacteria → septic thrombophlebitis develops in mesenteric veins (e.g., inferior mesenteric vein). The infected thrombus propagates through the portal venous system → septic emboli reach the liver → bacteria seed hepatic parenchyma, producing pyogenic liver abscesses visible on CT.

candidates.question: Which tumors are source-stated to invade or obstruct hepatic veins/portal veins in THAD-related cases?
candidates.answer: Tumor invading or obstructing veins: hepatocellular carcinoma > cholangiocarcinoma > metastases. Exam pivot: Portal venous invasion/obstruction can create THAD and carries poor prognosis related to the underlying tumor.

candidates.question: With hepatobiliary contrast agents on MRI, what gallbladder filling pattern supports acute cholecystitis?
candidates.answer: - Lack of filling or delayed filling of the gallbladder beyond 60 minutes supports acute cholecystitis - Normal filling within 60 minutes does not exclude acute cholecystitis - The gallbladder usually fills with contrast in chronic cholecystitis Exam pivot: Delayed/nonfilling supports acute cystic duct obstruction physiology, but normal filling does not completely rule out acute disease.

candidates.question: Why does papillary RCC usually enhance only mildly and often appear T2 hypointense?
candidates.answer: External literature source (not stated in Core/RadPrimer/STATdx/Radiopaedia). Source: https://doi.org/10.2214/AJR.08.1727 Papillary RCC is typically a relatively hypovascular RCC subtype, so less contrast enters the tumor during the arterial/nephrographic phases and enhancement is only mild compared with clear cell RCC. Its low T2 signal has been linked in prior imaging-pathology work to internal composition such as hemosiderin and compact tumor tissue rather than the highly vascular, more T2-bright phenotype of clear cell RCC. Because enhancement may be weak, some papillary RCCs can look almost nonenhancing on CT and may mimic a hemorrhagic cyst or fat-poor AML if MRI is not used carefully. Imaging pivot: a homogeneous renal tumor that is T2 dark and only mildly enhancing should push papillary RCC high on the differential.

candidates.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Introduction to Brain Neoplasms and Cysts::Colloid Cyst
candidates.question: What proportion of colloid cysts are asymptomatic versus associated with headache?
candidates.answer: Fact: 40-50% are asymptomatic and discovered incidentally; headache occurs in about 50-60%. Exam pivot: symptoms are common but absence of symptoms does not exclude a clinically important foramen of Monro lesion.

cards.question: What periportal mimic can make edema look like biliary dilation, and what check prevents the mistake?
cards.answer: Trap: Calling circumferential periportal fluid a dilated bile duct. Safety check: Identify the relationship to the portal vein and use MRCP/direct cholangiography or Doppler when needed. Key discriminator: Periportal edema surrounds the portal triad/portal vein; a dilated bile duct lies along one side of the accompanying portal vein. Why it happens: Both create branching low-attenuation or fluid-signal structures in the periportal region, and obstruction can produce both at once.

candidates.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
candidates.question: What scar-based pitfall can make FNH look like fibrolamellar HCC, and what imaging checks prevent the error?
candidates.answer: Trap: Treating every central scar as equivalent. Safety check: Compare scar T2 signal, calcification, enhancement timing, and hepatobiliary contrast behavior. Discriminator: FNH has a T2-hyperintense scar that enhances late with extracellular contrast and a lesion that retains hepatobiliary agent; fibrolamellar HCC has a fibrotic T1/T2-hypointense scar and commonly a calcified scar. Why it happens: Both may be large hypervascular liver masses with a central scar.

candidates.question: What sonographic mimic can make echogenic fecal material look like a dermoid, and how is the mistake avoided?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking echogenic fecal material in large bowel for an adnexal dermoid. Safety check: Confirm ovarian/adnexal localization with transvaginal imaging, repeat scanning, and bowel behavior; use MR when needed. Discriminator: A true dermoid remains linked to the ovary and contains source-supported teratomatous material clues rather than bowel contents. Why the error occurs: Echogenic feces can produce a mass-like sonographic appearance.

candidates.question: What visual pitfall does this image create, and what single check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking a dilated bile duct for a thrombosed portal vein, or letting the adjacent bile duct distract from the actual portal-vein abnormality. Safety check / maneuver: Use color Doppler to confirm which tubular structure is vascular and which is biliary. Key discriminator: A patent portal vein demonstrates flow; a bile duct does not. In this case, the portal vein itself is the abnormal structure because it shows no detectable internal flow with intraluminal echoes, while the dilated common bile duct is only an associated adjacent finding. Why the error occurs: In the porta hepatis, adjacent tubular structures can mimic one another on grayscale alone, especially when one is dilated and the other is thrombosed.

candidates.question: What MRI pitfall occurs when edema is obvious but a line is not, and what safety check prevents it?
candidates.answer: Trap: Stopping at marrow edema and failing to search for the fracture line. Safety check: Review other planes and use the correct plane/high-resolution imaging when the edema pattern is suspicious. Key discriminator: The source states the fracture line may not be visible if the correct plane and high resolution are not used, and a calcaneal case notes florid edema should prompt a search for fracture in other planes. Why it happens: The low-signal fracture line can be plane-dependent, while marrow edema is more diffuse and easier to see.

candidates.question: What is the pitfall when a mature post-pancreatitis collection looks simple on CT, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Labeling every delayed encapsulated post-pancreatitis collection a pseudocyst on CT alone. Safety check: Look for internal debris/solid material, and when the distinction matters use MR to determine whether the collection is truly simple or instead represents walled-off necrosis. Key discriminator: A pseudocyst is a delayed encapsulated simple fluid collection without debris; walled-off necrosis contains internal necrotic debris/blood products. Why the error occurs: CT can make a necrotic collection appear deceptively simple if internal solid material is not well appreciated.

candidates.question: What pitfall should be avoided, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking normal rotated sternal ossification centers for true bulbous posterior rib callus on oblique radiographs. Safety check: Correlate location/projection with other views and problem-solving imaging when needed; in this case, bone scan confirms true right rib fractures and identifies additional medial left posterior rib fractures. Key discriminator: Sternal ossification centers are projectional normal structures, while true fractures show healing/callus or focal radiotracer activity. Why it happens: On oblique views, sternal ossification centers can project over posterior ribs and visually mimic callus.

candidates.question: What pitfall can this appearance cause, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Mistaking echogenic renal sinus fat for a renal stone on ultrasound. Safety check: Confirm sharp posterior acoustic shadowing; use color Doppler twinkling as an additional aid when needed. Key discriminator: A true stone is an echogenic focus with posterior acoustic shadowing, whereas sinus fat may have similar echogenicity but lacks the same confirming stone features. Why the error occurs: Small stones can blend with central renal sinus fat on grayscale, so echogenicity alone can falsely suggest or falsely exclude a stone.

candidates.question: What diagnostic pitfall is demonstrated here, and what imaging safety check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking ileus with ascites (or recent bowel surgery) for small bowel obstruction (SBO) on plain films. Why it happens: Gas may collect only in nondependent bowel, while dependent small bowel and colon are fluid-filled and less dilated, creating an apparent segmental gas pattern. Safety check: Look for a true transition point or obstructing lesion. If unclear, obtain CT to confirm generalized dilation of small and large bowel without a transition zone. Key discriminator: Mechanical obstruction shows a discrete transition point with upstream dilation; ileus shows proportional dilation without a focal obstructing site.

candidates.question: What is the key pitfall in interpreting intraluminal portal-vein material here, and what check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Calling all portal-vein thrombus bland, or missing tumor thrombus by ignoring enhancement/vascularity within the intraluminal material. Safety check / maneuver: Assess whether the portal-vein material enhances or shows internal arterial flow; compare it with adjacent tumor when present. Key discriminator: Bland thrombus does not enhance on CEUS, whereas tumor thrombus enhances similarly to adjacent tumor and may show internal arterial vascularity. Why the error occurs: Both bland and tumoral material occupy the portal-vein lumen, so they can look similar unless enhancement behavior or internal vascularity is deliberately assessed.

candidates.question: What source-listed mimic can cause overcall, and what safety check helps prevent the error?
candidates.answer: Trap: Overcalling a metaphyseal spur as a classic metaphyseal lesion. Safety check: Look for an underlying lucency/fracture plane. Key discriminator: A metaphyseal spur is a distal extension of the SPBC beyond the chondroosseous junction and typically lacks underlying lucency; CML is a subphyseal fracture that undercuts the SPBC. Why the error occurs: Both can create a corner-like metaphyseal contour, especially near the distal femur.

candidates.question: What is the classic false-positive mimic of hydronephrosis in the renal sinus, and what imaging check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking peripelvic cysts for hydronephrosis. Safety check / maneuver: Determine whether the fluid spaces communicate with the pelvicalyceal system; if needed, use CT urogram to confirm a nondilated opacified collecting system rather than true collecting-system dilation. Key discriminator: Hydronephrosis consists of intercommunicating dilated calyces/pelvis, whereas peripelvic cysts are discrete noncommunicating renal sinus cysts. The article explicitly lists peripelvic cyst as a top differential and states CT urogram is confirmatory. Why this error happens: Both entities can appear as central anechoic renal sinus fluid on ultrasound, especially on limited views.

candidates.question: Portal venous Doppler pitfall in a transplant patient: what mimic can helical flow create, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking helical portal vein flow for hepatofugal flow from portal hypertension. Safety check / maneuver: Look for the elliptical color Doppler pattern and use the transplant history, especially donor-recipient main portal vein size mismatch, before calling true reversed flow. Key discriminator: Helical flow has the characteristic elliptical swirling color pattern rather than sustained true portal venous reversal. Why it happens: Helical flow commonly occurs in liver transplants when donor and recipient main portal veins are discrepant in size and can visually mimic hepatofugal flow.

cards.question: What periportal mimic can make thrombosed portal branches look like dilated bile ducts, and what check prevents the mistake?
cards.answer: Trap: Calling nonenhancing thrombosed portal branches dilated bile ducts. Safety check: Trace the vascular course, look for collateral veins, and confirm with contrast/Doppler or MRCP as appropriate. Key discriminator: Occluded portal branches occupy the portal-vein distribution and often coexist with collateral veins; true ducts follow the biliary tree and communicate on cholangiography/MRCP. Why it happens: Both can appear as branching nonenhancing tubular structures.

candidates.question: What is the pitfall when pancreatitis imaging coexists with a dilated pancreatic duct, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Stopping at the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis and failing to search for an underlying obstructing pancreatic mass. Safety check: If acute pancreatitis is accompanied by a dilated pancreatic duct or biliary obstruction, actively investigate for an underlying malignancy rather than assuming uncomplicated pancreatitis. Key discriminator: Routine acute pancreatitis does not usually explain a dilated obstructed pancreatic duct; an obstructing pancreatic adenocarcinoma can present as pancreatitis. Why the error occurs: The inflammatory findings are so visually dominant that the reader misses the malignant cause behind them.

candidates.question: What is the pitfall here, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking a renal sinus cyst for collecting-system dilatation or assuming any central renal fluid is hydronephrosis. Safety check: Confirm whether the fluid spaces are separate cysts or contiguous collecting-system dilatation; use excretory-phase contrast imaging when needed. Key discriminator: On excretory-phase CECT, water-attenuation renal sinus cysts remain separate from the enhanced renal collecting system. Why the error occurs: Both entities can appear as central renal fluid in the sinus region, especially when anatomy is crowded on a single image.

candidates.question: What is the key pitfall here, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Seeing an unusual vessel in the left lobe/falciform region and failing to recognize it as a recanalized paraumbilical collateral, thereby missing severe portal hypertension. Safety check / maneuver: On Doppler, trace the vessel to the left portal vein and assess whether it courses toward the anterior abdominal wall, which is the classic collateral pathway described in the source. Key discriminator: Continuity with the left portal vein identifies a portal-systemic collateral rather than a nonspecific superficial abdominal wall vessel. Why the error occurs: The vessel can look unfamiliar in location/course, so it is easy to dismiss it as incidental vascular anatomy instead of a major portal-hypertension sign.

candidates.question: What is the pitfall when pancreatitis-like inflammation is centered near the duodenum, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Calling a duodenal-centered inflammatory process pancreatitis simply because there is anterior pararenal fat stranding and edema near the pancreatic head. Safety check: Determine where the inflammation is centered; pancreatitis is centered on the pancreas, whereas perforated duodenal ulcer is centered on the duodenum, often best appreciated on coronal reformations. Key discriminator: Secondary pancreatic head edema can occur with perforated duodenal ulcer, but the primary inflammatory epicenter is duodenal rather than pancreatic. Why the error occurs: The reader anchors on nearby pancreatic edema and ignores the true compartment of origin.

candidates.question: What is the pitfall here, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking a hemorrhagic cyst with internal complexity on grayscale ultrasound for a cystic renal neoplasm. Safety check: Do not stop at grayscale complexity alone; evaluate for true internal enhancement with contrast-enhanced imaging when needed. Key discriminator: Internal echoes and septations can occur in hemorrhagic cysts, but enhancing mural nodules or enhancing soft-tissue components favor neoplasm. Why the error occurs: Blood products and clot can make a benign cyst look internally complex and falsely solid on baseline ultrasound.

candidates.question: What is the pitfall here, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Calling every multiloculated septated cystic renal mass with enhancement a cystic renal cell carcinoma. Safety check: Look specifically for the renal sinus or renal pelvis invagination clue before collapsing the case into Bosniak-malignant thinking alone. Key discriminator: Invagination into the renal sinus is a characteristic clue for adult cystic nephroma, even though overlap with cystic renal cell carcinoma remains substantial. Why the error occurs: Both adult cystic nephroma and cystic renal cell carcinoma can be multiloculated cystic masses with enhancing septa, so the dominant impression can default too quickly to malignancy.

candidates.question: What sonographic mimic can make echogenic fecal material look like a dermoid, and how is the mistake avoided?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking echogenic fecal material in large bowel for an adnexal dermoid. Safety check: Confirm ovarian/adnexal localization with transvaginal imaging, repeat scanning, and bowel behavior; use MR when needed. Discriminator: A true dermoid remains linked to the ovary and contains source-supported teratomatous material clues rather than bowel contents. Why the error occurs: Echogenic feces can produce a mass-like sonographic appearance.

cards.question: What is the periportal-edema pitfall after liver transplantation, and what check prevents overcalling graft injury?
cards.answer: Trap: Interpreting isolated early periportal edema as allograft injury or rejection. Safety check: Separate expected postoperative edema from specific vascular or biliary complications. Key discriminator: Periportal edema is a common recent-posttransplant finding; biliary necrosis/bilomas, vascular occlusion, or other direct complication signs require separate evidence. Why it happens: The postoperative lymphatic disruption can look striking despite being expected.

candidates.question: What lymph-node pitfall occurs in PSC, and what safety check prevents overcalling malignancy?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking common PSC-related lymphadenopathy for metastatic lymphadenopathy or lymphoma. Safety check: Interpret lymph nodes in context of the PSC biliary pattern and actively search for direct malignant features before assigning metastatic disease. Key discriminator: RadPrimer states extensive lymphadenopathy is common, particularly precaval/aortocaval or RUQ/retroperitoneal nodes, and should not be confused with metastatic lymphadenopathy or lymphoma. Why it happens: Enlarged nodes in a patient at risk for cholangiocarcinoma create an anchoring bias toward malignancy.

candidates.question: What is the pitfall when a dilated fallopian tube contains fluid, and what safety check prevents overcalling pyosalpinx?
candidates.answer: Trap: Calling any fluid-filled dilated tube pyosalpinx. Safety check: Interrogate the wall, intraluminal contents, folds, Doppler pattern, and surrounding pelvis. Discriminator: Hydrosalpinx has simple tubal fluid without wall thickening or surrounding inflammation; pyosalpinx has complex/debris-filled fluid with inflammatory wall/fold changes. Why it happens: Both entities share the same tubular shape, so content and inflammatory response - not dilation alone - provide the diagnostic separation.

candidates.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Brain::Primary Effects of CNS Trauma::Scalp and Skull Injuries
candidates.question: What is the pitfall here, and what safety check prevents it?
candidates.answer: Trap: treating a skull base fracture near vascular channels as an isolated bone injury. Safety check: evaluate whether the fracture involves the temporal bone, sphenoid/clivus, carotid canal, jugular foramen, or dural venous sinus; consider CTA/MRA when these high-risk pathways are involved. Key discriminator: fractures crossing the carotid canal, jugular foramen, or dural venous sinus region carry higher vascular or venous sinus injury risk. Why the error occurs: bone-window fracture detection can distract from the vascular-channel complication search.

candidates.question: What is the post-neoadjuvant MR pitfall with spiculations, and what safety check prevents the error?
candidates.answer: Trap: Assuming posttreatment spiculations automatically represent residual tumor. Safety check: Compare pre- and post-neoadjuvant MR side by side and look for T2 dark fibrosis or a split scar sign; use DWI/ADC change as an adjunct. Key discriminator: Persistent intermediate T2 signal favors residual tumor, whereas dark T2 fibrosis and the split scar sign favor treatment response. Why it happens: Posttreatment desmoplastic reaction can be depicted as spiculations and may be confused with tumor.

candidates.question: What is the major pitfall on this case, and what safety check prevents it?
candidates.answer: Trap: Misinterpreting medial left hepatic lobe enhancement from collateral venous flow as a hepatic mass. Safety check: Look for SVC occlusion, chest wall collateral veins, intrahepatic collaterals, and densely opacified medial segment/segment 4. Key discriminator: Third-inflow enhancement follows collateral venous pathways rather than forming a discrete spherical or oval mass. Why it happens: Alternative venous inflow can create focal hepatic hyperenhancement and nuclear medicine hot pseudolesions.

candidates.question: What is the pitfall here, and what safety check prevents it?
candidates.answer: Trap: Under-calling a Bosniak IV lesion as a “complex but probably benign cyst.” Safety check: actively search for thick enhancing septa and enhancing mural nodules rather than stopping at the word “cystic.” Key discriminator: enhancement of septal or nodular soft tissue converts the problem from benign complex cyst to malignant cystic renal neoplasm. Why it happens: hemorrhagic and proteinaceous cysts can look complex, but they should not contain truly enhancing nodular tissue.

candidates.question: What is the major pitfall on this case, and what safety check prevents it?
candidates.answer: Trap: Overestimating HCC tumor size by including adjacent THAD/perfusion abnormality as tumor. Safety check: Compare arterial and portal venous phases and separate the discrete tumor foci from the transient wedge-shaped perfusion territory. Key discriminator: The HCC masses show washout, while the THAD becomes less evident on portal venous phase. Why it happens: Tumor and adjacent perfusion abnormality can both be hypervascular on arterial phase.

candidates.question: What is the pitfall here, and what safety check prevents it?
candidates.answer: Trap: Treating renal vein/IVC thrombus as bland clot or failing to stage the venous system carefully in a renal mass. Safety check: inspect the renal vein and IVC on every study, and when thrombus is present, look for contiguous tumor, internal enhancement, or Doppler flow/arterial waveform within the thrombus. Key discriminator: enhancing or vascular thrombus contiguous with a renal mass is tumor thrombus and strongly favors RCC. Why it happens: both bland thrombus and tumor thrombus appear as filling defects unless vascularity is deliberately assessed.

candidates.question: What is the trap when a fracture site remains lucent, and what safety check prevents overcalling nonunion?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking persistent fracture lucency for nonunion when the fracture may be clinically stable from fibrous union. Safety check: Correlate with clinical union/stability and compare serial radiographs rather than relying on lucency alone. Key discriminator: Fibrous union is clinically successful union with fibrous tissue bridging the gap instead of bone and often fills in with bone later; nonunion means mature bone has not bridged the fragments and healing has arrested. Why it happens: Radiographic lucency can persist even when function and stability have returned.

candidates.question: What is the key diagnostic pitfall here, and what safety check prevents it?
candidates.answer: Trap: Calling an echogenic solid liver lesion a hemangioma just because it looks bright on grayscale US. Safety check: In an at-risk patient, do not assume hemangioma when a nodule is > 1 cm; characterize with multiphasic CECT, CEMR, or CEUS and look for the HCC dynamic pattern rather than relying on echogenicity alone. Key discriminator: The article states HCC can be hyperechoic because of fatty metamorphosis or hypervascularity, whereas hemangioma is unusual in a cirrhotic liver and benign labeling should not be based on brightness alone. Why this error occurs: Echogenic HCC visually overlaps with common benign echogenic liver lesions.

candidates.question: What is the pitfall here, and what safety check prevents it?
candidates.answer: Trap: Reassuring yourself that a solid renal mass is probably oncocytoma because it seems well-circumscribed or shows a spoke-wheel-type vascular pattern. Safety check: remember that oncocytoma cannot be reliably distinguished from RCC on cross-sectional imaging, and the spoke-wheel Doppler pattern is only a suggestive sign, not a rule-out sign. Key discriminator: there is no imaging feature sufficiently specific to safely dismiss RCC when a solid enhancing renal mass is present. Why it happens: classic “benign” descriptors are memorable but nonspecific, so they create premature closure.

candidates.question: What is the major pitfall on this case, and what safety check prevents it?
candidates.answer: Trap: Calling the perfusion wedge the whole lesion and missing the small causative tumor. Safety check: Inspect the apex of every wedge-shaped THAD on portal venous-phase and arterial-phase images. Key discriminator: The THAD is wedge-shaped and perfusional, while the causative tumor is a small rounded lesion at the apex of the wedge/triangle. Why it happens: The perfusion abnormality can be larger and more conspicuous than the small mass that causes it.

cards.question: What is the main imaging trap with peribiliary cysts, and what check prevents mistaking them for dilated bile ducts?
cards.answer: Trap: Calling periportal cystic/tubular structures biliary obstruction. Safety check: Assess biliary communication with MRCP/direct cholangiography and follow the relationship to portal veins. Key discriminator: Peribiliary cysts parallel portal veins but do not communicate with the biliary tree. Why it happens: Their elongated periportal distribution can closely mimic branching dilated ducts.

candidates.question: What is the imaging trap here, and what specific check helps prevent the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking a cystic hepatic metastasis for a simple hepatic cyst. Safety check / maneuver: Look carefully for mural nodularity and compare with prior imaging to see whether the lesion was previously solid. Key discriminator: A simple cyst should not have malignant mural nodularity or documented evolution from a prior soft tissue metastasis. Why the error occurs: Treated metastases can become near-water-density and deceptively benign in appearance.

candidates.question: What is the main diagnostic pitfall here, and what imaging check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking multiple renal sinus fluid spaces on ultrasound for hydronephrosis. Safety check: Prove communication with the collecting system. On ultrasound, look for continuity with the renal pelvis/proximal ureter; if uncertain, use delayed contrast-enhanced CT (pyelographic/excretory phase) to see whether the collecting system opacifies as one contiguous structure. Key discriminator: Peripelvic cysts are discrete, noncommunicating cysts within the renal sinus, while hydronephrosis is a contiguous dilated collecting system that contains excreted contrast on delayed imaging. Why the error occurs: Both entities can appear as echo-free renal sinus spaces on ultrasound, so the sonographic appearance alone can falsely suggest dilated calyces.

candidates.question: What is the imaging trap here, and what acquisition step prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Missing a hypervascular hepatic metastasis because it is nearly isodense or difficult to recognize on portal venous images alone. Safety check / maneuver: Obtain biphasic liver CT with an arterial phase when a hypervascular primary is known or suspected. Key discriminator: Hypervascular metastases may be conspicuous on arterial phase but become much less visible on venous phase. Why the error occurs: The lesion’s conspicuity depends on arterial perfusion, so venous-phase-only imaging can undercall or miss it.

candidates.question: What is the imaging trap here, and what check helps separate it from true cirrhosis?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking treatment-related pseudocirrhosis for primary chronic cirrhosis. Safety check / maneuver: Look for residual metastatic lesions and the source-supported history of lesion shrinkage with fibrosis producing contour distortion. Key discriminator: Pseudocirrhosis reflects post-treatment metastatic contraction and scarring rather than primary diffuse cirrhotic remodeling. Why the error occurs: Both processes can produce a nodular contour, fissural widening, and capsular retraction.

candidates.question: What is the imaging trap here, and what follow-up check helps prevent the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Miscalling diffuse hepatic metastatic infiltration as benign steatosis. Safety check / maneuver: Use complementary imaging such as contrast-enhanced CT, PET/CT, or ultrasound to look for innumerable focal lesions or FDG-avid abnormal liver. Key discriminator: True steatosis does not produce diffuse FDG-avid malignant replacement or innumerable hypoechoic metastatic nodules. Why the error occurs: Diffuse metastatic infiltration may lower liver attenuation globally and visually simulate fatty liver on CT.

candidates.question: What is the trap with orbital roof fractures, and what safety check prevents it?
candidates.answer: Trap: treating the injury as only an orbital fracture. Safety check: inspect for intracranial communication, pneumocephalus, anterior cranial fossa fragment displacement, frontal lobe injury, and orbital compartment complications. Discriminator: the orbital roof is also the floor of the anterior cranial fossa. Why it happens: orbital findings can distract from the skull base role of the same bone.

candidates.question: What is the pitfall when pancreatitis imaging coexists with a dilated pancreatic duct, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Stopping at the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis and failing to search for an underlying obstructing pancreatic mass. Safety check: If acute pancreatitis is accompanied by a dilated pancreatic duct or biliary obstruction, actively investigate for an underlying malignancy rather than assuming uncomplicated pancreatitis. Key discriminator: Routine acute pancreatitis does not usually explain a dilated obstructed pancreatic duct; an obstructing pancreatic adenocarcinoma can present as pancreatitis. Why the error occurs: The inflammatory findings are so visually dominant that the reader misses the malignant cause behind them.

candidates.question: What is the pitfall here, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking a hemorrhagic cyst with internal complexity on grayscale ultrasound for a cystic renal neoplasm. Safety check: Do not stop at grayscale complexity alone; evaluate for true internal enhancement with contrast-enhanced imaging when needed. Key discriminator: Internal echoes and septations can occur in hemorrhagic cysts, but enhancing mural nodules or enhancing soft-tissue components favor neoplasm. Why the error occurs: Blood products and clot can make a benign cyst look internally complex and falsely solid on baseline ultrasound.

candidates.question: What is the key pitfall in interpreting intraluminal portal-vein material here, and what check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Calling all portal-vein thrombus bland, or missing tumor thrombus by ignoring enhancement/vascularity within the intraluminal material. Safety check / maneuver: Assess whether the portal-vein material enhances or shows internal arterial flow; compare it with adjacent tumor when present. Key discriminator: Bland thrombus does not enhance on CEUS, whereas tumor thrombus enhances similarly to adjacent tumor and may show internal arterial vascularity. Why the error occurs: Both bland and tumoral material occupy the portal-vein lumen, so they can look similar unless enhancement behavior or internal vascularity is deliberately assessed.

candidates.question: What is the trap with NOE trauma, and what safety check prevents it?
candidates.answer: Trap: focusing only on nasal bones and medial orbit while missing anterior skull base and frontal sinus drainage involvement. Safety check: inspect cribriform plate, ethmoid roof, frontal sinus outflow region, and medial canthal tendon attachment region. Discriminator: NOE trauma can extend into the frontobasal skull base and can cause traumatic telecanthus when the tendon-bearing central fragment is displaced or comminuted. Why it happens: the injury looks facial, but its consequences may be skull base and lacrimal/orbital.

candidates.question: What visual pitfall does this image create, and what single check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking a dilated bile duct for a thrombosed portal vein, or letting the adjacent bile duct distract from the actual portal-vein abnormality. Safety check / maneuver: Use color Doppler to confirm which tubular structure is vascular and which is biliary. Key discriminator: A patent portal vein demonstrates flow; a bile duct does not. In this case, the portal vein itself is the abnormal structure because it shows no detectable internal flow with intraluminal echoes, while the dilated common bile duct is only an associated adjacent finding. Why the error occurs: In the porta hepatis, adjacent tubular structures can mimic one another on grayscale alone, especially when one is dilated and the other is thrombosed.

candidates.question: What is the pitfall here, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Calling every multiloculated septated cystic renal mass with enhancement a cystic renal cell carcinoma. Safety check: Look specifically for the renal sinus or renal pelvis invagination clue before collapsing the case into Bosniak-malignant thinking alone. Key discriminator: Invagination into the renal sinus is a characteristic clue for adult cystic nephroma, even though overlap with cystic renal cell carcinoma remains substantial. Why the error occurs: Both adult cystic nephroma and cystic renal cell carcinoma can be multiloculated cystic masses with enhancing septa, so the dominant impression can default too quickly to malignancy.

cards.question: What is the major gas-distribution pitfall in the liver, and what check separates pneumobilia from portal venous gas?
cards.answer: Trap: Treating all branching hepatic gas as the same process. Safety check: Assess central versus peripheral distribution and use spectral Doppler/clinical context when needed. Key discriminator: Pneumobilia is more central; portal venous gas extends to the liver periphery and may produce a spiky portal-venous Doppler waveform. Why it happens: Both can appear as branching echogenic foci with dirty shadowing on ultrasound.

candidates.answer: Trap: Misinterpreting medial left hepatic lobe enhancement from collateral venous flow as a hepatic mass. Safety check: Look for SVC occlusion, chest wall collateral veins, intrahepatic collaterals, and densely opacified medial segment/segment 4. Key discriminator: Third-inflow enhancement follows collateral venous pathways rather than forming a discrete spherical or oval mass. Key discriminator: Bland thrombus should not contain arterial neovascularity, whereas the article shows HCC tumor in vein with marked internal vascularity and arterialized spectral tracings. Why this error occurs: Both entities occupy the portal vein lumen, but only tumor thrombus contains viable hypervascular tumor tissue.

candidates.question: What is the key diagnostic pitfall here, and what safety check prevents it?
candidates.answer: Trap: Missing infiltrative HCC on ultrasound because there is no cleanly marginated focal mass. Safety check: Look for secondary mass effect clues, especially marked posterior displacement of hepatic vessels, and actively inspect for tumor in vein. Key discriminator: The article specifically says infiltrative tumor on US may be challenging to identify, but posterior displacement of hepatic vessels is a helpful clue and tumor in vein is often seen with large infiltrative HCC. Why this error occurs: Infiltrative tumor can blend into background liver and evade the usual find-the-round-mass search pattern.

candidates.question: What is the key diagnostic pitfall here, and what safety check prevents it?
candidates.answer: Trap: Seeing a central scar and reflexively calling the lesion focal nodular hyperplasia. Safety check: Step back and check whether the overall lesion behaves like a large malignant mass rather than a benign hyperplastic lesion; use the full pattern and patient context, not the scar alone. Key discriminator: Fibrolamellar carcinoma is a rare HCC subtype in young patients without chronic liver disease and is described as a large mass with a fibrous central scar, while FNH is a benign hypervascular lesion in which washout is uncommon. Why this error occurs: Both lesions can contain a central scar, so the scar by itself is a classic false reassurance cue.

candidates.question: What is the pitfall here, and what safety check prevents it?
candidates.answer: Trap: Calling an echogenic renal mass on ultrasound an angiomyolipoma by appearance alone. Safety check: confirm macroscopic fat on CT/MRI and remember that AML shadowing is specific when present, but echogenicity alone is not enough. Key discriminator: a non-calcified renal lesion with macroscopic fat supports AML; without macroscopic fat, RCC remains in play. Why it happens: AML and RCC overlap on ultrasound, and papillary RCC may be relatively hypovascular and deceptively bland.

candidates.question: What is the key diagnostic pitfall here, and what safety check prevents it?
candidates.answer: Trap: Dismissing a cirrhotic nodule as merely regenerative or dysplastic because the outer nodule looks relatively bland. Safety check: Search carefully for an internal focus that shows true HCC behavior, especially arterial hyperenhancement followed by late weak washout. Key discriminator: The article’s nodule-in-nodule case shows malignant transformation within a larger precursor nodule; regenerative and dysplastic nodules may be arterialized, but the source states they do not wash out on portal or delayed imaging like HCC. Why this error occurs: The larger background nodule can distract the reader from the smaller malignant inner component.

cards.question: What post-trauma periportal pitfall can confuse hemorrhage with resuscitation-related edema, and what check prevents the mistake?
cards.answer: Trap: Calling every post-trauma periportal low-density collar blood. Safety check: Search for a focal hepatic laceration/hematoma and compare with systemic hypervolemia signs such as a distended IVC. Key discriminator: Periportal blood usually accompanies another sign of hepatic injury and is generally limited to the injured lobe; resuscitation-related lymphedema is more diffuse and accompanies volume expansion. Why it happens: Both can track along portal tracts after trauma.

candidates.question: What is the pitfall when unexplained hemorrhage is seen in the pancreatic bed, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Attributing hemorrhage generically to hemorrhagic pancreatitis without searching for a vascular source. Safety check: When there is unexplained hemorrhage in the pancreatic bed, perform a deliberate search for a pseudoaneurysm and consider angiographic evaluation when appropriate. Key discriminator: A focal contrast-filled outpouching adjacent to an artery, often with surrounding hematoma, indicates pseudoaneurysm rather than nonspecific bleeding alone. Why the error occurs: The dramatic hemorrhage distracts from the smaller but more important culprit vascular lesion.

candidates.question: What is the key pitfall here, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Seeing an unusual vessel in the left lobe/falciform region and failing to recognize it as a recanalized paraumbilical collateral, thereby missing severe portal hypertension. Safety check / maneuver: On Doppler, trace the vessel to the left portal vein and assess whether it courses toward the anterior abdominal wall, which is the classic collateral pathway described in the source. Key discriminator: Continuity with the left portal vein identifies a portal-systemic collateral rather than a nonspecific superficial abdominal wall vessel. Why the error occurs: The vessel can look unfamiliar in location/course, so it is easy to dismiss it as incidental vascular anatomy instead of a major portal-hypertension sign.

candidates.question: What is the MRI pitfall when a complex adnexal lesion restricts diffusion, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Treating restricted diffusion as synonymous with abscess. Safety check: Confirm low ADC and then integrate T1/T2 signal, wall/septal enhancement, morphology, and the surrounding pelvic inflammatory response. Discriminator: Endometriomas and dermoids may also restrict diffusion; TOA is favored when restriction occurs inside a thick enhancing inflammatory adnexal lesion with pelvic inflammatory change. Why it happens: More than one common adnexal lesion in the source can show restricted diffusion, so a single sequence can falsely collapse the differential.

candidates.question: What diagnostic pitfall is demonstrated here, and what imaging safety check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking ileus with ascites (or recent bowel surgery) for small bowel obstruction (SBO) on plain films. Why it happens: Gas may collect only in nondependent bowel, while dependent small bowel and colon are fluid-filled and less dilated, creating an apparent segmental gas pattern. Safety check: Look for a true transition point or obstructing lesion. If unclear, obtain CT to confirm generalized dilation of small and large bowel without a transition zone. Key discriminator: Mechanical obstruction shows a discrete transition point with upstream dilation; ileus shows proportional dilation without a focal obstructing site.

candidates.question: What is the key pitfall here, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking gallbladder wall thickening in a cirrhotic patient with ascites for acute cholecystitis by default. Safety check / maneuver: Ask whether the wall thickening is a primary gallbladder process or part of a systemic edema state; specifically look for cirrhosis, ascites, and the source-stated hypoalbuminemic/hypoproteinemic setting. Key discriminator: In this source, the thickened wall is explicitly attributed to edema from hypoalbuminemia/hypoproteinemia, especially with ascites, rather than primary inflammatory gallbladder disease. Why the error occurs: Thickened gallbladder wall is visually nonspecific, so readers may jump straight to cholecystitis without recognizing the cirrhotic decompensation context.

candidates.question: What is the pitfall here, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking a renal sinus cyst for collecting-system dilatation or assuming any central renal fluid is hydronephrosis. Safety check: Confirm whether the fluid spaces are separate cysts or contiguous collecting-system dilatation; use excretory-phase contrast imaging when needed. Key discriminator: On excretory-phase CECT, water-attenuation renal sinus cysts remain separate from the enhanced renal collecting system. Why the error occurs: Both entities can appear as central renal fluid in the sinus region, especially when anatomy is crowded on a single image.

candidates.question: What pitfall makes coagulopathic hepatic hemorrhage mimic traumatic liver injury, and what checks prevent the error?
candidates.answer: Trap: Calling fracture-like hepatic defects traumatic lacerations. Safety check: Verify trauma history and search for a hematocrit sign or bleeding at multiple sites. Discriminator: The source anticoagulant case had fracture-like defects without trauma; the separate coagulopathy case showed hepatic and renal bleeding plus a hematocrit level. Why it happens: Intrahepatic hemorrhagic defects can resemble linear traumatic planes.

candidates.question: What is the post-neoadjuvant MR pitfall with spiculations, and what safety check prevents the error?
candidates.answer: Trap: Assuming posttreatment spiculations automatically represent residual tumor. Safety check: Compare pre- and post-neoadjuvant MR side by side and look for T2 dark fibrosis or a split scar sign; use DWI/ADC change as an adjunct. Key discriminator: Persistent intermediate T2 signal favors residual tumor, whereas dark T2 fibrosis and the split scar sign favor treatment response. Why it happens: Posttreatment desmoplastic reaction can be depicted as spiculations and may be confused with tumor.

cards.question: What malignant mimic can hepatic inflammatory pseudotumor create, and what check prevents an imaging-only overcall?
cards.answer: Trap: Calling periportal soft tissue that encases/narrows a portal vein cholangiocarcinoma with certainty. Safety check: Integrate the full imaging pattern with clinical/serologic evidence for a sclerosing inflammatory disorder and obtain tissue when the distinction remains unresolved. Key discriminator: Imaging overlap can be substantial; the source case required surgical pathology to show inflammatory pseudotumor. Why it happens: Lymphoplasmacytic inflammatory tissue can form a hilar/periportal mass and stricture that closely resembles malignancy.

candidates.question: What is the key hepatobiliary-phase pitfall in HCC, and what safety check prevents it?
candidates.answer: Trap: Excluding HCC because a lesion is isointense or hyperintense on hepatobiliary phase imaging. Safety check: Do not let hepatobiliary-phase signal override the dynamic hallmark pattern; integrate arterial hyperenhancement, washout, capsule, and the rest of the study. Key discriminator: The article states that uptake is related to OATP8 receptor behavior and that most HCCs are hypointense, but up to 10% of HCCs can be isointense or hyperintense on hepatobiliary phase. Why this error occurs: Readers may overgeneralize the usual hepatobiliary-phase appearance into an absolute rule.

candidates.question: What source-listed mimic can cause overcall, and what safety check helps prevent the error?
candidates.answer: Trap: Overcalling a metaphyseal spur as a classic metaphyseal lesion. Safety check: Look for an underlying lucency/fracture plane. Key discriminator: A metaphyseal spur is a distal extension of the SPBC beyond the chondroosseous junction and typically lacks underlying lucency; CML is a subphyseal fracture that undercuts the SPBC. Why the error occurs: Both can create a corner-like metaphyseal contour, especially near the distal femur.

candidates.question: What lymph-node pitfall occurs in PSC, and what safety check prevents overcalling malignancy?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking common PSC-related lymphadenopathy for metastatic lymphadenopathy or lymphoma. Safety check: Interpret lymph nodes in context of the PSC biliary pattern and actively search for direct malignant features before assigning metastatic disease. Key discriminator: RadPrimer states extensive lymphadenopathy is common, particularly precaval/aortocaval or RUQ/retroperitoneal nodes, and should not be confused with metastatic lymphadenopathy or lymphoma. Why it happens: Enlarged nodes in a patient at risk for cholangiocarcinoma create an anchoring bias toward malignancy.

candidates.question: What is the pitfall when a hepatobiliary-phase liver lesion looks like FNH, and what safety check prevents the error?
candidates.answer: Trap: Assuming hepatobiliary-phase uptake/retention always proves FNH. Safety check: Check for inflammatory HA risk factors and the full imaging pattern, because a minority of adenomas are iso- to hyperintense on hepatobiliary phase and inflammatory HA can mimic FNH. Key discriminator: FNH usually retains gadoxetate and contains bile ductules/Kupffer cells; adenoma often lacks substantial retention, but exceptions exist. Why it happens: Both lesions are hepatocellular and hypervascular, so hepatobiliary-phase behavior can overlap.

candidates.question: What is the tumor-mimic pitfall in pelvic stress fracture, and what safety check prevents it?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking stress-fracture marrow edema for metastatic disease, myeloma, or lymphoma. Safety check: Look for a discrete fracture line and the geometry of the marrow abnormality. Key discriminator: Insufficiency fracture edema is band-like or has straight/rectilinear margins; tumor marrow replacement tends to be rounded and usually lacks a discrete fracture line. Why the error occurs: Marrow edema can be extensive, and femoral neck fatigue fracture may even have a rounded edema appearance, so CT may be useful when it shows the fracture line more distinctly than MR.
