candidates.question: What visual pitfall can occur on this stereotactic MR image, and what safety check prevents it?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking enhancement along the cyst margins for true cyst-wall rim enhancement. Safety check: Trace the enhancing margins anatomically as displaced internal cerebral and septal veins when they course along the lateral cyst margins. Key discriminator: true rim enhancement surrounds the cyst wall; in this case the source states the enhancement represents displaced veins, not rim enhancement. Why it happens: venous structures displaced around a foramen of Monro cyst can visually simulate a thin enhancing cyst wall.

candidates.question: Portal venous Doppler pitfall: what false interpretation can low PRF create, and what safety check prevents it?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking color aliasing for hepatofugal portal venous flow. Safety check / maneuver: Increase pulse repetition frequency and optimize Doppler settings before calling true flow reversal. Key discriminator: True hepatofugal flow persists after proper Doppler optimization; aliasing-related apparent reversal does not. Why it happens: Low PRF causes color wraparound in the portal venous system, creating an artifactual appearance of reversed flow.

candidates.question: What is the trap when abundant callus is present near a fracture, and what safety check prevents overcalling union?
candidates.answer: Trap: Assuming that abundant peripheral callus means the fracture is united. Safety check: Confirm that callus actually crosses the fracture line, ideally on at least two projections or with multiplanar CT if radiographs are inconclusive. Key discriminator: Hypertrophic nonunion has abundant peripheral callus that never crosses the fracture line; radiographic union requires bridging ossified callus. Why it happens: Callus volume can look reassuring even when the biologically important bridge across the fracture gap is absent.

candidates.question: What pitfall makes coagulopathic hepatic hemorrhage mimic traumatic liver injury, and what checks prevent the error?
candidates.answer: Trap: Calling fracture-like hepatic defects traumatic lacerations. Safety check: Verify trauma history and search for a hematocrit sign or bleeding at multiple sites. Discriminator: The source anticoagulant case had fracture-like defects without trauma; the separate coagulopathy case showed hepatic and renal bleeding plus a hematocrit level. Why it happens: Intrahepatic hemorrhagic defects can resemble linear traumatic planes.

candidates.question: What early-radiograph pitfall can lead to a miss, and what safety check prevents it?
candidates.answer: Trap: Calling the study negative because no fracture line is visible. Safety check: Actively inspect for focal periosteal reaction and compare all projections, including the lateral view for dorsal soft-tissue swelling in metatarsal cases. Key discriminator: The source states focal periosteal reaction is often the earliest radiographic sign and that dorsal soft-tissue swelling on lateral view may be the only clue to metatarsal stress fracture. Why it happens: Early stress fracture may be radiographically insensitive, so the indirect repair/inflammatory clues appear before the fracture line.

candidates.question: Portal venous Doppler pitfall in a transplant patient: what mimic can helical flow create, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking helical portal vein flow for hepatofugal flow from portal hypertension. Safety check / maneuver: Look for the elliptical color Doppler pattern and use the transplant history, especially donor-recipient main portal vein size mismatch, before calling true reversed flow. Key discriminator: Helical flow has the characteristic elliptical swirling color pattern rather than sustained true portal venous reversal. Why it happens: Helical flow commonly occurs in liver transplants when donor and recipient main portal veins are discrepant in size and can visually mimic hepatofugal flow.

candidates.question: What is the pitfall when pancreatitis-like inflammation is centered near the duodenum, and what safety check prevents the mistake?
candidates.answer: Trap: Calling a duodenal-centered inflammatory process pancreatitis simply because there is anterior pararenal fat stranding and edema near the pancreatic head. Key discriminator: Secondary pancreatic head edema can occur with perforated duodenal ulcer, but the primary inflammatory epicenter is duodenal rather than pancreatic. cards.question: For ascending cholangitis, what ultrasound/Doppler pattern should be recognized?

candidates.answer: Bright homogeneous arterial enhancement except for the central scar; later the lesion becomes isoattenuating to liver, with delayed scar enhancement around 5 minutes. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive. Recognition pivot: Homogeneous arterialization plus late scar enhancement is the classic CT pattern.

candidates.question: For primary sclerosing cholangitis, what biliary and hepatic CT pattern should be recognized when fissures are widened?
candidates.answer: Irregular duct dilatation alternating with strictures creates a beaded appearance. Widened fissures, peripheral atrophy, and relative central/caudate hypertrophy can accompany it; advanced disease may show varices. Interpretation pivot: Ductal beading distinguishes a cholangiopathic cause from isolated cirrhotic volume loss. The captured Core report includes common and intrahepatic ducts; the selected CT depicts intrahepatic beading.

candidates.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
candidates.question: For FNH, what MRI and hepatobiliary-contrast pattern should be recognized?
candidates.answer: Typically isointense to liver on routine MRI; central scar is subtly T2 hyperintense. Arterial hyperenhancement; delayed scar enhancement with extracellular agents. Hepatobiliary phase: lesion iso-/hyperintense from retained Eovist, while the scar does not retain it. Recognition pivot: Hepatobiliary retention strongly separates FNH from adenoma.

candidates.question: For hepatic lymphoma, what ultrasound pattern should be recognized?
candidates.answer: Hepatic lymphoma may be hypoechoic on ultrasound. In a liver that appears diffusely low in attenuation on CT, focal lesions plus splenomegaly or lymphadenopathy raise infiltrative disease. Ultrasound appearance is nonspecific; systemic findings or tissue diagnosis may be required.

cards.question: For choledocholithiasis, what ultrasound/Doppler pattern should be recognized?
cards.answer: Ultrasound: echogenic stones within the bile duct, often with posterior shadowing; stones Large stones may cause upstream biliary dilation; Doppler distinguishes the avascular duct from adjacent vessels. Recognition pivot: directly visualized intraductal stones plus upstream dilation strongly support choledocholithiasis.

candidates.question: For FNH, what ultrasound and Doppler pattern should be recognized?
candidates.answer: Ultrasound appearance is nonspecific; the central scar is rarely seen. Doppler may show a spoke-wheel configuration of arterial vessels. Imaging specificity: Nonspecific. Recognition pivot: Use Doppler as supportive, not definitive, evidence.

candidates.question: For HCC, what ultrasound and Doppler pattern should be recognized?
candidates.answer: Core: HCC has a variable ultrasound appearance. High Doppler flow may be present, especially at the periphery, due to arteriovenous shunting. Imaging specificity: Nonspecific on grayscale alone. Recognition pivot: A new mass in a cirrhotic liver requires cross-sectional characterization.

candidates.question: For cavernous hemangioma, what ultrasound pattern should be recognized?
candidates.answer: Circumscribed, homogeneously echogenic mass with no flow on color Doppler; posterior acoustic enhancement may be present. A hypoechoic halo/target sign should not be seen and suggests malignancy. Recognition pivot: Classic echogenic avascular morphology supports hemangioma in an otherwise normal liver.

candidates.question: For hepatic steatosis, what MRI pattern should be recognized?

candidates.question: For THAD/THID, what ultrasound appearance is source-supported?
candidates.answer: - Ultrasound: no corollary findings are expected. - Exception: contrast-enhanced ultrasound with microbubble contrast agent may show a correlate. Exam pivot: Do not invent grayscale or Doppler findings for THAD unless contrast-enhanced ultrasound is specifically being used.

candidates.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
candidates.question: What ultrasound features favor a benign or normal cervical lymph node?
candidates.answer: Benign cervical nodes are typically ovoid or elliptical, hypoechoic, and contain an echogenic hilum. Power Doppler should show hilar vascularity; in reactive nodes, cortical hypertrophy may occur but the hilum and radiating hilar vascularity are preserved.

cards.question: For hepatic artery calcification, what ultrasound pattern should be recognized?

candidates.answer: Trap: Stopping after the dermoid diagnosis and missing the superimposed emergency. candidates.question: In a cystic hepatic lesion, what CT finding should make metastatic or other neoplastic disease a leading concern?
candidates.answer: A true mural nodule or enhancing solid component in an otherwise cystic mass raises concern for neoplasm; multiple lesions or a known cancer history increase concern for metastases. Pitfall: Nodularity does not establish a primary site or prove malignancy. The source also illustrates tiny biliary hamartomas with enhancing wall nodules.

candidates.question: How can hair appear on ultrasound in mature cystic teratoma?
candidates.answer: Hair can appear as punctate echoes in one plane and linear echoes in an orthogonal plane; mobile hair in fluid can produce the dot-dash-dot appearance. Exam pivot: Hair echoes plus a Rokitansky nodule/dermoid plug strongly favor mature cystic teratoma. Source: RadPrimer + STATdx master source.

candidates.question: What CT findings should be sought in orbital roof fracture?
candidates.answer: Depression into the orbit; elevation into the anterior cranial fossa; orbital hematoma; superior rectus/levator-related involvement; proptosis; globe injury; pneumocephalus.

cards.question: For an intrahepatic portosystemic shunt, what Doppler pattern should be recognized?

candidates.answer: CT: Homogeneous water attenuation (0-20 HU), a thin/nearly imperceptible wall, and no enhancement. Interpretation pivot: Thick enhancing wall, enhancing septa, or a true mural nodule requires characterization as a complex lesion; fluid attenuation alone is insufficient.

cards.answer: CT: a low-density periportal collar surrounding portal venous branches together with a distended IVC. Recognition pivot: systemic venous distention supports overhydration/hypervolemia rather than focal periportal hemorrhage.

candidates.question: For radiation hepatitis, what CT distribution is the key discriminator?
candidates.answer: A low-attenuation region corresponding to the external-beam treatment field or radioactive bead distribution, with a sharply demarcated boundary. Recognition pivot: a straight field-conforming boundary is more characteristic than the vessel-traversing geographic pattern of steatosis.

candidates.question: For hepatic angiosarcoma, what CT pattern should raise concern?
candidates.answer: Bizarre or peculiar eccentric hypervascular enhancement; may resemble hemangioma, with multiple lesions in liver and spleen in the article. Imaging specificity: Nonspecific. candidates.question: What CT pattern suggests internal hernia as a cause of SBO?
candidates.answer: Cluster of dilated small bowel segments. Crowding, twisting, displacement of mesenteric vessels. Dilated segment entering hernia; collapsed segment leaving hernia. Exam pivot: Mesenteric vessel crowding + clustered loops strongly suggests internal hernia rather than adhesive SBO.

candidates.question: For hepatic sarcoidosis, what CT pattern should raise the diagnosis?
candidates.answer: Low-density enlarged liver or innumerable small hypodense granulomas; hepatic and splenic granulomas may coexist. Look for thoracic and abdominal lymphadenopathy. Recognition pivot: combined liver/spleen granulomatous lesions plus adenopathy favor sarcoidosis over isolated steatosis. Imaging specificity: Requires correlation.

candidates.question: On T2-weighted MRI, what ovarian pattern supports adnexal/ovarian torsion?
candidates.answer: High-signal edematous stroma with peripheral hyperintense follicles supports torsion. Dark tissue may indicate infarcted or nonviable tissue. Exam pivot: MRI can preserve the same morphology learned on ultrasound: edema/enlargement plus peripheral follicles and abnormal position.

candidates.answer: Multiple spherical subcapsular/peripheral masses that may coalesce; halo/target appearance and capsular retraction are key clues. candidates.question: In splenic trauma, how common is traumatic splenic infarction and what CT pattern/risk does the source state?
candidates.answer: Frequency: unusual, less than 2% of traumatic splenic injury cases. CT pattern: wedge-shaped hypoattenuation, which can be segmental or complete. Proposed cause: probably arterial thrombosis after intimal injury. Risk: delayed rupture or abscess formation. Exam pivot: traumatic infarction is rare but complication-prone; do not confuse it with the more common laceration/hematoma pattern.

candidates.question: For splenic trauma, what CT attenuation thresholds support hemoperitoneum or perisplenic clot?
candidates.answer: Hemoperitoneum: greater than 30 HU. Perisplenic clot: greater than 45 HU. Sentinel clot sign: highest-density blood localizes adjacent to the injury site. Exam pivot: Dense blood adjacent to the spleen can reveal occult splenic injury even without a visible laceration.

cards.question: For chemotherapy-induced cholangitis/biliary injury, what CT pattern should be recognized?
cards.answer: CT may show moderate irregular intrahepatic ductal dilation after hepatic arterial chemotherapy; the pattern can resemble PSC and may include mural thickening/enhancement, edema, or adjacent hepatoduodenal-ligament fat stranding. Imaging specificity: Requires treatment-history correlation. Recognition pivot: irregular sclerosing-type duct injury in the direct hepatic-artery treatment setting supports chemotherapy-related cholangiopathy.

candidates.question: For Budd-Chiari syndrome, what CT pattern should be recognized?
candidates.answer: Look for hepatic-vein or IVC obstruction/thrombus, collateral vessels, caudate preservation or hypertrophy, and peripheral hepatic injury or volume loss. Direct demonstration of hepatic venous outflow obstruction is the decisive clue; caudate enlargement alone does not establish the diagnosis.

candidates.question: For primary sclerosing cholangitis, what biliary and hepatic CT pattern should be recognized when fissures are widened?
candidates.answer: Irregular duct dilatation alternating with strictures creates a beaded appearance. Widened fissures, peripheral atrophy, and relative central/caudate hypertrophy can accompany it; advanced disease may show varices. Interpretation pivot: Ductal beading distinguishes a cholangiopathic cause from isolated cirrhotic volume loss. The captured Core report includes common and intrahepatic ducts; the selected CT depicts intrahepatic beading.

cards.question: After recent liver transplantation, how should isolated periportal edema be interpreted?
cards.answer: Periportal edema is a common normal postoperative finding and does not by itself imply allograft injury. Report pivot: do not label graft injury from edema alone; separately assess hepatic arterial patency, portal/hepatic veins, and biliary complications when the study shows specific abnormalities.

candidates.question: How should a liver measuring at least 25 HU below the spleen on portal-venous-phase CT be interpreted?
candidates.answer: The captured Core criterion supports steatosis, but contrast-enhanced attenuation assessment is less reliable than unenhanced CT. Do not interchange this portal-phase threshold with the unenhanced 10-HU comparison. Use morphology and chemical-shift MRI when fat versus infiltration remains uncertain.

candidates.question: What is the most common tumor associated with portal-vein tumor thrombus?
candidates.answer: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is the most common tumor associated with portal-vein tumor thrombus. Exam pivot: If intraluminal portal-vein material shows enhancement or internal arterial flow, HCC should be the first malignant cause you consider.

candidates.question: How should the orbital roofs be traced?
candidates.answer: Trace each orbital roof from anterior to posterior and look for depression into the orbit or elevation into the cranial fossa.

candidates.question: In a patient with cirrhosis, how often should surveillance for hepatocellular carcinoma be performed according to the source?
candidates.answer: Every 6 months. Exam pivot: Cirrhosis is an HCC-surveillance disease state, so the follow-up interval itself is testable.

candidates.question: What clinical presentation should raise immediate concern for testicular torsion?
candidates.answer: Acute scrotal or inguinal pain with a swollen erythematous hemiscrotum, abnormal testicular lie, pain not relieved by elevation, and absent cremasteric reflex. Younger prepubertal children may present only with groin or lower abdominal pain. Exam pivot: torsion is a surgical emergency even when the scrotal complaint is atypical.

candidates.question: After identifying an EDH on trauma CT, what source-supported search-pattern pivot remains important?
candidates.answer: - EDH can coexist with SDH, SAH, or contusion. - Continue the search pattern after finding the epidural collection. - CT comma sign indicates coexisting EDH and SDH and may change treatment planning because compartments can require separate surgical planning. Exam pivot: Do not stop at the first extraaxial hematoma.

candidates.question: After localization, what imaging features should be assessed for an orbital lesion?
candidates.answer: Determine whether it is solid or cystic, whether it contains fluid, fat, blood, or soft tissue, whether it is well defined or infiltrative, whether there is bony remodeling or destruction, and the degree/homogeneity of enhancement.

candidates.question: What are the Milan criteria for liver transplantation in hepatocellular carcinoma?
candidates.answer: Solitary HCC ≤ 5 cm, or up to 3 HCC nodules each ≤ 3 cm, with no vascular invasion or extrahepatic tumor. Exam pivot: These are the key transplant-selection size/number thresholds to know for board-style HCC questions.

candidates.question: What is cavernous transformation of the portal vein?
candidates.answer: Network of collateral venous channels replacing chronically thrombosed portal vein. example of case Cavernous transformation of portal vein | Radiology Case | Radiopaedia.org

candidates.question: What are the most common locations for CML, and what medial/lateral pattern is source-stated?
candidates.answer: Most common: distal femur, proximal tibia, distal tibia; proximal humerus is also a listed location. At distal femur/proximal and distal tibia, CML is more commonly medial. Lateral and anterior fractures were always accompanied by medial fractures in a series of cases. Exam pivot: Search the medial metaphysis carefully around knee and ankle.

candidates.question: What Rodriguez et al. pediatric 1-hour emptying threshold is listed for delayed emptying?
candidates.answer: Exam pivot: Pediatric criteria are variable and not well established.

candidates.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::FacialTraumaandH&NEmergencies::Skull Base and Facial Trauma Overview
candidates.question: Mandibular fracture reporting pivot: what special implication follows fracture extension into the periodontal ligament space of an erupted tooth?
candidates.answer: A mandibular fracture that extends into the periodontal ligament space of an erupted tooth is managed as an open (contaminated) fracture. Exam pivot: Tooth socket involvement changes the practical severity of the fracture and must be reported explicitly.

cards.question: For the periportal region, what anatomy-based clue separates edema from a dilated bile duct?
cards.answer: Periportal edema surrounds the portal triad/portal venous branch; a dilated bile duct runs along one side of the accompanying portal vein. Recognition pivot: use this relationship first, then confirm uncertain branching structures with Doppler, MRCP, or direct cholangiography.

candidates.question: For biliary hamartomas, what MRCP finding separates them from Caroli disease?
candidates.answer: MRCP: innumerable small T2-hyperintense lesions that do not communicate with the biliary tree. Key differentiator: noncommunication favors biliary hamartomas; Caroli disease is dilated intrahepatic bile ducts that communicate. Imaging specificity: Strongly suggestive.

candidates.question: For arterioportal shunts in cirrhosis, what imaging pattern distinguishes them from HCC?
candidates.answer: Usually small (often ≤1.5 cm), peripheral, and wedge-shaped with straight margins; arterial hyperenhancement becomes isodense/isointense on portal/delayed imaging. No corresponding precontrast T1/T2 abnormality; early filling of a portal vein branch is a key clue. Recognition pivot: Transient perfusion geometry rather than a persistent mass.

candidates.question: For peripheral mass-forming cholangiocarcinoma, what enhancement pattern separates it from HCC and hemangioma?
candidates.answer: Delayed/progressive persistent enhancement, sometimes with capsular retraction, favors peripheral mass-forming cholangiocarcinoma. Unlike typical hemangioma, enhancement need not match blood pool; the source case becomes denser than liver and vessels on delayed imaging. HCC more characteristically shows washout.

candidates.deck: Corebook::Neuro::Head & Neck::Suprahyoid and Infrahyoid Neck::Cervical Lymph Nodes
candidates.question: What feature separates a level IIA node from a level IIB node?
candidates.answer: A level IIB node lies posterior to the IJV with a visible fat plane between the node and the vein. A posterior node that directly contacts the IJV without an interposed fat plane is still classified as level IIA.

candidates.deck: Corebook::GI::Peritoneum, Mesentery, and Abdominal Wall::Spigelian Hernia
candidates.question: For Spigelian hernia, what CT anatomy establishes the diagnosis?
candidates.answer: Defect in the internal oblique/transversus abdominis aponeurosis with herniated omentum and/or bowel. Typical position: lateral to rectus and caudal/lateral to the umbilicus. External oblique muscle/fascia usually remains intact over the sac. Exam pivot: The intact superficial external oblique layer is a key discriminator.

candidates.question: How is the vermis organized, and which fissure separates superior from inferior vermis?
candidates.answer: Superior vermis: lingula, central lobule, culmen, declive, folium. Inferior vermis: tuber, pyramid, uvula, nodulus. The horizontal (petrosal) fissure separates superior from inferior vermis.

candidates.question: On grayscale ultrasound, what is the best diagnostic clue for biliary ductal dilatation?
candidates.answer: Tubular, anechoic, fluid-filled structures accompanying portal veins in the extrahepatic and intrahepatic segments. Exam pivot: The key recognition pattern is a periportal branching or tubular fluid-filled structure that follows the biliary tree.

candidates.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
candidates.question: For hepatic adenoma, what chemical-shift MRI clue should be recognized?
candidates.answer: Some adenomas contain intracellular lipid and show T1 hyperintensity with signal loss on out-of-phase images. Recognition pivot: Out-of-phase signal loss supports a fat-containing adenoma subtype and helps explain apparent central heterogeneity.

candidates.question: What is the imaging trap here, and what check helps separate it from true cirrhosis?
candidates.answer: Trap: Mistaking treatment-related pseudocirrhosis for primary chronic cirrhosis. Safety check / maneuver: Look for residual metastatic lesions and the source-supported history of lesion shrinkage with fibrosis producing contour distortion. Key discriminator: Pseudocirrhosis reflects post-treatment metastatic contraction and scarring rather than primary diffuse cirrhotic remodeling. Why the error occurs: Both processes can produce a nodular contour, fissural widening, and capsular retraction.

candidates.deck: Corebook::GI::Liver::Liver Mass With Central or Eccentric Scar
candidates.question: For hepatic metastases, what CT phase usually gives the best conspicuity?
candidates.answer: Most metastases are hypovascular and are best appreciated on the portal venous phase as hypoattenuating masses. Recognition pivot: Portal venous phase is the default detection phase for most metastases, unlike hypervascular HCC.

candidates.question: For ankle/foot stress fracture, what nuclear medicine appearance is expected?
candidates.answer: Bone scan: focal abnormal increased uptake in one or more bones of the foot. Morphology: may or may not be linear. Timing: uptake may take up to 48 hours after injury to manifest. Technique pivot: pinhole collimation is useful for better anatomic detail. Source attribution: RadPrimer article; unsupplied Core three-phase bone-scan language removed.

candidates.question: What is the normal direction of portal venous flow, and what direction indicates severe portal hypertension?
candidates.answer: Hepatopetal flow is normal. Hepatofugal flow is a sign of severe portal hypertension. Exam pivot: Reversed portal flow is a hemodynamic severity marker, not just a descriptive Doppler curiosity.
